💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s been two weeks since the release of DeepSeek R1 and just a week since we started the open-r1 project to replicate the missing pieces, namely the training pipeline and the synthetic data.
  • It should serve both as an enhancement on the project and as a collection of interesting resources around DeepSeek-R1.
  • Let’s start by looking at the progress we made on Open-R1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s been two weeks since the release of DeepSeek R1 and just a week since we started the open-r1 project to replicate the missing pieces, namely the training pipeline and the synthetic data. This post summarizes:.

It should serve both as an enhancement on the project and as a collection of interesting resources around DeepSeek-R1.

Let’s start by looking at the progress we made on Open-R1. We started Open-R1 just one week ago and people across the teams as well as the community came together to work on it and we have some progress to report.

The first step in reproduction is to verify that we can match the evaluation scores. We are able to reproduce Deepseek's reported results on the MATH-500 Benchmark:.

You can find the instructions to run these evaluations in the open-r1 repository.

One observation we have made is the enormous size of the generations from the DeepSeek models, which makes even evaluating the model challenging. Here we show DeepSeek-R1 response lengths in the OpenThoughts dataset:.

Distribution of R1’s responses shows that they are on average very long with the average response being 6,000 tokens long and some responses containing more than 20,000 tokens. Worth noting that the average page contains ~500 words and one token is on average slightly less than a word, which means the many reponses are over 10 pages long. (src: https://x.com/gui_penedo/status/1884953463051649052).

The length of responses will make GPRO training challenging, as we will have to generate long completions which will require a significant proportion of GPU memory to store the activations / gradients for the optimization step.

In order to share our progress publicly, we have created an open-r1 evaluation leaderboard, so the community can follow our reproduction efforts (space is here):.

In a recent development, following the release of Open R1, GRPO (Grouped Relative Policy Optimization) was integrated into the latest TRL release (version 0.14). This integration enables training any model with one or multiple reward functions or models. The GRPO implementation integrates with DeepSpeed ZeRO 1/2/3 for parallelized training that scales to many GPUs, and uses vLLM for fast generation, which is the primary bottleneck in online training methods.

There are still some limitations relating to the use of high memory usage, and progress is being made to profile and reduce them.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most exciting findings of the R1 report was that the main model can be used to generate synthetic reasoning traces and smaller models fine-tuned on this dataset see similar performance gains as the main model. So naturally we want to re-create the synthetic reasoning dataset as well such that the community can fine-tune other models on it.

With a model as massive as R1 the main challenge is scaling up generation efficiently and fast. We spent a week tinkering with various setups and configurations.

According to recent reports, the model fits on two 8xH100 nodes so naturally we started experimenting with that setup and used vLLM as inference server. However, we rapidly noticed that this configuration is not ideal: the throughput is sub-optimal and only allows for 8 parallel request, because the GPU KV cache fills up too quickly. What happens when the cache fills up ist that the requests which use a lot of cache are preempted and if the config uses PreemptionMode.RECOMPUTE the requests are scheduled again later when more VRAM is available.

According to recent reports, we then switched to a setup with 4x 8xH100 nodes, so 32 GPUs in total. This leaves enough spare VRAM for 32 requests running in parallel with barely any of them getting rescheduled due to 100% cache utilization.

Originally we started querying the vLLM servers with batches of requests but noticed quickly, that straggles in the batches would cause the GPU utiliziation to vary since a new batch would only start processing once the last sample of the previous batch is done. Switching the batched inference to streaming helped stabilize the GPU utilization significantly:.

It has been revealed that it only required changing the code sending requests to the vLLM servers. The code for batched inference:.

The latest code for streaming requests:.

We are generating at a fairly constant rate but might still explore a bit further if for example switching to the CPU cache is a better strategy when long queries get preempted.

The current inference code can be found here.

Other mentions: Washington Post, Financial Times, Financial Times, Fortune, Fortune, The Verge, Financial Review, Tech Crunch, Die Zeit, Financial Times, Fresh York Times, The Wall Street Journal, EuroNews, Barrons, New York Times, Vox, Nature, SwissInfo, Handelsblatt, Business Insider, IEEE Spectrum, MIT Tech Review, LeMonde.

While the community is still digesting DeepSeek-R1’s results and report, DeepSeek has captured broader public attention just two weeks after its release.

After a relatively calm first week post-release, the second week saw significant market reactions, prompting responses from multiple AI research labs:.

In parallel, several companies worked on providing the DeepSeek models through various platforms (non-exhaustive list):.

According to recent reports, there has been a lot of interest around the proclaimed cost of training V3/R1. While the exact number probably doesn’t matter so much, people worked on some back-of-the-envelope calculations to verify the order of magnitude here. TL;DR the numbers seem generally in the right order of magnitude, as seen in these discussions:.

As many groups are working on reproducing the training pipeline, we’ll get more evidence on the possible training efficiency for the model.

Sources indicate that last week some speculations surfaced that DeepSeek might have been using OpenAI outputs to train its models. See for example the Financial Times. However, it is unclear at this point what the consequences of these allegations will be.

The open source community has been extremely active around DeepSeek-R1 and many people started building interesting projects around the model.

There have been a number of projects that try to reproduce the basic learning mechanics at smaller scale, so you can test the basic learning principles at home.

The community has been busy on a number of dataset efforts related to R1, some highlights include:.

This list only covers a small number of reasoning and problem solving related datasets on the Hub. We’re excited to see what other datasets the community build in the coming weeks.

In a recent development, we are just getting started and want to finish the training pipeline and try it on smaller models and use the scaled up inference pipeline to generate high quality datasets. If you want to contribute check out the open-r1 repository on GitHub or follow the Hugging Face open-r1 org.

Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips.
  • Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made notable progress toward solving this problem.
  • Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This indicates that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an key step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made notable progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This indicates that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an key step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors.

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

It has been revealed that this effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%.

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results revealed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

In a recent development, when the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

It has been revealed that the team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the newly introduced technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error.".

A Newly introduced Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors.

According to recent reports, the findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

Sources indicate that this is especially vital for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

In a recent development, "By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," claims Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations.".

Sources indicate that the broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

I'm having a much better time in GTA 6 now I've disabled its pesky Criminal Profile pings

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Do you think you'd enjoy invasive UI elements in real life?
  • According to recent reports, I think it'd be tortuous.
  • So why is it any different in GTA 6?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Do you think you'd enjoy invasive UI elements in real life? You crouch to fuss your dog, and a little ping activates in your retina, informing you that you've just earned plus-three serotonin. Your boss chews you out for coming into work 15 minutes late thanks to a traffic accident holding you up on your way to work, a notification pings: "-10 percent motivation (lasts 24 hours)". Maybe you eat a bang-up meal, flirt with a hot stranger, beat your personal best on a run - ding, ding, ding. Well done, you win at being a human.

According to recent reports, I think it'd be tortuous. I think it would interact with my already-questionable perception of reality, and send my neurodivergent coping mechanisms into overdrive. I already see time 'in blocks', and am incapable of breaking tasks down to anything less than 15 minute chunks - I can't imagine how ill I'd get if I could begin ascribing status buffs and debuffs to those blocks, too. We're all different, of course - such is the beauty of life - but I think most people would be pushed to the point of meltdown if every action they took had a quantifiable mechanical system attached to it.

So why is it any different in GTA 6? The game, after all, is the most effective simulation we've ever seen about modern life. Aside from the rampant crime sprees you can engage with, there's so much mundanity in the game it's beyond impressive: I spent the opening 10-or-so hours in the game with a very strict morning routine. I'd get up, work out, shower, feed Dolores the snake, drink a protein shake, then head to one of the local businesses to get some breakfast. Every day! I'm a busy person; I'm playing GTA 6 for fun, yes, but also as part of my job - I need to be making progress. Yet, Rockstar's invisible hand is so competently realised, so artisanally implemented, that I bow to its insistence that I live life properly and engage with all the systems suggested to me like a good little drone.

So, after being low-key brainwashed by the initial tutorialisation, it stands to reason that I'm open to Rockstar's other suggestions. And - right on cue - you get a mission early on that introduces you to what is perhaps the most hotly debated aspect of the game so far: the Criminal Profile. If you're unaware, this new mechanic is a bit like the Honour System in Red Dead Redemption 2. It's broken down into five levels: professional, hardened, violent, psycho, and irredeemable. If you hit that final bracket, irredeemable, you can never go back: it's essentially GTA 6's criminal version of 'being cancelled', only here there are real, serious consequences that will actually ruin your life forever.

The game tracks how you behave when you're playing as both Jason and Lucia. They have separate criminal profiles. If, for example, you fudge a robbery on a cartel's pill-shipping operation and fight for your life, you can certainly kill everyone in the room - that's still fine. This is still Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar isn't trying to make you play this game like Thief or Deus Ex or something. You can go for total stealth runs, but incapacitating enemies without killing them and getting away cleanly will only grant 'professional' points. You get the same assessment if you 'go loud' and aim for the hands, knees, feet of the people trying to kill you. I am currently about 30 hours in, and every single encounter has been either 'no casualties' or 'low casualties', and I promise I've not even been trying that hard to 'be good' (and there are always settings you can change to help you out if you're struggling, too).

It has been revealed that there has been a certain amount of online discourse pointing towards this system as 'immersion ruining' or 'systematically inhibiting'. There's this idea that, in order to get a number of the game's 'good' endings, you need to play like a saint the whole way through the game. This is untrue. It's actually weighted more towards the opposite: in order to get the more nefarious ranks, you need to intentionally play like a sociopath. Wing a goon, see him lying on the floor in agony, and then go over and shoot his other kneecap? Yeah, you're going to get those unpopular purple devil points. Kick a dog in the street for no reason? Devil points. Taking a shotgun to a mall and opening fire on unarmed, un-implicated civilians? Devil points.

In a recent development, I'm enjoying the role-playing aspect of the game, because in my head-canon Jason and Lucia are doing what they can to survive. It may not be pretty, and I probably wouldn't want to know them in real life, but - as far as this work of fiction goes - I think playing them as criminals-on-the-run, trying to draw as little attention to themselves as possible is a great iteration of the series' core themes. I don't want to play as another Tommy Vercetti, or CJ, or Trevor. I want something different, and this game is giving it to me.

"The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper," explains Michael Wiafe, writer at Rockstar, in materials shared with Eurogamer ahead of the game's release. "[They're] full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn’t necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don’t attempt to make excuses for them. What’s key is how they resonate, no matter where you’re experiencing the game in the world." I think this indicates, quite well, what the Criminal Profile mechanic sets out to achieve in GTA 6: it's Rockstar saying 'these people are forced into certain situations by us, the developers, but you get to figure out how they respond to what life is giving them'.

Sources indicate that and you know what? I'm glad GTA 6 punishes you for playing like a psychopath. The world of Leonida is analogous to the real world, and things would start going wrong for you if you started attacking pedestrians randomly on the street. Other civilians and cops would start defending themselves and resisting you if you instigated a rampage of indiscriminate violence. The only time I've been victim to the devil icon in my game so far is when a Kingfisher accidentally shot out my (very expensive) windshield whilst aiming for Jason. So I kneecapped him, stole his beer, drank the whole bottle, then threw the bottle at his head. I acted like an idiot, and got treated as such. Good!

Recent findings suggest that but I don't want to see that. I want to roleplay as Jason and Lucia and act as I think they would. I don't need the game telling me, like a little voice in my head, 'hm, actually, that was a pretty weird thing to do, we're going to write that down'. So I have turned the notifications off. It's a simple process: simply open Settings, and then navigate to UI, and head down to the 34/70 area and you'll see all the HUD notifications settings. I play with both Criminal Profile and Relationship settings turned off - I prefer to have all that happening in the background, ticking over as I play, rather than constantly reminding me there's some secret meter somewhere judging me for what I'm doing.

If my relationship is turning sour, I trust my instincts (and Rockstar's grounded, well-structured writing) to tell me that. Jason is getting a bit cold, Lucia doesn't want to jump my bones, like, all the time, the two aren't holding hands at every opportunity like lovesick puppies… Much like in my real-life relationships, I trust the process. And I think more people should, because the role-playing in this game is fantastic, and we've been given a real rich text to engage with. I think that the fact that certain corners of the internet are upset because they're being treated badly for being bad people is a better level of satire than anything GTA 6 has put in-game, to be honest.

Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a fresh generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity.
  • A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them.
  • Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a fresh generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an key role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers.

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also notable to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," mentioned Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an key advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time.

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

According to recent reports, in the latest study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

According to recent reports, "For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing.

According to recent reports, understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly vital if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

According to recent reports, the findings therefore offer more than a fresh way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

Sources indicate that "The findings give us newly introduced insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become key for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling latest computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

Tech Report: DABStep: Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning

📅 04 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2366 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that language models are becoming increasingly capable and can solve tasks autonomously as agents.
  • To tackle this challenge, Adyen and Hugging Face built the Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning (DABstep) together.
  • Our findings reveal that DABstep presents a significant challenge for current AI models, with the most capable reasoning-based agents achieving only 16% accuracy, highlighting significant progress to be made in the field.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that language models are becoming increasingly capable and can solve tasks autonomously as agents. There are many exciting use cases, especially at the intersection of reasoning, code, and data. However, proper evaluation benchmarks on real-world problems are lacking and hinder progress in the field.

To tackle this challenge, Adyen and Hugging Face built the Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning (DABstep) together. DABstep consists of over 450 data analysis tasks designed to evaluate the capabilities of state-of-the-art LLMs and AI agents.

Our findings reveal that DABstep presents a significant challenge for current AI models, with the most capable reasoning-based agents achieving only 16% accuracy, highlighting significant progress to be made in the field.

In this blog post, we'll cover the design and construction of the benchmark, explore evaluation results, and discuss the significant gap between current models and the ability to solve complex data analysis tasks effectively.

Industry observers note that data analysis is both an art and a science that requires technical skill, domain knowledge and creativity, and thus, it’s rarely straightforward. Even seasoned data analysts face challenges like:.

In a recent development, at companies like Adyen, analysts tackle a spectrum of problems, from routine queries to complex workflows requiring creativity, precision, and iterative reasoning. Access to a capable data analysis agent that can automate simple and repetitive tasks and assist with complex tasks would allow analysts to work faster, reduce mental strain, and focus on solving more impactful problems. That would be a pivotal moment for many industries that need data analysis and insights, such as finance.

According to recent reports, recent advancements in agentic workflows — where LLMs equipped with tools independently execute multi-step tasks — have shown tremendous promise across domains like coding, open QA, software engineering, and even Kaggle competitions. These systems aren’t just theoretical; they've been driving real-world productivity gains.

So, the question becomes: Can agentic workflows reshape the way we approach data analysis?

In a recent development, progress in machine learning is fueled by high quality benchmarks that yield reliable progress signals. Thus, we are excited to introduce the Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning (DABstep), a latest benchmark for evaluating and advancing agentic workflows in data analysis.

Here's what makes DABstep unique:.

How does DABstep achieve all this and remain a simple to run benchmark? Let’s take a look at its design!

Sources indicate that DABstep has been designed for low-barrier usage, quality evaluation and increasing difficulty levels. To this end, we are opening up the following items as part of DABstep: Datasets, Tasks, Evals, Real-time Leaderboard and Baselines.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest challenges analysts must overcome, when working on real-world problems, is balancing domain knowledge and technical skills. To this end, DABstep contains both unstructured and structured data to measure domain knowledge and technical skills respectively.

Table 1 indicates a snapshot of some of the dataset we are releasing with the benchmark.

Table 1: The benchmark is composed of various datasets across various tasks including the financial payments sector.

Some of the structured datasets include CSV and JSON files representing real-world data, such as transaction telemetry and business metadata (e.g., merchant category codes). Additionally, we have unstructured data such as documentation, lengthy manuals, and detailed handbooks that, for example, are issued by networks, regulators, and processors.

All of these datasets were extracted from real-world tasks at Adyen.

Based on the new datasets included in DABstep, we are releasing several tasks with increasing difficulty levels designed to test an AI agent’s accuracy.

Each task contains the following items:.

None of the tasks can be solved with 1-shot of code; in other words, they cannot be solved by reasoning alone, but rather, they require sequential steps of iterative problem-solving. For example, at the minimum, the agent must at least know what columns exist in the respective dataset to answer a question. This is contrasted with popular benchmarks like GAIA, MATH and SimpleQA, where it's possible to answer multiple questions with 1-shot of code correctly.

Two example tasks are shown in Figure 1, and an example human-made reference solution is shown in Figure 2.

Figure 1: On the left is an example Risk/Fraud question from the Easy Set. Solution requires referencing at least 2 data sources and 3-shots of code. On the right is an example Scheme Fees question from the Hard Set. The solution requires referencing at least 2 data sources and multiple shots of code. The included answers are just for demonstration purposes and are withheld from the dataset.

The benchmark consists of two difficulty levels:.

Recent findings suggest that as an example of a multi-step reasoning problem, The following code highlights a snippet of the human-made reference solution to a Hard Level task. Overall, it is broken down into four(4) sequential steps including the development of various support macros. In order to code this solution, the agent would have to have specific domain knowledge and the ability to work in sequential steps of iterative reasoning.

Figure 2: The 220 line reference solution to a question in the Hard Set: “If the merchant {merchant} had switched its MCC code to {target_mcc} prior to the start of 2023, how much of a difference in fees would they have to pay for the year 2023?” The solution requires multiple steps of inductive reasoning difficult for 1 shot code generation.

Some quick comments on how we are hoping to encourage generalization with the benchmark.

Symbolic Reasoning: In the spirit of GSM-Symbolic, tasks have been exploded in cardinality using permutations of time ranges, merchant names, etc. The rationale is to remove the chance of “lucky guesses” and validate core reasoning (repeatability of reasoning) and generalization.

In a recent development, hidden Test Set: We have opted not to divide the dataset into validation and test sets and are only releasing a heldout test set. This is because a data analyst agent should be able to generalize across various analysis tasks not per se captured in this benchmark version.

Dev Set: Given this hard generalization setting, the scale of the benchmark (450 questions), and in the spirit of developer friendliness, we have also released a dev set, which is a representative subset of the full test set, including answers. The spirit of this dev set is to allow researchers to configure their E2E submission pipeline locally, including evaluation and fast feedback loops, and then submit to the leaderboard proper.

Industry observers note that to test broad generalization, DABstep should not be benchmarked alone, and it should be seen in combination with other benchmarks that test overall generalization and problem-solving (e.g. MMLU, SuperGlue, GPQA).

According to recent reports, for simplicity, we have opted for a factoid-based answer evaluation system. This means that answers to benchmark questions should be simple words, numbers or multiple-choice combinations. This allows for unbiased, scaled and model-free evaluations. (This is as opposed to natural language answer submissions evaluated by a judge LLM).

According to recent reports, given that, we didn’t intend answer formatting to be the focus of the benchmark. To that end, we implemented a series of flexible evaluation methods that ensure that the focus remains on the accuracy of the answers rather than their formatting. As examples, we use adaptive tolerance to compare numerical values, allowing for variations in precision and formatting. Strings are normalized and compared using fuzzy matching with a similarity ratio threshold. Lists are evaluated element-wise after normalization.

Recent findings suggest that DABstep features a real-time leaderboard hosted on Hugging Face, where participants can submit their answers to be graded instantly. You can see your standing against others around the globe with instant feedback.

It has been revealed that view of the leaderboard with the best ranked submissions. Link: DABstep Leaderboard.

We are providing a set of baseline evaluations across popular open and closed models.

Figure 3: Performance (on Hard set) across closed and open models/providers. * The Reasoning Models did not work well on the unified ReAct prompt we were using across all chat models, so we had to craft a special Reasoning Prompt. See baseline implementation and prompt details here. We benchmarked the commercial offering of DeepSeek-V3.

From Figure 3 we can see that there is a lot of progress to be made, even with the best agents available not crossing the 20% line.

It has been revealed that the best performing agents were based on the latest reasoning models with o3-mini coming out on top at 16% accuracy and R1 coming in at 13%**. The closest chat-based model was Claude Sonnet at 12% the open DeepSeek V3 coming in at 6%.

Industry observers note that one surprising finding was that while instruct models perform well out of the box with a ReAct prompt, reasoning models don’t and achieve 0% accuracy. Common failure modes include poor instruction following, invalid code syntax, closing code blocks (lack of), use tools (improper) and 1-turn dialogs (i.e., no sequential steps). It required multiple iterations on the prompt to get the reasoning models to perform well on this benchmark.

The baselines provided as part of the benchmark are standardized prompts across the chat and reasoning models, and thus, they should be considered non-optimized and a lower bound on performance.

*We had to design a special prompt for the reasoning models because our unified ReAct prompt, although performing excellently on chat models, performed exceptionally poorly on all the reasoning models.

** R1 performance is extrapolated from a sample due to the prolonged outage at the time of this publication.

Additionally, we tracked the cost to run the full benchmark for each commercial offering and compare them in Table 2 below:.

Table 2: Costs for commercial models. Due to subjectivity/variance, we did not include price analysis of open models. Cost/Perf % is explored in Figure 4.

We break down the economics in Figure 4 by looking at the Accuracy vs Cost tradeoff.

Figure 4: Curve w/ performance and cost tradeoff between commercial providers.

Arguably, the economics of DeepSeek R1 are ideal as there is essentially no tradeoff between performance and cost.

Now, let’s have a look at how you can run these benchmarks yourself and evaluate your own models.

We are mindful that doing agentic research by interacting with the benchmark requires an execution environment and involves costs. We are lowering the barrier by providing access to HuggingFace's Inference API and smolagents. With these tools, researchers get 1k free LLM requests daily and access to a secure local code execution environment.

For convenience, we provide an example notebook: a ready-to-go solution for submitting an entry at zero cost (quickstart.ipynb).

By eliminating friction, DABstep ensures that anyone, from seasoned researchers to curious newcomers, can contribute to advancing agentic workflows in data analysis.

Industry observers note that we are really excited about the release of DABstep and think it will help test the state of data analysis agents today. However, this release marks just the first step and we blueprint to evolve the benchmark over time.

At the rate of progress in AI, we foresee that the benchmark will eventually be considered solved in its current state. However, the benchmark is designed to be valid for a longer time by increasing the difficulty in many dimensions. We will be building on the benchmark with full backwards compatibility. Below are some broad avenues on which we will improve the baseline.

Recent findings suggest that tasks: The current tasks are very narrow and limited in scope, encompassing mostly fraud and payment fees. This is a subset of the real world, as there are many other dimensions and variables at play. In the future, we will expand the same benchmark, including tasks in the area of approval rates (issuer refusals), authentication drop-offs, and real-time situations over a wider time span such as seasonal components. This would test the capacity of agents to balance several variables at the same time and execute trade-offs on multiple dimensions.

In a recent development, domains: The benchmark currently revolves around tasks from the financial sector. However, we invite researchers and practitioners from other fields, such as health, biology, insurance, telecommunication etc. to contribute fresh subsets to the benchmark so we can evaluate the performance across many domains.

Sources indicate that data scale: The structured data will eventually not be able to fit in memory. They will be analyzed with standard tooling, requiring the analysts to use distributed computing engines or scheduling workflows for later evaluation.

Documentation: The unstructured data that maps the domain knowledge will explode with more files containing time evolution (e.g., bulletins), different formats (e.g., PDF), and also different versions of similar but different logic that map each scheme, acquirer, or partner. The context will reach a step that will logically not fit the current and future token cardinality allowed in the context windows.

Industry observers note that multimodal: Agents should also become multimodal. To this end, we will enhance the benchmark with tasks that require extracting logic by interpreting and creating plots and graphs.

Existing benchmarks for evaluating AI in data analysis have advanced the field and DABstep is built on top of their foundations.

DS Bench evaluates 466 questions from Modeloff competitions, primarily designed for Excel-based workflows. While effective for small-scale tasks, Excel does not support the iterative, code-driven workflows common in real-world data analysis (e.g., Jupyter notebooks). Additionally, reliance on GPT-4 as an evaluator introduces bias and reduces generalizability.

DS 1000 tests Python-based data analysis tasks sourced from StackOverflow, curated to avoid memorization. However, its tasks are short and single-shot, lacking real datasets and iterative reasoning. This limits its ability to evaluate end-to-end workflows or multimodal capabilities.

For example, fraud rates have been intentionally elevated for the purpose of this exercise.

Getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show. This plan breaks preparation into eight skill areas, pairs each one with a learning option and a hands-on task, and gives you a simple test for knowing when to move on.

Many people preparing for their first analyst role study for months and still struggle to get interviews. Their CVs list SQL, Excel and Tableau, yet nothing on the page indicates those tools being used to answer a real question. Recruiters reading dozens of similar applications need something more concrete.

It has been revealed that A course can give your learning a sensible order, but a completion badge indicates little about how you think. A small analysis that states its question, explains its method and admits its limits tells a hiring manager far more. This strategy aims to collect that kind of proof while you learn, not after.

According to recent reports, start by collecting ten to twenty entry-level postings in the industry you want to join, and tally the tools and tasks they mention. You will quickly see a pattern. Some roles are built around Excel and routine reporting, while others want SQL, a BI platform and a bit of Python.

The wider market follows a similar shape. Jobright’s 2026 analysis of data analyst hiring, which looked at 2025–2026 postings from LinkedIn, Indeed and Levels.fyi, found that more than 80% of data analyst jobs mention SQL, over 60% mention Excel or Google Sheets, and roughly half mention Python or R. Let your own tally decide the order you learn in, but expect SQL to sit near the top.

As you work through each area below, finish with something you can show someone: a query, a tidied dataset, a chart, a one-page report or a portfolio project. Free material is often enough if you can stay disciplined. Pay for teaching only when it gives you something you cannot get alone, such as feedback, accountability or a fixed timetable.

Sources indicate that SQL is how analysts pull, join and summarise records from a database, and a tool like Tableau lets other people explore what you found. Treat them as one workflow rather than two subjects: frame a question, write the query, sanity-check the numbers and present the result so a non-technical reader can follow it.

SQLBolt offers free, bite-sized SQL lessons that run in the browser, and Tableau publishes free training videos on connecting to data and building dashboards. Used together, they are enough to produce a small end-to-end project.

According to recent reports, if you learn better with a set schedule and an instructor checking your work, you could learn to analyse data with SQL and Tableau from scratch through a guided programme at Heicoders Academy in Singapore. Whichever route you take, compare what is covered, how feedback is given, when sessions run and the full cost against what free resources already offer.

Proof you can show: A working SQL query set and your first published dashboard.

Move on when: You can take a question from idea to dashboard on your own, without following a tutorial line by line.

Spreadsheets are still where much of a team’s day-to-day reporting lives, especially when colleagues don’t write SQL. Get comfortable with filtering, pivot tables, and lookup functions, and learn to spot quiet errors like dates saved as text or one category spelled three different ways.

The next step is automating the cleanup so it doesn’t have to be repeated by hand each month. Microsoft’s Power Query documentation shows how to import and reshape data in recorded steps that refresh when latest data arrives. The same ideas apply in other spreadsheet tools too.

Proof you can show: A messy export turned into a summary that refreshes itself.

Move on when: You can clean an untidy CSV and build a report that updates when the source file changes.

Industry observers note that for most junior analyst roles, the technical interview is a SQL test. Basic SELECT statements won’t be enough; interviewers like to probe joins, subqueries, common table expressions and window functions, which answer everyday questions such as running totals or each customer’s first purchase.

Practise with timed problem sets and review your answers for correctness as well as speed.

Proof you can show: Confidence going into a live or take-home SQL test.

Move on when: You can solve intermediate problems in around 15 to 20 minutes each without looking up syntax.

Sources indicate that take-home assignments often come with data that has been made messy on purpose. Reviewers want to see how you deal with missing values, duplicates and inconsistent formats, and whether they can follow your reasoning afterwards.

It has been revealed that keep a short cleaning log as you work, noting each change and why you made it. A separate sheet tab or a list of comments in a notebook both work.

Proof you can show: A take-home submission a reviewer can audit step by step.

Move on when: Every change to your dataset is written down with a reason.

Recent findings suggest that case-study questions test whether you can read numbers sensibly, not just produce them. A working grasp of distributions, means and medians, spread, correlation and sampling will keep you away from the mistakes that undo otherwise good answers, such as quoting an average that a few extreme values have pulled out of shape.

Proof you can show: Clear, careful answers in case-study interviews.

Move on when: You can explain in everyday language why two things moving together doesn’t mean one causes the other.

In a recent development, every chart should help someone answer a specific question. Learn where bars, lines, scatter plots and simple tables each work best, and how axis ranges, labels and colour can nudge a reader towards the wrong conclusion. On a dashboard, the most important finding should be the first thing people see.

Industry observers note that datawrapper’s guidance on picking chart types is a useful free reference. As practice, show the same result in two different chart types and decide which one represents the data more honestly.

Proof you can show: Portfolio charts that make a point, not just show off features.

Move on when: A person who has never seen your data can spot the main finding and its caveat at a glance.

What counts as a useful metric depends on the role. Marketing analysts focus on conversion and retention, operations analysts on delivery times and capacity, and finance analysts on margins and cash flow. Choose one sector and learn exactly how its key measures are defined.

Proof you can show: A project built around the questions your target industry actually asks.

Move on when: You can define several sector metrics and describe how a manager would use each one.

Recent findings suggest that your portfolio is where the other seven areas come together. Two or three deep, well-documented projects will say more about you than a long list of quick ones. Give each project a README that sets out the question, the data, your method, the findings and the limitations.

Proof you can show: A portfolio link and a write-up you can talk through in an interview.

Move on when: Every project clearly explains what it asked, how you answered it and what you found.

Recent findings suggest that there is no need to finish all eight areas before you apply. Once you can use the tools your target roles mention, speak honestly about your work and point to two or three clearly explained projects, start sending applications and keep learning alongside them.

Adjust each application to the job. Lead with a reporting example for spreadsheet-heavy roles, a query that solved a real problem for SQL roles, and a chart that supported a decision for visualisation roles. Be upfront about which work you built independently and which came from guided exercises.

Do I really need eight courses? No. These are skill areas, not eight required qualifications. A single resource can cover several of them, and practice you do on your own counts as much as classroom learning.

Is it possible to prepare using only free material? Yes. Free tutorials, open textbooks, official documentation and public datasets cover the fundamentals well. The harder parts are sticking to a routine and finding people who will give you honest feedback.

Which should come first, SQL or spreadsheets? It depends on the jobs you want. Spreadsheets are an easy starting point for reporting roles, while SQL is expected wherever databases are involved. You will want both eventually, so start with whichever your target postings stress most.

How many portfolio projects should I have? Two or three solid ones are a good start. Each should show a clear question, steps someone else could repeat and an honest reading of the results, rather than several near-identical dashboards.

Recent findings suggest that do I need a certificate before I apply? Not usually. Some employers ask for one, but many judge skills through interviews, take-home tasks and tests instead. Go by what each posting actually requires.

A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • In a recent development, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • In a recent development, the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

In a recent development, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

In a recent development, the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

Sources indicate that conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

Sources indicate that the term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

According to recent reports, "Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

In a recent development, superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the latest approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

It has been revealed that the researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Industry observers note that crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

Recent findings suggest that "It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

According to recent reports, the first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

Recent findings suggest that "Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

Recent findings suggest that this means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

It has been revealed that ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

Sources indicate that "Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

Recent findings suggest that "We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

It has been revealed that in quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

Recent findings suggest that this fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

Industry observers note that the approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

Industry observers note that these calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

According to recent reports, the results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

It has been revealed that however, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely upcoming materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain vital challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

Recent findings suggest that from the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

Recent findings suggest that from a technological perspective, the study highlights how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising latest way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

It has been revealed that robert Heinlein suggests that a well-rounded person should be capable of handling a wide range of tasks—both intellectual and physical—rather than being narrowly specialized in one field. Drawing a parallel between a well-rounded person and machine intelligence: AI systems vary widely, but human intelligence excels in versatility—adapting to tasks, environments, and surprises. While large language and vision-language models (LLMs, VLMs) show promise, they lack interaction with the physical world. To bridge this gap, we need models trained on robotic data. Generalist robot models can enhance adaptability, using diverse data to improve generalization and robustness. Instead of training on isolated tasks, pre-training on varied robotic data—similar to LLMs—boosts efficiency and performance.

Developing generalist robot policies, or robot foundation models, presents three key challenges:.

The need for large-scale research to fully leverage pre-training benefits.

Industry observers note that designing model architectures that can integrate diverse data sources while capturing complex physical interactions. A key challenge in this regard is cross-embodiment training, where a model must learn from diverse robot types with varying configurations, control spaces, and action representations. Existing approaches tackle this by:.

Crafting an effective training recipe, as recent advances in NLP and vision have heavily relied on careful pre-training and post-training strategies.

In this post, we introduce π0 and π0-FAST, prototype models and learning frameworks developed by Physical Intelligence, designed to overcome these challenges.

π0 (Pi-Zero) is a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, developed by the Physical Intelligence team designed for generalist robot control. It builds upon large-scale pretraining and flow matching-based action generation, enabling robots to perform dexterous manipulation tasks across different embodiments.

π0 is trained on data from 7 robotic platforms and 68 unique tasks, demonstrating strong zero-shot and fine-tuned performance on complex, real-world tasks such as laundry folding, table bussing, grocery bagging, box assembly, and object retrieval.

Unlike standard robotic policies, π0 employs flow matching to produce smooth, real-time action trajectories at 50Hz, making it highly efficient, precise, and adaptable for real-world deployment. Flow matching was used in continuous normalizing flows and improved generation quality in diffusion models. The denoising process π0 used works in the same way, starting with a random noise that progressively converges towards a sequence of motor actions that make sense.

In a recent development, vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) share a common foundation: transformers. However, the key distinction lies in action representation. While VLMs process and generate multimodal representations (images and text), VLAs extend this by incorporating action and observation state tokens. With these additional tokens in place, the next challenge is understanding how attention is computed.

Let’s expand our vocabulary and introduce key terms:.

They are appended after the prefix portion (images + text), so the prefix serves as context (e.g., a scene image, language instructions like "be a good robot" or "transfer the cube"), while the suffix captures policy‐specific features.

Recent findings suggest that however, efficiently handling attention in π0 comes with its own set of challenges. The unique shape of its attention mask influences how attention is computed—let’s dive into the details!

According to recent reports, the resulting 2D causal mask exhibits strong block sparsity, but defining the boundaries of each block—especially in a batch of samples—is a bit tricky. We are used to causal masks with triangular structures for autoregressive modeling, but this is not one of those cases.

In a recent development, as you can see in this example below: the image (first element) has some padding tokens, representing empty cameras. Then, text tokens and state tokens are added. This "prefix" part forms a fully noncausal attention, as in PaliGemma. Then, the "suffix" (state + action/time tokens) has a causal-block structure. The eager naive implementation performs matrix multiplications and applies softmax across the entire input, making it highly inefficient.

Now that we know actions are simply n-dimensional vectors that can be tokenized, we can explore the challenges of action representation in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The way actions are represented directly impacts efficiency, generalization, and execution fidelity.

One approach is semantic action representation, where actions are described as high-level concepts like sub-tasks or keypoints. While this allows for few-shot and zero-shot learning, it often relies on hand-designed low-level controllers, limiting flexibility across different robots. In contrast, low-level control representations map actions directly to motor commands, enabling precise movements but making training less stable and harder to scale.

Industry observers note that most existing VLAs use discrete action tokenization, converting continuous actions into discrete tokens generated autoregressively. The most common method—per-dimension, per-timestep binning—struggles with high-frequency control tasks, leading to lossy representations and inefficient training. Alternatives like vector quantization (VQ) and time-series compression help, but VQ is sensitive to hyperparameters, making it less reliable for diverse robot designs.

To address these issues, Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization (FAST) introduces a novel time-series compression approach using the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). FAST reduces redundancy, improves efficiency, and enhances action fidelity.

With this, we present π0-FAST, faster and autoregressive version of π0 also available in Lerobot repo, an extension of π0, which leverages this new tokenizer for better action representation.

Paper | Jax Code | Our implementation in Lerobot.

π0-FAST is an autoregressive version of π0, introducing **FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization)**—a new tokenization scheme that enhances efficiency and performance.

🔗 The π0-FAST tokenizer can be accessed here: FAST Tokenizer.

🔗 Pretrained weights can be accessed here: Pi0+FAST.

It has been revealed that FAST uses the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to compress continuous action sequences into discrete tokens. The process, illustrated in Figure 2, begins with normalizing raw robot actions, mapping the 1st and 99th quantiles of each action dimension to the range [-1,1]. This normalization is used to ensure consistency across different robotic systems and improve robustness against outliers.

Each action dimension is then transformed independently using DCT, converting the time-domain signal into the frequency domain. To reduce redundancy, insignificant coefficients are removed through a scale-and-round operation, where a hyperparameter balances compression rate and reconstruction accuracy. The resulting DCT coefficient matrix, often sparse, is flattened into a one-dimensional sequence of integers, interleaving low-frequency components first across dimensions to preserve critical information.

Recent findings suggest that to further compress the sequence, Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is applied. As usual, BPE merges frequently occurring patterns across dimensions while maintaining a fixed-size vocabulary.

Figure 2: The FAST action tokenization pipeline.

Industry observers note that since all operations are invertible, actions can be reconstructed efficiently and losslessly from tokens. The tokenization pipeline has only two hyperparameters: the scaling coefficient applied before rounding and the BPE vocabulary size. Both parameters remain robust across different datasets.

Sources indicate that additionally, a universal version of FAST, called FAST+, has been trained on one million action sequences from single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation robots, making it applicable across diverse robotic setups. FAST+ is available as a Hugging Face AutoProcessor, allowing users to tokenize action sequences with just a few lines of code.

Sources indicate that for optimal compression, input actions should be quantile-normalized to [-1,1] before tokenization. With the AutoProcessor module, the users can train a custom FAST tokenizer on their own datasets.

🔗 Code for the usage and training custom action tokenizers in the official FAST Repo.

FAST is integrated into Hugging Face Transformers and can be easily used for encoding and decoding robot action sequences.

Sources indicate that with π0 and π0-FAST, we take a significant step towards generalist robot intelligence, bringing scalable, efficient, and versatile Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to LeRobot. By leveraging FAST tokenization, we enhance action representation, enabling robots to perform a diverse range of tasks with higher efficiency and adaptability. These steps open the door for future multi-embodiment, real-time robotic policies, pushing the boundaries of what robots can achieve in the real world. 🚀.
