Tech Report: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • It has been revealed that but position and time are different.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

It has been revealed that but position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

According to recent reports, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Recent findings suggest that understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

In a recent development, at RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with crucial changes taking place over just attoseconds.

According to recent reports, to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

It has been revealed that making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

Industry observers note that in the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It revealed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

Sources indicate that what makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

In a recent development, raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

In a recent development, in other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a fresh aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists upcoming ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

Industry observers note that "In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

Sources indicate that "In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the presently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

Recent findings suggest that that possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a latest foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

A new leak suggests that Samsung is preparing to copy the iPhone’s Dynamic Island feature in the not-too-distant future, to an extent that not many other Android brands have even done thus far.

Copying the Dynamic Island was briefly like a rite of passage for some Android brands, with many wasting almost no time in delivering their own version of the feature. But, on many of those devices, it’s a surface-level ripoff at best. The feature is primarily limited to music apps and timers, rarely working with any third-party apps in meaningful ways. Android has a built-in feature similar to Apple’s but not in the same styling.

Samsung is now preparing its own version of the Dynamic Island, and it seems this one has a bit more meat on its bones.

In a recent development, samMobile on Twitter/X posted a video and two still images of what appears to be a Dynamic Island clone coming to Galaxy devices. It’s mentioned as potentially coming to the Galaxy S27 series (so, One UI 9.5) and being called “Moment Effects.” A portion of the software explicitly mentions integration with Google Sports, the leak claims, while it seems Samsung is using Live Notifications here, which already support a number of third-party apps.

The current implementation of live activities showing the "chip" in the top bar is honestly far from good.

It negates one of the major pros of Android over iOS: being able to see notification icons in the top bar.

As when the "chip" of the live activity is active/shown, all notification icons will get hidden, even if there's a ton of space left between the "chip" and the constraint of the front camera area - an implementation that makes no sense whatsoever.

I honestly can't fathom how could Google come out with such poor implementation.

I don't particularly like this one from Samsung, but it surely is 1000000 times better from a UX perspective.

The kicker from a UX perspective is that Samsung’s interpretation allows you to swipe between activities, similar to Apple, but the core premise is similar with the island showing around the selfie camera cutout.

Industry observers note that when this feature might surface does remain unclear, but a One UI 9.5 debut would make plenty of sense. That update is in beta now and due to launch on the Galaxy S27 series early next year.

What do you think of Samsung’s alleged Dynamic Island clone? Personally, I’m on board as long as it proves useful, and it seems to be on the right track compared to most other copycats.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

It has been revealed that your accessibility check in CI is green. axe-core ran, zero violations, and the badge in the README looks great. Your site can still fail WCAG 2.2.

Sources indicate that that isn't a bug in axe. WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2023. It added nine success criteria and dropped one (4.1.1 Parsing), and most of the new ones can't be judged by reading the DOM. Deque said as much when it shipped the first WCAG 2.2 support in axe-core 4.5: the target-size rule would probably be the only new-criterion rule they added, because the others can't be automated without a lot of false positives.

So the rest is on you. This article covers the one criterion axe can check and three it can't (focus not obscured, dragging movements, accessible authentication), with Playwright tests you can drop into a project. I ran all of them against a small test page that fails every criterion on purpose, and against a fixed version of the same page. If you want a plain-language rundown of every change first, WCAG 2.2 vs 2.1 goes through them. Here I only care about what you can put in a pipeline.

In a recent development, level A and AA are what most contracts and laws point at, so those are the ones that matter first. The AAA criteria are still worth knowing about.

In a recent development, that's four AA criteria with something you can script, one of which axe already handles. The rest of this article goes through those four.

Industry observers note that the AA rule is smaller than most people expect: a pointer target should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or sit far enough from its neighbours that a 24px circle centred on it wouldn't overlap another target or that target's own circle. There are exceptions, including inline links in a sentence, and targets whose size the browser controls.

According to recent reports, axe-core has a target-size rule for this. One catch: it isn't part of a default run. In my setup (axe-core 4.14.1 through @axe-core/playwright 4.14.0), a plain analyze() on the broken page reported nothing at all. The rule only showed up once I asked for it:.

It has been revealed that on the broken page this lists the three 16px toolbar buttons by selector. On the fixed page, with 32px buttons, it passes. If you've been running axe for years and never seen a target-size result, this is why.

Some context on how common the problem is. In the scan data behind my last SitePoint article, 34.5% of the 1,025 sites had controls below a stricter 44px threshold. That is a tougher standard than the 24px that AA asks for, so don't read it as "a third of sites fail 2.5.8". Plenty of those would pass. But it does show how many production sites ship tiny controls.

If you'd like a quick look at one page before wiring anything up, browser tools such as axe DevTools, WAVE, or a WCAG checker will show the same thing.

Industry observers note that axe can't test it, because you have to press Tab and look at where the browser scrolled. Two details caught me out building this:.

The check below samples a grid of points inside the visible part of the focused element and asks the browser what's on top at each one. If none of the points land on the element or its children, it's covered.

On my broken page it reported nine hits: links hidden behind the footer going forward ("Section 4 link", "Section 10 link", "Section 16 link") and the toolbar buttons and a few links hidden behind the header coming back. The output names the element and the key, which is what you want when you're staring at a failed build.

The fix is one CSS rule, sized to your sticky elements:.

That tells the browser to leave room when it scrolls a focused element into view. With it in place the same test passes.

Recent findings suggest that be aware of what this can't see: a modal that opens over the page, or a chat widget that only appears after a delay, will not show up unless your test opens or waits for them. Adrian Roselli's piece on 2.4.11 and adversarial conformance is worth reading for the awkward cases.

It has been revealed that anything you can do by dragging needs a way to do it with a single click or tap, unless dragging is essential. Sortable lists, sliders, kanban cards, file reorderers: all of them.

You can't prove a drag alternative works from a script. But you can catch the obvious mistake, which is a draggable item with no button anywhere near it:.

The limit is real. It only recognises the native draggable attribute. Libraries built on pointer events, such as dnd-kit, don't set it, so this test will walk right past them. If you use one of those, replace the selector with whatever your component renders, or add a test per drag component. Treat it as a tripwire for the common case, not a verdict.

The fix, in the fixed page, is a pair of "Move up" and "Move down" buttons on each item, each with an accessible name that indicates which item it moves.

According to recent reports, this dispatches a synthetic paste event and checks whether anything called preventDefault() on it. It catches the old onpaste="return false" trick, and it catches script-based blockers too. It does not tell you whether your login has a CAPTCHA that needs an alternative, or an emailed one-time code you must retype. Those need a person.

On a pull request, a plain GitHub Actions job is enough:.

Industry observers note that point PAGE_URL at a running preview, and run the tests against the pages that matter most: sign-in, checkout, anything with a sticky element. Don't try to crawl everything on the first pass. A test that fails for reasons nobody owns gets deleted within a month.

Four things I haven't tried to automate, and wouldn't:.

In a recent development, automation will keep the regressions out. It won't tell you the work is finished. A green build and a conformant site are different things, and WCAG 2.2 widened the gap between them.

Industry observers note that the tests and both test pages are small enough to read in one sitting. Copy what's useful, change the selectors, and keep the broken page around: it's a handy way to check that a test fails when it should.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Nest app has been on life support for years now.
  • Realistically, even long-time Nest users have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.

The Nest app has been on life support for years now. Google has been migrating legacy products into the Home app for a while and the last few puzzle pieces came in Nest Protect support, the death of the earliest Nest Thermostats, and other assorted adjustments.

Realistically, even long-time Nest users have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.

Industry observers note that having been personally, deeply invested in Google’s vision for the smart home over the past decade, I’ll say that the Google Home app we have today is better than the Nest app ever was or ever could be. A huge part of that comes from Google Home’s ability to pull together devices from third-party ecosystems. Being able to control your entire smart home from a single app is how the smart home always should have been, and between Google’s work and the Matter standard, we’re finally able to enjoy that pretty seamlessly for the most part. Automations, Google’s actually-useful AI features, and more only sweeten the deal. I’m also a massive fan of what the Home app has become from a UX perspective. While there are always rough edges and bugs to clean up, the customizable homepage and well-organized sections make for a good – not perfect, but good – experience for the end user.

That remarked, there is one thing that the Nest app’s limited scope benefitted from, and that’s a focus on making your own product great.

Google’s move to the Home app for Nest devices has been a 5-year run of trying to clean things up, improve on the app, and basically bring back the way things were in the Nest app as far as the first-party cameras and thermostats are concerned. It’s taken ages, but we’re finally up to speed, mostly. I still hate that you have to reset Nest Cams to change Wi-Fi when the Nest app just let you change it, and the Nest app’s settings were much less overwhelming, but I’d say the pros far outweigh the cons at this point.

The Nest app was good at its job, but the Google Home app is a worthy successor, finally, and now the Nest app can finally rest. I mostly think the same applies to Gemini vs Google Assistant, with the newer assistant a better overall experience, but it’s easier to poke holes in that argument.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • According to recent reports, by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a upcoming form of computer memory.

According to recent reports, by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," notes Yiwen Chu.

Industry observers note that the breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

It has been revealed that chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

According to recent reports, quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the upcoming system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

Sources indicate that however, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

Upcoming Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

Recent findings suggest that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

It has been revealed that to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two notable computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

According to recent reports, "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the fresh architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

One of the most significant findings is that the latest system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

Industry observers note that however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

In a recent development, chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Industry observers note that practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising newly introduced route toward making those machines a reality.

Open-source DeepResearch – Freeing our search agents

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday, OpenAI released Deep Research, a system that browses the web to summarize content and answer questions based on the summary.
  • One of the main results in the blog post is a strong improvement of performances on the General AI Assistants benchmark (GAIA), a benchmark we’ve been playing with recently as well, where they successfully reached near 67% correct answers on 1-shot on average, and 47.6% on especially challenging “level 3” questions that involve multiple steps of reasoning and tool usage (see below for a presentation of GAIA).
  • DeepResearch is composed of an LLM (which can be selected from the current list of LLMs provided by OpenAI, 4o, o1, o3, etc) and an internal “agentic framework” which guide the LLM to use tools like web search and organize its actions in steps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, OpenAI released Deep Research, a system that browses the web to summarize content and answer questions based on the summary. The system is impressive and blew our minds when we tried it for the first time.

One of the main results in the blog post is a strong improvement of performances on the General AI Assistants benchmark (GAIA), a benchmark we’ve been playing with recently as well, where they successfully reached near 67% correct answers on 1-shot on average, and 47.6% on especially challenging “level 3” questions that involve multiple steps of reasoning and tool usage (see below for a presentation of GAIA).

DeepResearch is composed of an LLM (which can be selected from the current list of LLMs provided by OpenAI, 4o, o1, o3, etc) and an internal “agentic framework” which guide the LLM to use tools like web search and organize its actions in steps.

It has been revealed that while powerful LLMs are now freely available in open-source (see e.g. the recent DeepSeek R1 model), OpenAI didn’t disclose much about the agentic framework underlying Deep Research….

So we decided to embark on a 24-hour mission to reproduce their results and open-source the needed framework along the way!

Industry observers note that the clock is ticking, let’s go! ⏱️.

Almost everyone has already experienced how powerful LLMs can be simply by playing with chatbots.. However, what not everyone is aware of yet is that integrating these LLMs into agentic systems can give them real superpowers!

Here is a recent example comparing the performance of a few frontier LLMs with and without an agentic framework (in this case the simple smolagents library) - using an agentic framework bumps performance by up to 60 points!

In fact, OpenAI also highlighted in its release blogpost how Deep Research performed dramatically better than standalone LLMs on the knowledge-intensive "Humanity’s Last Exam" benchmark.

So, what happens when we integrate our current top LLM in an agentic framework, to work toward an open-DeepResearch ?

Industry observers note that A quick note: We’ll benchmark our results on the same GAIA challenge but keep in mind that this is a work in progress. DeepResearch is a massive achievement and its open reproduction will take time. In particular, full parity will require improved browser use and interaction like OpenAI Operator is providing, i.e. beyond the current text-only web interaction we explore in this first step.

Let’s first understand the scope of the challenge: GAIA.

GAIA is arguably the most comprehensive benchmark for agents. Its questions are very difficult and hit on many challenges of LLM-based systems. Here is an example of a hard question:.

Which of the fruits shown in the 2008 painting "Embroidery from Uzbekistan" were served as part of the October 1949 breakfast menu for the ocean liner that was later used as a floating prop for the film "The Last Voyage"? Give the items as a comma-separated list, ordering them in clockwise order based on their arrangement in the painting starting from the 12 o'clock position. Use the plural form of each fruit.

You can see this question involves several challenges:.

Solving this requires both high-level planning abilities and rigorous execution, which are two areas where LLMs struggle when used alone.

So it’s an excellent test set for agent systems!

On GAIA’s public leaderboard, GPT-4 does not even reach 7% on the validation set when used without any agentic setup. On the other side of the spectrum, with Deep Research, OpenAI reached 67.36% score on the validation set, so an order of magnitude better! (Though we don’t know how they would actually fare on the private test set.).

Let’s see if we can do better with open source tools!

In a recent development, the first improvement over traditional AI agent systems we’ll tackle is to use a so-called “code agent”. As shown by Wang et al. (2024), letting the agent express its actions in code has several advantages, but most notably that code is specifically designed to express complex sequences of actions.

Consider this example given by Wang et al.:.

This highlights several advantages of using code:.

The advantages above were confirmed by our experiments on the agent_reasoning_benchmark.

According to recent reports, from building smolagents we can also cite a notable additional advantage, which is a better handling of state: this is very useful for multimodal tasks in particular. Need to store this image/audio/other for later use? No problem, just assign it as a variable in your state and you can re-use it 4 steps later if needed. In JSON you would have to let the LLM name it in a dictionary key and trust the LLM will later understand that it can still use it.

Now we need to provide the agent with the right set of tools.

1. A web browser. While a fully fledged web browser interaction like Operator will be needed to reach full performance, we started with an extremely simple text-based web browser for now for our first proof-of-concept. You can find the code here.

2. A simple text inspector, to be able to read a bunch of text file format, find it here.

According to recent reports, these tools were taken from the excellent Magentic-One agent by Microsoft Research, kudos to them! We didn’t change them much, as our goal was to get as high a performance as we can with the lowest complexity possible.

Here is a short roadmap of improvements which we feel would really improve these tools’ performance (feel free to open a PR and contribute!):.

In our 24h+ reproduction sprint, we’ve already seen steady improvements in the performance of our agent on GAIA!

We’ve swiftly gone up from the previous SoTA with an open framework, around 46% for Magentic-One, to our current performance of 55.15% on the validation set.

Sources indicate that this bump in performance is due mostly to letting our agents write their actions in code! Indeed, when switching to a standard agent that writes actions in JSON instead of code, performance of the same setup is instantly degraded to 33% average on the validation set.

Here is the final agentic system.

We’ve set up a live demo here for you to try it out!

However, this is only the beginning, and there are a lot of things to improve! Our open tools can be made better, the smolagents framework can also be tuned, and we’d love to explore the performance of better open models to support the agent.

We welcome the community to come join us in this endeavour, so we can leverage the power of open research together to build a great open-source agentic framework! It would allow anyone to run a DeepResearch-like agent at home, with their favorite models, using a completely local and customized approach!

While we were working on this and focusing on GAIA, other great open implementations of Deep Research emerged from the community, specifically from.

It has been revealed that each of these implementations use different libraries for indexing data, browsing the web and querying LLMs. In this project, we would like to reproduce the benchmarks presented by OpenAI (pass@1 average score), benchmark and document our findings with switching to open LLMs (like DeepSeek R1), using vision LMs, benchmark traditional tool calling against code-native agents.

OpenAI’s Deep Research is probably boosted by the excellent web browser that they introduced with Operator.

Recent findings suggest that so we’re tackling that next! In a more general problem: we’re going to build GUI agents, i.e. “agents that view your screen and can act directly with mouse & keyboard”. If you’re excited about this project, and want to help everyone get access to such cool capabilities through open source, we’d love to get your contribution!

We’re also hiring a full time engineer to help us work on this and more, apply if you’re interested 🙂.

Industry News: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," mentioned Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

It has been revealed that for decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

The upcoming findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

Industry observers note that at Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

According to recent reports, when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

According to recent reports, another notable discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

In a recent development, this distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

In a recent development, A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

Industry observers note that the participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler stated. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

According to recent reports, the research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Sources indicate that rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

Industry News: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • Sources indicate that the approach has already revealed latest candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • In a recent development, one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

Sources indicate that the approach has already revealed latest candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

In a recent development, one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

In a recent development, this capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Recent findings suggest that although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

Industry observers note that these imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

It has been revealed that finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

In a recent development, by "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

Recent findings suggest that "Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more promptly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Upcoming Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Recent findings suggest that light plays an crucial role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Industry observers note that much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

In a recent development, the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Industry observers note that beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

It has been revealed that martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

It has been revealed that "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

#150748. The Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard 2

The Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard 2

📅 10 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the growing availability of LLMs supporting Arabic, both as monolingual and multilingual models, prompted the community to create dedicated Arabic language leaderboards.
  • While these approaches helped spark initial interest in Arabic benchmarking, they also introduced several challenges:.
  • These limitations underscore the need for a more unified, accessible, and transparent benchmarking platform—one that not only enables but encourages genuine and reproducible experimentation for the entire Arabic NLP community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the growing availability of LLMs supporting Arabic, both as monolingual and multilingual models, prompted the community to create dedicated Arabic language leaderboards. Previously, Arabic-focused leaderboards were typically confined to narrow benchmarks introduced by specific authors, often as demos for their work. In these cases, the authors would set up leaderboards to demonstrate how models performed on a particular task or dataset. Alternatively, other leaderboards required owners to run evaluations on their own computing resources and then submit a JSON file containing their results for display.

While these approaches helped spark initial interest in Arabic benchmarking, they also introduced several challenges:.

These limitations underscore the need for a more unified, accessible, and transparent benchmarking platform—one that not only enables but encourages genuine and reproducible experimentation for the entire Arabic NLP community. To address these problems, in May 2024, 2A2I, TII, and HuggingFace launched the first version of the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard - OALL [1], featuring 14 benchmarks across a wide range of tasks including reading comprehension, sentiment analysis, and question answering among others.

It has been revealed that in September 2024, a collaboration between SDAIA and the King Salman Global Academy for Arabic Language introduced the Balsam Index, which includes approximately 1,400 datasets with 50,000 questions covering 67 tasks, such as grammar correction, paraphrasing, cause-and-effect classification, and text comprehension ... etc.

Later that year, on December 5th, Inception and MBZUAI announced the AraGen Leaderboard, the first generative tasks leaderboard for Arabic, introducing the 3C3H evaluation metric, which uses dynamic evaluation cycles with private test, and provides a native-Arabic and culturally-aware generative tasks dataset, AraGen Bench, to assess LLMs across four main tasks.

According to recent reports, and to end the year strong, on 19th of December 2024, Scale's Safety, Evaluations, and Alignment Lab (SEAL) published an Arabic leaderboard as part of their multilingual leaderboards. The benchmark empowering this leaderboard remains always private like all the other languages within their family of leaderboards, and relies on human-preference evaluation, using a dataset of 1,000 Arabic prompts designed to enhance chatbot interaction capabilities across complex and culturally nuanced conversations.

Sources indicate that in less than 7 months after its launch, the first version of the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard swiftly became a vital platform for the Arabic AI community, attracting over 46,000 visitors and more than 2,000 visits in the past month (January 2025). The HuggingFace space received over 100 likes and 8 citations on Google Scholar. The community submitted more than 700 models, ranging from 1B to over 70B parameters. The submitted models originate from more than 180 unique organizations making it one of the most active LLM evaluation leaderboards. Since its launch, the leaderboard sparked numerous engaging discussions across social media, HuggingFace, Reddit, making it the most prominent Arabic leaderboard to date.

As depicted in Figure 1, among the ~700 models submitted to the initial version of the leaderboard, the majority are chat and finetuned models, comprising over 70%, whereas pretrained models constitute only 11%. In terms of model size, more than 50% of the models are smaller than 7B parameters.

Compared to leaderboards for other languages and as shown in Figure 2, the Open Arabic LLM leaderboard stands out as one of the most active, following closely behind the Korean, Polish, and Portuguese leaderboards, all within less than a year of its launch. Considering that Arabic is one of the most spoken languages globally, yet has relatively limited content available on the internet, these figures carry even greater significance compared to other languages.

Recent discussions within the community, including critiques of the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard (OALL) and similar initiatives, have highlighted key shortcomings in current benchmarking practices [2]. Many researchers, developers, and language enthusiasts have emphasized the need for more direct evaluations of Arabic-specific tasks, increased transparency in how benchmarks are created, and the inclusion of more diverse datasets that reflect the breadth of Arabic dialects, domains, and real-world applications. These insights have played a central role in shaping the updated leaderboard.

The Arabic language presents unique challenges and characteristics that require specialized evaluation beyond what general NLP tasks can capture. These include intricate grammar, rich and complex morphology, the diversity of spoken dialects, and culturally nuanced safety-related considerations. A leaderboard that addresses these factors can provide a clearer picture of how well models perform in real-world Arabic language contexts.

Sources indicate that in the first iteration of OALL, a large portion of datasets and tasks originated from non-Arabic-speaking contexts. When adapted to Arabic, these tasks often failed to reflect real-world use cases or meet the practical needs of Arabic-speaking communities. Many tasks were direct translations from English, which frequently introduced linguistic and contextual mismatches. This approach overlooked Arabic’s unique morphological and syntactic complexities, making the tasks less effective in measuring true language understanding and modeling capabilities.

Sources indicate that additionally, some benchmarks from the first version of OALL became less effective over time as models achieved near-perfect scores, limiting their ability to differentiate incremental improvements. In response, the fresh leaderboard replaces these saturated benchmarks, introducing a more relevant and up-to-date suite of evaluation tasks.

To address these gaps, the new leaderboard incorporates tasks that are natively developed in Arabic. These tasks are designed to capture the language’s distinctive features—such as its rich morphology, subtle syntax, and context-specific usage—elements that are often lost in translation-based benchmarks. This shift ensures that evaluations are more authentic and better aligned with the realities of Arabic language use.

Recent findings suggest that furthermore, we identified a silent bug in one of the main tasks, AlGhafa, which inadvertently impacted model rankings. The glitch stemmed from a mismatch in how answer choices were checked—rather than verifying their indices, the task evaluated responses based on the choices themselves. While this was not entirely incorrect, it affected small/weak models disproportionately. Some models experienced score drops of up to 20 points, while stronger models remained relatively unaffected. This issue compromised the consistency, fairness and uniformity of the evaluations.

In reforming the leaderboard, we follow two guiding principles: remove saturated and machine translated tasks, due to inherent lower quality and possible cultural bias, and add newly available high quality native or human curated benchmarks to increase the coverage of the evaluation.

From the first version of the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard (OALL), we keep the following benchmark datasets:.

We enrich the leaderboard by adding the following datasets, released in the past year:.

Finally, we introduce the ALRAGE benchmark: Arabic Language Retrieval Augmented Generation Evaluation. It introduces a comprehensive framework for evaluating Large Language Models' retrieval-augmented generation capabilities in Arabic. Built upon a meticulously curated dataset sourced from 40 Arabic books spanning diverse topics, from Arts & Literature to Technology & Innovation, the benchmark was created using meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-70B for synthetic generation and validated by native Arabic speakers with a community sprint with Argilla. The dataset structure includes questions, ground-truth answers, candidate contexts retrieved through the BAAI/bge-m3 embedding model, and target candidate indices, all designed to authentically simulate real-world RAG scenarios in Arabic.

The innovative aspect of ALRAGE lies in its evaluation methodology, which implements a LLM-as-judge metric within the lighteval framework. Using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct as the judge model, the system evaluates generated responses through a structured Arabic prompt that compares the model's output against gold answers. The evaluation employs a nuanced 0-10 scoring rubric that assesses answer accuracy, relevance, and quality, with scores normalized to a 0-1 range for standardization. This technical implementation, manifested through a custom JudgeMetricWrapper class, provides a rigorous, reproducible method for evaluating Arabic language generation while maintaining sensitivity to Arabic linguistic nuances, effectively addressing the critical need for sophisticated evaluation metrics in Arabic NLP.

Table 1 summarizes the datasets kept from the first version of the leaderboard as well as the latest datasets introduced in this second version.

To assess the impact of the second iteration of the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard, we conducted a series of statistical comparisons between the two versions.

Sources indicate that figure 3 displays the performance scores across six benchmarks for Versions 1 and 2. Notably, ACVA and Toxigen demonstrate saturation effects at various model sizes. Alghafa in Version 1 exhibits lower saturation, which we hypothesize is due to the inclusion of both native and translated Arabic benchmarks. In contrast, the models' performance for AraTrust, ALRAGE, and Alghafa form v2 is more dispersed with respect to model size.

It has been revealed that to examine the correlation between OALL and other Arabic LLM leaderboards, we compared the relative rankings of five open Arabic LLMs: google/gemma-2-27b-it, CohereForAI/aya-23-35B, CohereForAI/aya-expanse-32b, inceptionai/jais-adapted-70b-chat, and meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, across three leaderboards: OALL v2, SEAL Arabic, and AraGen. As illustrated in Figure 4, a correlation between the leaderboards is notable, with the Llama3.3-70-instruct model ranking first on both OALL v2 and AraGen, and third on SEAL. *As a clarification, AraGen presently only features the scores for inceptionai/jais-adapted-70b-chat, and the Arabic SEAL leaderboard only includes Jais Adapted 70B, so presumably the pretrained model. As we could not fully solve this discrepancy, we decided to evaluate inceptionai/jais-adapted-70b-chat on OALL v2 for this comparison.

To further explore the differences between the two versions of OALL, we present in Figure 5 the top models across two categories: pretrained and chat. For models submitted to OALL v1, Qwen2.5 establishes itself as a strong baseline for Arabic in all categories, particularly for pretrained models. In OALL v2, Qwen models also dominate the pretrained models category, however the Qwen/Qwen2-72B model surpasses Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B as the best pretrained/continually pretrained model, and Llama3.3-70B-instruct emerges as the leader in all categories, surpassing calme-2.1-qwen2.5-72b in performance. Overall, some model rankings have shifted in v2, while others have remained consistent. We attribute these changes to two key factors: first, the robustness of models with respect to Arabic-native benchmarks, safety, and trustworthiness; and second, the evaluation of over 700 models in OALL v1 compared to 80 models in v2, including a few recent models that might not be present in v1. We anticipate that the community will contribute to expanding the leaderboard following its release.

Finally, we analyzed the average scores on OALL v1 and v2 for two model families: AceGPT and Jais. As depicted in Figure 6, the trend is consistent across both versions: larger models tend to achieve higher average scores, with the exception of inceptionai/jais-family-30b-8k, that surpasses the larger inceptionai/jais-adapted-70b model on OALL v2. Overall, the average scores in v2 are higher than in v1, except for the 7B models in both families. We hypothesize that this discrepancy is due to the lower performance of smaller models on ALRAGE, as it is a generative task, which typically favors larger models.

Recent findings suggest that in this blog post, we introduced the second version of the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard. We analyzed the existing Arabic leaderboards as well as the first version of the OALL, remarking issues such as the saturation of specific benchmarks that were removed in this second iteration. We also removed machine-translated benchmarks and retained only the Arabic native and human-translated benchmarks. Finally, we introduced new benchmarks such as Aratrust, MadinaQA, native MMLU, human translated MMLU (MMLU-HT) and ALRAGE. Our goal is to offer the community an objective evaluation of Arabic LLMs, aiding in the understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each submitted model.

Looking ahead, we hope to see the release of additional Arabic benchmarks, particularly in areas such as mathematics, reasoning, hallucination and both general and domain-specific benchmarks.

Sources indicate that the authors would like to thank Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) for providing some of the upcoming native benchmarks we are using in this version, including the new MMLU-HT dataset. We also extend our gratitude to TII for their generous sponsorship of the inference hardware needed for the evaluation backend. We also thank our friends at Hugging Face for their continuous support and being always 🤗 whenever needed. Thanks to all people focusing on evaluation and leaderboards for their languages and tasks. Lastly, we thank the community for their engagement and valuable feedback on the first version of the OALL. Looking forward to seeing many models on the leaderboard 🚀.
