Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • Industry observers note that quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Industry observers note that quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

According to recent reports, the breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

Recent findings suggest that quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can promptly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

Sources indicate that but quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," notes Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the upcoming approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify crucial interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

According to recent reports, to evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

Industry observers note that after this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an crucial step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

Recent findings suggest that the next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

Sources indicate that "After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," claims Peter Zoller.

This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

Sources indicate that the findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

Open R1: Patch #2

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are now two weeks into the Open R1 project which aims to reconstruct the missing pieces of DeepSeek R1—specifically, the training pipeline and synthetic data.
  • In this post, we are happy to share the construction of OpenR1-Math-220k: our first large-scale dataset for mathematical reasoning!
  • We also take a look at some exciting developments from the community towards curating small, high-quality datasets for fine-tuning, along with insights into how to control the length of the chain-of-thought from reasoning models at both train-time and inference-time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are now two weeks into the Open R1 project which aims to reconstruct the missing pieces of DeepSeek R1—specifically, the training pipeline and synthetic data.

In this post, we are happy to share the construction of OpenR1-Math-220k: our first large-scale dataset for mathematical reasoning!

We also take a look at some exciting developments from the community towards curating small, high-quality datasets for fine-tuning, along with insights into how to control the length of the chain-of-thought from reasoning models at both train-time and inference-time.

One of the key advantages of DeepSeek R1 is its ability to transfer advanced reasoning capabilities to smaller models through distillation. The DeepSeek team demonstrated this by generating 600k reasoning traces and fine-tuning a series of Qwen and Llama models, showing that direct distillation from R1 can achieve competitive reasoning performance without reinforcement learning. Notably, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B achieved 55.5% on AIME 2024, surpassing larger models like QwQ-32B-Preview.

However, the reasoning traces used for distillation have not been released publicly, prompting the community to independently recreate similar datasets. So far, multiple open datasets have been released by the community, including OpenThoughts-114k, Bespoke-Stratos-17k, Dolphin-R1, and LIMO.

Sources indicate that 🐳  Introducing OpenR1-Math-220k, a large-scale math reasoning dataset generated locally on 512 H100s, with multiple answers per problem. To create OpenR1-Math-220k, we collaborated with Numina who have developed a brand new version of their popular NuminaMath-CoT dataset.

What’s new in OpenR1 dataset compared to existing datasets:.

By demonstrating scalable, high-quality reasoning data generation, we hope this pipeline can be extended beyond math to domains like code generation.

Recent findings suggest that to build OpenR1-220k, we prompt DeepSeek R1 to generate solutions for 400k problems from NuminaMath 1.5. We follow the model card’s recommended parameters and prepend the following instruction to the user prompt:.

"Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.".

Industry observers note that we set a 16k token limit per generation, as our analysis demonstrated that only 75% of problems could be solved in under 8k tokens, and most of the remaining problems required the full 16k tokens. Initially, we used vLLM for inference, achieving a throughput of 15 generations per hour per H100, and shared our generation scripts in previous updates and on the OpenR1 repo. Recently, we started experimenting with SGLang and we were able to generate 25 solutions per hour per H100 (almost 2x speedup!), enabling us to generate 300k problem solutions per day on 512 H100s. This allowed us to produce 800k reasoning traces in just a few days.

We generate two solutions per problem—and in some cases, four—to provide flexibility in filtering and training. This approach allows for rejection sampling, similar to DeepSeek R1’s methodology, and also makes the dataset suitable for preference optimisation methods like DPO.

The scripts for the data generation are available here: https://github.com/huggingface/open-r1/tree/main/slurm.

The unfiltered dataset is available here: https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-r1/OpenR1-Math-Raw.

To retain only high-quality, correct reasoning traces, we leverage Math Verify, a robust mathematical expression evaluation system designed to assess LLM-generated answers. We extract the final answers from model generations and compare them against ground truth answers in the dataset.

We find that 55% of problems have at least one correct answer. However, some ground truth answers in NuminaMath 1.5 were empty or not in a verifiable format, making automatic validation challenging. While we have improved Math-Verify to more accurately handle these more uncommon output formats (see Math-Verify improvements below), we also explored an alternative method to recover valid solutions from rejected samples: using Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct as a judge on a subset of rejected problems. Before running this verification step, we filter out samples that are incomplete or that contain an empty ground truth answer, ensuring that only well-formed responses with a clearly boxed final answer are considered. This process successfully retrieves 28,000 of previously rejected problems.

We prompt Llama3.3-70B-Instruct as follows:.

Recent findings suggest that by combining rule-based verification (Math Verify) with LLM-based evaluation, we improve dataset quality while maintaining scale. The final dataset consists of 220k problems with verified reasoning traces, making it a valuable resource for training reasoning models. Providing multiple solutions per problem gives the community flexibility to filter for better generations and apply more targeted refinements based on NuminaMath data sources and problem types.

The dataset is available in two splits:.

Industry observers note that for rows with multiple correct answers, we also tried applying a Reward Model (RM) as a final filter to select the best response. For each row with multiple correct generations by R1, we extracted the final answer by removing the thinking tokens (…), and then pass the problem + the extracted answer to Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-RM-72B served using vLLM to get an score. Using these scores, we built a ranking for each row containing more than one correct response. The top-1 correct generations were selected and included in the training dataset, but sadly the training ablations showed that this approach doesn’t help to improve model performance with respect to selecting one random correct generation. A possible improvement could be to include the reasoning trace rather than just the final answer when scoring with the RM.

According to recent reports, we fine-tune Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct for 3 epochs on the default split of the dataset using a learning rate of 5e-5. To extend the context length from 4k to 32k, we increase RoPE frequency to 300k. The training follows a linear learning rate schedule with a 10% warmup phase. The table below compares the performance of OpenR1-Qwen-7B to DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-7B and OpenThinker-7B using lighteval.

This dataset represents an initial version, providing a foundation for further refinement. The community can explore additional filtering strategies to improve performance, such as rejection sampling, which was used in DeepSeek R1 to enhance quality.

Industry observers note that we identified several failure cases in Math-Verify during our inspection of the verification results. To address these concerns, we implemented significant improvements and fixes. We strongly recommend updating to the latest version (0.5.2) to benefit from these enhancements:.

The following is the summary of the most vital improvements:.

This week saw the community explore GRPO from many different angles, while multiple research labs have shown that only ~1000 high quality training samples may be sufficient to elicit reasoning in existing open models.

The first part of the AIME 2025 was released this week, which consists of 15 difficult math problems that are used to train high school students for the International Math Olympiad. In the past year, AIME 2024 has stood as the main benchmark to probe the mathematical capabilities of LLMs and the community was excited to see how well models performs on a new set of unseen problems:.

An interesting newly introduced research paper reveals that by using a recurrent language model, it is possible to scale test-time compute by implicitly reasoning in latent space. This resembles Meta’s Coconut work to train language models in latent space, but now adapted to reasoning tasks. The advantage of these methods is that they are far more compute efficient: by exploring the latent, one does not need to generate huge amounts of “thinking” tokens to obtain high performance.

While DeepSeek R1 leveraged 600k reasoning traces for distillation, recent work suggests that complex reasoning can emerge in language models not through massive-scale training, but through a small number of carefully curated samples.

Recent findings suggest that one example of this approach is the s1K dataset. It consists of 1,000 carefully selected math questions with distilled reasoning traces from Gemini Flash. The selection approach focuses on difficulty, diversity, and quality. The authors fine-tune Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on s1K and manage to exceed OpenAI’s o1-preview on competition math benchmarks by up to 27%.

It has been revealed that another dataset, LIMO, pushes this idea further, achieving strong performance on AIME and MATH benchmarks using only 817 training samples. The authors hypothesize that when a model has already acquired extensive domain knowledge during pre-training, only a small number of well-structured examples may be needed to unlock advanced reasoning capabilities.

One crucial ingredient allowing the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model from s1K to reach such strong performance is budget forcing, a test-time compute technique that either extends or truncates reasoning by appending “Wait” or an end-of-thinking token delimiter to the model’s generation, respectively. This tool allowed the authors to vary thinking time and conclude that their model exhibits test-time scaling: as thinking time increases, so does accuracy on different math benchmarks.

Sources indicate that similarly, Demystifying Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs (Yeo et al.) also studies the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) length on model performance. They introduce the Cosine Reward — a novel reward function that they use to incentivize shorter CoTs for correct generations and longer CoTs for wrong generations — which stabilizes RL training, particularly when the model has relatively limited max context size and average response length could explode. Repetition penalty is also employed when the model starts to show signs of reward hacking on hard questions, by artificially increasing CoT length through repetition instead of attempting to solve the problem.

Recent findings suggest that now that GRPO is humming in TRL, we are running an extensive set of experiments to understand which hyperparameters and reward functions have the greatest impact on training. You can follow our progress in the community tab and will write up our findings in the next upgrade!

If you want to contribute check out the open-r1 repository on GitHub or follow the Hugging Face open-r1 org.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A short clip can help a project in different ways. It can show an idea you have not filmed, put an existing design in motion, or give an announcement something to look at. The same approach will not work if the clip needs to demonstrate a real feature or show exactly what happened. Before choosing a generator, decide what the viewer needs to learn from the shot.

Sources indicate that this article uses Kling 4.0 as a worked example, but the decision process applies to any AI video generator. It covers how these tools turn prompts and images into video, how Kling 4.0 and a few alternatives differ, how to choose a starting mode, how to add exact text and branding outside the generated clip with a short ffmpeg script, and when real footage is the better choice. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you proposal a production.

● Generated video is best for imagined shots. It suits concepts, backgrounds and early explorations, not instructions or faithful records.

According to recent reports, ● Your starting material decides the mode. A written idea, a reference image or a pair of opening and closing frames each call for a different input.

It has been revealed that ● Keep exact wording out of the generated clip. Titles, dates and logos belong on separate layers in an editor.

Sources indicate that ● Tools differ on control, cost and licensing. Compare inputs, length, resolution, credits and terms before you commit.

According to recent reports, ● Always review. Watch the whole clip at its final size and check it against the real product or design.

Most current systems extend diffusion models across time. A model learns to turn noise into a coherent set of frames guided by a prompt, and sometimes by an image or a clip. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequences are easy to observe.

According to recent reports, ● The prompt describes change over time. One visible change and one camera instruction usually work better than a long list of actions.

It has been revealed that ● Reference material steers but does not lock. A picture can suggest shape and colour without guaranteeing an exact match.

According to recent reports, ● Longer clips give more room for drift. Faces, logos and fine text are the first things to change between frames.

● Cost grows with length and resolution. Most hosted tools charge credits per second, so short previews are cheaper than full shots.

Sources indicate that if you only have an idea, start with text. For a short announcement, you might ask for a band of light to move across a wall of coloured tiles. No one needs to recognise a particular wall, so the model can decide how it looks. Give it one visible change and a clear view of the subject. A prompt such as Soft morning light travels slowly across a wall of blue ceramic tiles. Fixed camera, no lettering is enough to see whether the idea works.

If you already have an illustration or a photo, reference mode gives you another starting point. Suppose you want a short concept clip for a desk accessory that only exists as a drawing. The picture can show the general shape and colour while the prompt describes the view you want. A video reference can help when it is the motion that is hard to explain, such as a slow camera slide. Say what each asset is meant to guide, and do not add a clip just because you have one.

It has been revealed that use keyframes when a particular view matters at a particular moment. Start with an opening image. If a short reveal also needs to end with the object facing forward, add an ending image to show that view. That is different from a reference image that mainly reveals what the object looks like. Neither method guarantees an exact match, so check the result rather than assuming the uploaded picture has locked the design.

Recent findings suggest that no single tool fits every project. The table summarizes what each option’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Sources indicate that reading the table: hosted studios such as the one on JXP are the quickest way to test an idea and need no setup, but you pay per second and work within their supported inputs. Kling’s own site is the place to check announcements and API options directly, since its page states little about durations or resolution. Runway positions its models for motion quality and prompt following, while Google’s Gemini API video documentation suits teams building generation into their own products. The Diffusers video guide covers open-source pipelines for developers who want local control and are ready to manage GPUs and licences.

Trying an idea before making it. An illustrator might want to see how an imagined landscape feels when the light changes. A quick clip gives the team something to discuss: is the change visible, and does it happen at the right pace? It does not need to be the final animation to answer those questions.

Sources indicate that showing a product concept. A rotating view or a slow camera move can help people discuss how a design might be presented. It is useful early, when the shape and lighting are still being explored. Once the clip represents a product someone can buy, the standard changes. If a port moves or a button appears that the real product does not have, it is the wrong clip for that job.

Industry observers note that making a short visual for a post. A few seconds of moving colour can give an event announcement or a project patch a distinctive opening. Put the name, date and other exact wording in your editor so they are readable and easy to change. The background only needs to support the message. If it competes with the text, use less movement or keep the background still.

According to recent reports, generated video is unreliable at lettering, so add titles in an editor or with a script. The command below overlays a title on a generated background and then checks the file properties. It assumes you already have a clip named background.mp4 and ffmpeg installed.

-vf "drawtext=text='Launch Night | 12 March':fontcolor=white:fontsize=64:x=(w-text_w)/2:y=(h-text_h)/2:box=1:boxcolor=black@0.35:boxborderw=24" \.

-c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -an announcement.mp4.

ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \.

-show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,duration \.

-of default=noprint_wrappers=1 announcement.mp4.

In a recent development, because the text lives in the command, you can reuse the same background for three events by changing one string. The font may need to be set with a fontfile option on some systems. This is the practical version of keeping the moving background in one file and the editable details in another.

If people will follow the clip as instructions, use real footage or a screen recording for the steps. A convincing shot of an app is not proof that a button is in the right place. A generated close-up of a product is not a reliable way to show how its parts fit. You can still use an imagined opening, but make the switch to the real demonstration clear.

According to recent reports, think about revisions, too. If your team expects to adjust the same title, logo or date every week, put those elements on separate layers in an editor. And if the only movement you need is a slow zoom on an approved picture, apply that zoom directly. There is no reason to risk changing the picture when a simple edit will do.

This matters when someone else will maintain the video. A reusable announcement template is easier to hand over if the moving background is one file and the event details are editable. If the team likes the movement but needs three versions with different dates, they can reuse the same clip. If every change calls for a new generation, the time you saved on the first version may disappear on the second.

Recent findings suggest that the Kling 4.0 video generator on JXP right now offers 720p and 1080p settings and clip lengths from 3 to 30 seconds. According to its page, reference mode accepts up to 10 images and 5 videos, keyframe mode takes a first frame, middle frames and an optional last frame, and credits are charged per second with a higher rate at 1080p. For a first attempt, choose the frame shape you proposal to use and make the clip only as long as it needs to be. Check the displayed credit cost before generating, because a short preview can tell you whether the direction works before you spend on a longer shot.

According to recent reports, decide what a good result looks like before you generate it. For the tile background, you need to see the light move without distracting from the words you will add. For a product concept, check whether the shape stays recognisable as the viewpoint changes. Watch the whole clip at the size the audience will see it. If the shot misses the point, revise one thing at a time: the motion, the framing or the source image.

It has been revealed that ● Read the licence. JXP’s page lists a commercial use license on each plan and notes outputs are for creative and lawful use, with the user responsible for reviewing them. Other tools have different terms.

● Do not misrepresent products or events. A generated clip should not suggest features or footage that do not exist.

● Consider provenance. C2PA is an open standard for Content Credentials that records where content came from and how it was edited, and some tools support it.

● Disclose where required. Follow platform and advertising rules on labelling AI-generated or altered content.

● Fine text, logos, hands and fast motion can drift or flicker between frames.

● Reference images and keyframes steer the result but do not guarantee an exact match.

● Vendor specifications, such as resolution and length, can differ between a model announcement and a particular platform.

● Credit costs and strategy terms change, so check them on the day you generate.

● Long or exact sequences are often cheaper and safer to film than to generate.

Short imagined shots, concept clips and moving backgrounds, where some details can be left open and the clip is reviewed before use.

Use text when you only have an idea, reference mode when you have a picture or clip to guide the look, and keyframes when specific views matter at specific moments.

Sources indicate that not reliably. Use real footage or a screen recording for instructions and demonstrations.

No. Hosted studios, vendor sites, developer APIs and open-source pipelines all exist. Compare supported inputs, length, resolution, cost and licensing against your project.

Kling 4.0 is a good candidate when the missing piece is an imagined shot and you can describe what it needs to do. Pick one such shot, try it, and put it next to the material you already have, and compare at least one alternative before you commit. Samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, meanwhile, is designed to be a normal smartphone on the outside, hiding a tablet within. Finally, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the new kid on the block, offering a compact outer display that opens up to a media-friendly, wider inner panel.

According to recent reports, each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs. Here’s a quick rundown of the key details on each device:.

Starting with the displays, the book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra both provide outer displays that are fully usable as standard smartphones, while the inner display is useful for multitasking, media, or just getting more space for reading a website or e-book. Samsung’s top-tier specs deliver performance for everything you’d need, with Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy powering everything from demanding games or media-editing apps to day-to-day use.

Cameras, battery life, content consumption, and size are some of the most important points to consider, so let’s take a look one-by-one.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to cameras, foldables have a tough time. There’s only so much physical space to fit the camera sensors and, with cameras, having more space generally results in a battery overall camera.

Runner-up here is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers a pair of 50MP cameras for wide and ultrawide shots. All three devices also use their foldable nature to let you capture full-quality selfies using the rear cameras, which always have better quality than the 10MP dedicated front-facing cameras.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the best places to score a great deal with solid trade-in values and deep discounts around Black Friday and throughout the holiday season.

(This post was authored by hlky and Sayak).

Tooling for image generation datasets is well established, with img2dataset being a fundamental tool used for large scale dataset preparation, and complemented with various community guides, scripts and UIs that cover smaller scale initiatives.

Our ambition is to make tooling for video generation datasets equally established, by creating open video dataset scripts suited for small scale, and leveraging video2dataset for large scale use cases.

“If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants”.

In this post, we provide an overview of the tooling we are developing to make it easy for the community to build their own datasets for fine-tuning video generation models. If you cannot wait to get started already, we welcome you to check out the codebase here.

Sources indicate that typically, video generation is conditioned on natural language text prompts such as: "A cat walks on the grass, realistic style". Then in a video, there are a number of qualitative aspects for controllability and filtering, like so:.

According to recent reports, video generation models are only as good as the data they are trained on. Therefore, these aspects become crucial when curating the datasets for training/fine-tuning.

Our 3 stage pipeline draws inspiration from works like Stable Video Diffusion, LTX-Video, and their data pipelines.

Like video2dataset we opt to use yt-dlp for downloading videos.

We create a script Video to Scenes to split long videos into short clips.

Recent findings suggest that florence-2 microsoft/Florence-2-large to run Florence-2 tasks , , and on extracted frames. This provides different captions, object recognition and OCR that can be used for filtering in various ways.

We can bring in any other captioner in this regard. We can also caption the entire video (e.g., with a model like Qwen2.5) as opposed to captioning individual frames.

In the dataset for the model finetrainers/crush-smol-v0, we opted for captions from Qwen2VL and we filtered on pwatermark < 0.1 and aesthetic > 5.5. This highly restrictive filtering resulted in 47 videos out of 1493 total.

Let's review the example frames from pwatermark -.

Two with text have scores of 0.69 and 0.61.

The "toy car with a bunch of mice in it" scores 0.60 then 0.17 as the toy car is crushed.

Industry observers note that all example frames were filtered by pwatermark < 0.1. pwatermark is effective at detecting text/watermarks however the score gives no indication whether it is a text overlay or a toy car's license plate. Our filtering required all scores to be below the threshold, an average across frames would be a more effective strategy for pwatermark with a threshold of around 0.2 - 0.3.

Let's review the example frames from aesthetic scores -.

The pink castle initially scores 5.5 then 4.44 as it is crushed.

The action figure scores lower at 4.99 dropping to 4.84 as it is crushed.

The shard of glass scores low at 4.04.

In our filtering we required all scores to be below the threshold, in this case using the aesthetic score from the first frame only would be a more effective strategy.

It has been revealed that if we review finetrainers/crush-smol we can notice that many of the objects being crushed are round or rectangular and colorful which is similar to our findings in the example frames. Aesthetic scores can be useful yet have a bias that will potentially filter out good data when used with extreme thresholds like > 5.5. It may be more effective as a filter for bad content than good with a minimum threshold of around 4.25 - 4.5.

Here we provide some visual examples for each filter as well as the captions from Florence-2.

We have created various datasets with the tooling in an attempt to generate cool video effects, similar to the Pika Effects:.

Sources indicate that we then used these datasets to fine-tune the CogVideoX-5B model using finetrainers. Below is an example output from finetrainers/crush-smol-v0:.

According to recent reports, we hope this tooling gives you a headstart to create small and high-quality video datasets for your own custom applications. We will continue to add more useful filters to the repository, so, please keep an eye out. Your contributions are also more than welcome 🤗.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones.
  • Another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones.
  • Recent findings suggest that “After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year,” states Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA travel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that another Thanksgiving week is upon us, which means tens of millions of Americans will once again travel by plane, train, and automobile to see their loved ones. However, this Thanksgiving period will be a little different than in recent years—at least when it comes to transportation. That’s because the American Automobile Association (AAA) indicates that, for the first time in several years, fewer Americans will be traveling. “After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year,” says Stacey Barber, vice president of AAA travel. “But travelers won’t notice much of a difference on the roads and at the airports, since projected volumes remain near record levels.”  That means that despite fewer travelers, the roads are still expected to be packed at times. With that in mind, here are the best and worst times to travel by car over the 2026 Thanksgiving period. Best times to hit the roads for the Thanksgiving travel period For the 2026 Thanksgiving period, AAA expects 72.9 million people to travel to their holiday destinations by car. That’s down from last year’s 73.1 million automobile travelers, but still a significant amount. AAA defines the 2026 Thanksgiving period as the seven days lasting from Tuesday, November 24 to Monday, November 30, 2026. But despite the expected 72.9 million road travelers, how congested the streets will be depends heavily on when you travel during the period. AAA says these are the best times to be on the road (ie: the times with the expected lowest congestion) over the period, according to transportation data and insights provider INRIX data compiled by the auto organization: Tuesday, November 24: Before 1:00 PM Wednesday, November 25: Before 12:00 PM  Thursday, November 26 (Thanksgiving): Minimal Traffic Impact Expected  Friday, November 27: Before 12:00 PM  Saturday, November 28: Before 11:00 AM  Sunday, November 29: Before 11:00 AM  Monday, November 30: Before 1:00 PM  Worst times to hit the roads for the Thanksgiving travel period INRIX data indicates that the worst days to travel over the Thanksgiving period—that is, the days the congestion is expected to be the highest—are the Tuesday and Wednesday before Thanksgiving, and the Sunday and Monday after. Those are the days when most people choose to travel to and from their holiday destinations. As for the individual times that are expected to be the worst to travel by car, those are: Tuesday, November 24: 2:00 PM to 8:00 PM  Wednesday, November 25: 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM  Thursday, November 26 (Thanksgiving): Minimal Traffic Impact Expected  Friday, November 27: 1:00 PM to 7:00 PM  Saturday, November 28: 12:00 PM to 9:00 PM  Sunday, November 29: 12:00 PM to 8:00 PM  Monday, November 30: 2:00 PM to 7:00 PM  Fewer total travelers are expected over the Thanksgiving 2026 period When combining all modes of transportation—auto, air, and “other,” which includes bus, boat, and train—AAA says 81.48 million people in America are expected to travel over the 2026 Thanksgiving period. That’s about 121,000 fewer than the 81.61 million who traveled during the 2025 Thanksgiving period. Still, 2026’s expected numbers far surpass the 77.78 million people who traveled in 2019, the last year before the pandemic. The expected decline in travelers this year is mainly due to higher travel costs, especially gas prices, AAA says. Besides a decline of about 200,000 car travelers, AAA says there will also be a drop in air travelers by about 0.2% to 5.96 million (versus 5.97 million in 2025). However, more people will travel by “other” modes during this period than last year. “Other” includes travel by bus, train, and cruise. In the 2026 Thanksgiving period, the other travel segment is expected to reach 2.6 million travelers—up 4.1% from 2.49 million in 2025.

#150738. From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub

📅 12 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1543 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub

📅 12 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Content-defined chunking (CDC) plays a central role in enabling deduplication within a Xet-backed repository.
  • Sources indicate that in practice, it's more complex.
  • On Hugging Face's Xet team, we're bringing CDC from theory to production to deliver faster uploads and downloads to AI builders (by a factor of 2-3x in some cases).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content-defined chunking (CDC) plays a central role in enabling deduplication within a Xet-backed repository. The idea is straightforward: break each file’s data into chunks, store only unique ones, reap the benefits.

Sources indicate that in practice, it's more complex. If we focused solely on maximizing deduplication, the design would call for the smallest possible chunk size. By doing that, we’d create significant overheads for the infrastructure and the builders on the Hub.

On Hugging Face's Xet team, we're bringing CDC from theory to production to deliver faster uploads and downloads to AI builders (by a factor of 2-3x in some cases). Our guiding principle is simple: enable rapid experimentation and collaboration for teams building and iterating on models and datasets. This means focusing on more than just deduplication; we’re optimizing how data moves across the network, how it’s stored, and the entire development experience.

It has been revealed that imagine uploading a 200GB repository to the Hub. Today, there are a number of ways to do this, but all use a file-centric approach. To bring faster file transfers to the Hub, we've open-sourced xet-core and hf_xet, an integration with huggingface_hub which uses a chunk-based approach written in Rust.

If you consider a 200GB repository with unique chunks, that's 3 million entries (at ~64KB per chunk) in the content-addressed store (CAS) backing all repositories. If a latest version of a model is uploaded or a branch in the repository is created with different data, more unique chunks are added, driving up the entries in the CAS.

With nearly 45PB across 2 million model, dataset, and space repositories on the Hub, a purely chunk-based approach could incur 690 billion chunks. Managing this volume of content using only chunks is simply not viable due to:.

In short, network requests balloon, databases struggle to manage the metadata, and the cost of orchestrating each chunk skyrockets all while you wait for your files to transfer.

These challenges lead to a key realization:.

Deduplication is a performance optimization, not the final goal.

According to recent reports, the final goal is to improve the experience of builders iterating and collaborating on models and datasets. The system components from the client to the storage layer do not need to guarantee deduplication. Instead, they leverage deduplication as one tool among many to aid in this.

By loosening the deduplication constraint, we naturally arrive at a second design principle:.

Avoid communication or storage strategies that scale 1:1 with the number of chunks.

What does this mean? We scale with aggregation.

Aggregation takes chunks and groups them, referencing them intelligently in ways that provide clever (and practical) benefits:.

It has been revealed that together, blocks and shards unlock significant benefits. However, when someone uploads a fresh file, how do we know if a chunk has been uploaded before so we can eliminate an unnecessary request? Performing a network query for every chunk is not scalable and goes against the “no 1:1” principle we mentioned above.

The solution is key chunks which are a 0.1% subset of all chunks selected with a simple modulo condition based on the chunk hash. We provide a global index over these key chunks and the shards they are found in, so that when the chunk is queried, the related shard is returned to provide local deduplication. This allows us to leverage the principles of spatial locality. If a key chunk is referenced in a shard, it’s likely that other similar chunk references are available in the same shard. This further improves deduplication and reduces network and database requests.

The Hub presently stores over 3.5PB of .gguf files, most of which are quantized versions of other models on the Hub. Quantized models represent an interesting opportunity for deduplication due to the nature of quantization where values are restricted to a smaller integer range and scaled. This restricts the range of values in the weight matrices, naturally leading to more repetition. Additionally, many repositories of quantized models store multiple different variants (e.g., Q4_K, Q3_K, Q5_K) with a great deal of overlap.

A good example of this in practice is bartowski/gemma-2-9b-it-GGUF which contains 29 quantizations of google/gemma-2-9b-it totalling 191GB. To upload, we use hf_xet integrated with huggingface_hub to perform chunk-level deduplication locally then aggregate and store data at the block level.

Once uploaded, we can start to see some cool patterns! We’ve included a visualization that indicates the deduplication ratio for each block. The darker the block, the more frequently parts of it are referenced across model versions. If you go to the Space hosting this visualization, hovering over any heatmap cell highlights all references to the block in orange across all models while clicking on a cell will select all other files that share blocks:.

A single block of deduplication might only represent a few MB of savings, but as you can see there are many overlapping blocks! With this many blocks that quickly adds up. Instead of uploading 191GB, the Xet-backed version of the gemma-2-9b-it-GGUF repository stores 1515 unique blocks for a total of approximately 97GB to our test CAS environment (a savings of ~94GB).

It has been revealed that while the storage improvements are significant, the real benefit is what this means for contributors to the Hub. At 50MB/s, the deduplication optimizations amount to a four hour difference in upload time; a speedup of nearly 2x:.

In a recent development, similarly, local chunk caching significantly speeds up downloads. If a file is changed or a newly introduced quantization is added that has significant overlap with the local chunk cache, you won’t have to re-download any chunks that are unchanged. This contrasts to the file-based approach where the entirety of the new or updated file must be downloaded.

Taken together, this demonstrates how local chunk-level deduplication paired with block-level aggregation dramatically streamlines not just storage, but developing on the Hub. By providing this level of efficiency in file transfers, AI builders can move faster, iterate quickly, and worry less about hitting infrastructure bottlenecks. For anyone pushing large files to the Hub (whether you're pushing a new model quantization or an updated version of a training set) this helps you shift focus to building and sharing, rather than waiting and troubleshooting.

Industry observers note that we’re fast at work, rolling out the first Xet-backed repositories in the coming weeks and months! As we do that, we will be releasing more updates to bring these speeds to every builder on the Hub to make file transfers feel invisible.

Follow us on the Hub to learn more about our progress!

How can we find the chunk content using chunk hash?

Sources indicate that chunk hash is calculated via content-defined chunking (CDC), which means that if two chunks have the same content they will share the same hash. CDC removes the need to store the mapping between chunk hash -> chunk content because we know if two chunks share the same hash, they will have identical content.

The CAS system only stores "block_hash -> block_content", Where does the map of chunk to block?

It has been revealed that this is explained in the "key chunks" section in the blog post above. Essentially we only store a tiny subset of chunk -> block by leveraging spatial locality in the file. Trying to store every mapping of chunk -> block can get impractical very swiftly.

Sources indicate that what does the shards store? Is it "file_name, shard_id, chunk_hash, block_hash".

You can think of the shards as storing mappings between file (identified via file hash) to list of chunks that make up the file.

I hope this help explains our underlying tech better!

If we don't store every chunk hash to block hash, how can we download a model file. For example if a model does not have a key chunk, the shard info only contains "file hash -> list of chunks", the CAS only has "block hash -> block content", how can we know which block is needed ?

For example if a model does not have a key chunk.

Two points of clarification might be in order concerning the above point:.

If we don't store every chunk hash to block hash, how can we download a model file.

In a recent development, when downloading a model file, a request is made to our services with the file hash. This is mapped to a list of block subranges. Logically these are chunks, but by storing the offsets we save on the metadata storage and ultimately many offsets will share boundaries inside a block (allowing us to group them together in a response) providing benefits when sending the content back to the client.

Industry News: 6 tips to use this Thanksgiving when family asks about your career

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, evan Reece has a few strategies for handling unwelcome questions about his career when he gathers with family.
  • According to recent reports, evan Reece has a few strategies for handling unwelcome questions about his career when he gathers with family.
  • Industry observers note that have a short, confident response or two ready for the job-related queries you think might come up, remarked Melody Wilding, an executive coach and author of “Managing Up.”For example, if you’re unemployed, you could say, “I’m taking time to find the right fit and not rushing into something fresh.” Or if you’ve made an unconventional career move, say, “I know it’s not what everyone would choose, but I’m excited about it,” Wilding said.“Then redirect the conversation nicely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, evan Reece has a few strategies for handling unwelcome questions about his career when he gathers with family. He founded and ran a ski lift ticket platform for 15 years, but it went out of business during the COVID-19 pandemic. Reece then started a career management platform. He’s its sole employee and earns less than he did before.At family parties, he sometimes feels pressure to explain why he doesn’t get a full-time job working for someone else. When he’s asked such questions, he reminds himself that people usually ask because they care.“Oftentimes, if we’re stressed about something that we don’t have an answer to, the question feels like an interrogation, when that’s rarely the intention of the person asking the question,” mentioned Reece, 48, who runs the career management platform Truest.me.A simple “How’s your job going?” can feel like an ambush when you’re unemployed, underemployed or working in jobs your friends and relatives don’t understand or may regard as frivolous. These queries can bring up painful experiences like layoffs. Advice can sound like criticism to recent graduates in a seemingly impenetrable job market, while curiosity about someone’s income can feel like judgment.Even inquiries motivated by a genuine desire to connect can come across as invasive or awkward in a group setting.With holiday gatherings approaching, here are some tips and potential scripts to help you handle tricky career conversations with relatives and feel less defensive. The same strategies can be applied when faced with scrutiny about getting married or having children. Anticipate questions and strategy responses in advance Have a short, confident response or two ready for the job-related queries you think might come up, said Melody Wilding, an executive coach and author of “Managing Up.”For example, if you’re unemployed, you could say, “I’m taking time to find the right fit and not rushing into something newly introduced.” Or if you’ve made an unconventional career move, say, “I know it’s not what everyone would choose, but I’m excited about it,” Wilding said.“Then redirect the conversation nicely. You might say, ‘Tell me about you,’ or ‘I’d love to hear about your recent trip,'” she added. Be a boomerang when fielding questions Turning the inquiries around on the questioner can deflect attention and be entertaining.“If someone is willing to ask you a question that requires tremendous vulnerability out of you, then they should be willing to answer one too,” Reece said.When a relative asks if you’re “still job searching” or “Why did you leave a good job?” get curious before you get defensive, Wilding suggested. Instead of immediately responding to their question, try to understand the motivation behind it by countering, “Why do you ask?” or “What makes you say that?” Wilding said.“Maybe they’re just making conversation, which saves you from launching into a full defense of your choices,” she said. Turn it into a game If someone asks about an unstable job or recent layoff, you can say it’s been challenging and then suggest, “Let’s play a game. Everybody tell a story about the worst job they ever had,” Reece said. “Anybody who’s ever worked has a story. And they’re usually amazing.”For recent graduates or those who are trying to figure out what’s next, you could be honest about your uncertainty and reply, “Everybody go around and talk about a time in their career when they weren’t sure what to do next and what you did,” Reece suggested. Let others take the spotlight Hope Bond, 53, spent a decade working as an editor in the magazine industry. She left the field for a few years to raise her young children, then did some freelance editing jobs. When she sought to return to full-time work in 2020, she couldn’t find a position. Bond began working as a site manager for a movie production location in 2024.She loves the job, despite its erratic hours, instability and hourly pay. But at gatherings with her family of lawyers and bankers, she often felt singled out by probing questions about her work.After years of answering their questions, she now redirects them and encourages others to be the star of the conversation, especially her children.“I stay on the periphery. The younger generations are the ones who are bringing the great energy, so I like them to have the floor,” Bond said. “I don’t insert myself into conversation if we’re talking about career or money. Those are my two boundaries. Even with a family that is loving and supportive and wants the best for me, it is just awkward.” Share context about the job market When people feel scrutinized after layoffs or extended unemployment, Avigail Lev, a psychologist at the Bay Area CBT Center in San Francisco, suggests explaining to family members how the job market has changed and how artificial intelligence has impacted their fields.“The first thing you need to say is to speak to the context that things are different, and the decisions about work are very different right now,” Lev said.Many of Lev’s clients work in technology or at AI companies and worry about losing their jobs, while some have already been laid off, she said.“Some people are very depressed right now about not having work or not knowing what’s next. And having a relative blame you for something that’s not in your control is the last thing that you need right now,” Lev said. Choose what you reveal One way to avoid unnecessary judgment is to choose whom you share details about your professional life with.Rishabh Dutta, 25, of Mumbai, India, quit his marketing job for Bollywood movies after stress and long hours led to hair loss. For the next few months, “everyone was constantly asking me what I was doing, if I had found something else,” he said.The next time Dutta left a job, he kept it to himself for a few months. “I just decided not to tell them, and honestly I don’t regret it,” he said. Share your stories and questions about workplace wellness at cbussewitz@ap.org. Follow AP’s Be Well coverage, focusing on wellness, fitness, diet and mental health at https://apnews.com/hub/be-well. —Cathy Bussewitz, AP Business Writer.

This Fitbit Air app buzzes your wrist with phone notifications, finds a lost tracker, more

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The era of vibe-coding has been very swiftly bringing ideas to reality, and these new Fitbit Air notification apps are a great example.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Fitbit Air is a simple screenless fitness tracker, but it can do a bit more, and now someone has built an app that lets the Air buzz your wrist when phone notifications come through.

The era of vibe-coding has been very swiftly bringing ideas to reality, and these new Fitbit Air notification apps are a great example.

According to recent reports, “Air Relay” is the result of a developer managing to reverse-engineer a way to control haptics on the Fitbit Air via Bluetooth without affecting Google Health sync. “Cuff” uses the same method while also showing health stats if you don’t want to use Google Health.

The idea here is pretty simple. You can have apps on your phone ping your Fitbit Air as you choose. “Air Relay” lets you pick select apps and even change the vibration pattern or strength based on the app. You can set “Quiet hours” to prevent notifications while you’re sleeping, and there’s a WhatsApp-specific setting that lets you only get notifications from specific groups or people. A “Find My Air” setting uses Bluetooth strength you help you track down a lost tracker.

While a big part of the appeal of Fitbit Air is its screenless, disconnected nature, having the option to set up alerts for key apps or contacts is certainly a useful option.

“Air Relay” is free on Google Play, and Fitbit Air is available for $99.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the manufacturer’s board is joining him at the center of scrutiny.The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia’s president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” President Donald Trump noted he believes his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement.Just six days earlier, the board was singing a different tune.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the manufacturer’s board is joining him at the center of scrutiny.The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia’s president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” President Donald Trump noted he believes his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement.Just six days earlier, the board was singing a different tune. Board members had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation following his admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board did not intend to reinstate him, Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of a quarterly earnings call.“To bow to pressure to bring someone back who has hurt the reputation of the company is crazy,” said Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.The board’s stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump’s role means for the meeting of business and politics. Concerns swirl about corporate governance and Trump’s intervention Nvidia’s board includes both business leaders with longstanding ties to the company and a group of more recent additions who have experience at significant-name companies including Taco Bell, PepsiCo and Eli Lilly.Some experts have called for the board to resign in the wake of the havoc.Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasized that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.“The shareholders should demand a upcoming board,” she said.Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.“Traditionally, it’s a good practice” to limit how long people can sit on a board, said Nada Kakabadse, professor of policy, governance and ethics at the University of Reading’s Henley Business School. “They should be eight years maximum. Four years, plus another four years if they’re performing well. But beyond that, they really become not independent anymore, right?”It’s not unusual for U.S. tech bosses to stuff their boards with allies or high-profile figures who might not be aware of what’s happening at the company, Kakabadse said.American business has a culture of “leader heroes” — entrepreneurs who founded companies and are seen as the only ones who can steer them through tough times, she said. But at some point, the companies can get so big that “you need proper corporate structure, you need proper governance.”Many people are also questioning what “input” the company received from senior government leaders and why it persuaded the board to make a complete turnaround.“The board should have listened to the president’s request and stuck to its position that it was time to find a new CEO,” said Peter Cohan, an associate professor of management practice at Babson College. “In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company. That’s because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it.”The idea of an independent board of experts looking out for the long-term interests of the company and its shareholders “sort of goes out the window” if the sitting president “essentially tells them what to do,” said Daniel Kinderman, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Delaware.“This is really the mark of crony capitalism, right?” he said.Kinderman said the episode might “open the door a little bit more for more aggressive actions on behalf of elected representatives” in their relationships with businesses. Lawmakers call for accountability from the board The Nvidia saga has made waves in Washington, particularly in conversations around export controls. Huang’s affair raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with those restrictions. The reinstatement has renewed fervor on Capitol Hill for more transparency from both Huang and the board.Elected officials from both parties were quick to respond to the reinstatement with criticism and skepticism.Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, said the decision to bring Huang back was “reckless.” She wrote in a statement Monday that it does not change the fact that Huang, Nvidia executives and the company’s board “still owe Congress answers.”Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, called for both Huang and the board to testify publicly to Congress. “A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk,” she said in a statement Monday.California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is investigating Nvidia in connection with Huang’s affair, said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that the president’s intervention “does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favor.”The California Department of Justice said Thursday that it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public. Some members joined the Nvidia board in the 1990s Two board members, Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, joined the board in 1993 when Nvidia was founded. Stevens and Coxe were both previously venture capitalists who made early investments in Nvidia.Two other long-serving board members, Jones and Brooke Seawell, are the former chief executive and chief financial officer, respectively, of Synopsys, which makes chip-design software and counted Nvidia as its first customer. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, while Seawell joined four years later.Stephen Neal, who’s designated as the board’s “lead independent director,” joined in 2019. He’s the chairman emeritus of Cooley LLP, Nvidia’s longtime law firm, and has advised the company in “various governance matters,” according to his bio.Other board members have less of a direct link to Nvidia.Melissa Lora, former president of Taco Bell International, spent 31 years at the fast food company and joined Nvidia’s board in 2023. Aarti Shah, formerly a senior vice president and chief digital officer at pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, joined in 2020.John Dabiri, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology whose lab researches fluid mechanics, was added to the board in 2020. Dawn Hudson was the NFL’s chief marketing officer and a former CEO of Pepsi-Cola’s North American division who’s been on the board since 2013. Suzanne Nora Johnson was a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs who joined the board in July.None of the board members provided comment in response to requests from The Associated Press. This story corrects that Shah joined the Nvidia board in 2020, not 2021. —Kaitlyn Huamani and Kelvin Chan, Associated Press.

Jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the organization’s board is joining him at the center of scrutiny.The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia’s president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” President Donald Trump remarked he believes his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement.Just six days earlier, the board was singing a different tune. Board members had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation following his admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board did not intend to reinstate him, Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of a quarterly earnings call.“To bow to pressure to bring someone back who has hurt the reputation of the company is crazy,” said Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.The board’s stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump’s role means for the meeting of business and politics.

Nvidia’s board includes both business leaders with longstanding ties to the manufacturer and a group of more recent additions who have experience at massive-name companies including Taco Bell, PepsiCo and Eli Lilly.Some experts have called for the board to resign in the wake of the havoc.Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasized that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.“The shareholders should demand a new board,” she said.Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.“Traditionally, it’s a good practice” to limit how long people can sit on a board, said Nada Kakabadse, professor of policy, governance and ethics at the University of Reading’s Henley Business School. “They should be eight years maximum. Four years, plus another four years if they’re performing well. But beyond that, they really become not independent anymore, right?”It’s not unusual for U.S. tech bosses to stuff their boards with allies or high-profile figures who might not be aware of what’s happening at the company, Kakabadse said.American business has a culture of “leader heroes” — entrepreneurs who founded companies and are seen as the only ones who can steer them through tough times, she said. But at some point, the companies can get so big that “you need proper corporate structure, you need proper governance.”Many people are also questioning what “input” the company received from senior government leaders and why it persuaded the board to make a complete turnaround.“The board should have listened to the president’s request and stuck to its position that it was time to find a new CEO,” said Peter Cohan, an associate professor of management practice at Babson College. “In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company. That’s because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it.”The idea of an independent board of experts looking out for the long-term interests of the company and its shareholders “sort of goes out the window” if the sitting president “essentially tells them what to do,” said Daniel Kinderman, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Delaware.“This is really the mark of crony capitalism, right?” he said.Kinderman said the episode might “open the door a little bit more for more aggressive actions on behalf of elected representatives” in their relationships with businesses.

Recent findings suggest that the Nvidia saga has made waves in Washington, particularly in conversations around export controls. Huang’s affair raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with those restrictions. The reinstatement has renewed fervor on Capitol Hill for more transparency from both Huang and the board.Elected officials from both parties were quick to respond to the reinstatement with criticism and skepticism.Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, said the decision to bring Huang back was “reckless.” She wrote in a statement Monday that it does not change the fact that Huang, Nvidia executives and the firm’s board “still owe Congress answers.”Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a Fresh York Democrat, called for both Huang and the board to testify publicly to Congress. “A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk,” she said in a statement Monday.California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is investigating Nvidia in connection with Huang’s affair, said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that the president’s intervention “does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favor.”The California Department of Justice said Thursday that it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public.

Two board members, Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, joined the board in 1993 when Nvidia was founded. Stevens and Coxe were both previously venture capitalists who made early investments in Nvidia.Two other long-serving board members, Jones and Brooke Seawell, are the former chief executive and chief financial officer, respectively, of Synopsys, which makes chip-design software and counted Nvidia as its first customer. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, while Seawell joined four years later.Stephen Neal, who’s designated as the board’s “lead independent director,” joined in 2019. He’s the chairman emeritus of Cooley LLP, Nvidia’s longtime law firm, and has advised the company in “various governance matters,” according to his bio.Other board members have less of a direct link to Nvidia.Melissa Lora, former president of Taco Bell International, spent 31 years at the fast food company and joined Nvidia’s board in 2023. Aarti Shah, formerly a senior vice president and chief digital officer at pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, joined in 2020.John Dabiri, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology whose lab researches fluid mechanics, was added to the board in 2020. Dawn Hudson was the NFL’s chief marketing officer and a former CEO of Pepsi-Cola’s North American division who’s been on the board since 2013. Suzanne Nora Johnson was a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs who joined the board in July.None of the board members provided comment in response to requests from The Associated Press.

This story corrects that Shah joined the Nvidia board in 2020, not 2021.

—Kaitlyn Huamani and Kelvin Chan, Associated Press.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you’ve optimized your model. Your pipeline is running smoothly. But now, your cloud bill has skyrocketed. Running 1B+ classifications or embeddings per day isn’t just a technical challenge—it’s a financial one. How do you process at this scale without blowing your budget? Whether you're running large-scale document classification or bulk embedding pipelines for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), you need cost-efficient, high-throughput inference to make it feasible, and you get that from having a well optimized configuration.

Recent findings suggest that these tasks often use encoder models, which are much smaller than modern LLMs, but at the 1B+ inference request scale it's still quite a non-trivial task. Just to be clear, that's English Wikipedia 144x over. I haven’t seen much information on how to approach this with cost in mind and I want to tackle that. This blog breaks down HOW to calculate cost and latency for large scale classification and embedding. We’ll analyze different model architectures, benchmark costs across hardware choices, and give you a clear framework for optimizing your own setup. Additionally we should be able to build some intuition if you don't feel like going through the process yourself.

You might have a couple questions:.

Here is the code to make it happen: https://github.com/datavistics/encoder-analysis.

To evaluate cost and latency we need 4 key components:.

I’ll be leveraging Inference Endpoints for my Hardware Options, as it allows me to choose from a wide range of hardware choices. Do note you can replace that with your GPUs of choice/consideration. For the Deployment Facilitator I'll be using the ever so useful Hugging Face Hub Library which allows me to programmatically deploy models easily.

According to recent reports, for the Inference Server I’ll also be using Infinity which is an amazing library for serving encoder based models (and more now!). I’ve already written about TEI, which is another amazing library. You should definitely consider TEI when approaching your use-case, though this blog focuses on methodology rather than framework comparisons. Infinity has a number of key strengths, like serving multimodal embeddings, targeting different hardware (AMD, Nvidia, CPU and Inferentia) and running any latest models that contain remote code that have not been integrated into huggingface’s transformer library. The most notable of these to me is that most models are compatible by default.

For Load Testing I'll be using k6 from Grafana which is an open-source load testing tool written in go with a javascript interface. It’s easily configurable, has high performance, and has low overhead. It has a lot of built-in executors that are super useful. It also pre-allocates Virtual Users (VUs), which can be much more realistic than throwing some testing together yourself.

I'll go through 3 use-cases that should cover a variety of interesting points:.

Optimization is a tricky glitch, as there is a lot to consider. At a high level, I want to sweep across notable load testing parameters and find what works best for a single GPU, as most encoder models will fit in a single GPU. Once we have a baseline of cost for a single GPU, the number of GPUs and throughput can be scaled horizontally by increasing the number of replica GPUs.

For each use-case this is the high-level flow I’ll use:.

Since you have the code, feel free to adjust any part of this to your:.

Sources indicate that VUs and Batch Size are important because these influence how well we take advantage of all the compute available in the GPU. A large enough Batch Size makes sure we are fully utilizing the Streaming Multiprocessors and VRAM. There are scenarios where we have VRAM left over but there is a bandwidth cost that prevents throughput from increasing. So experimentation can help us. VUs allow us to make sure we are fully utilizing the batch size we have available.These are the main parameters I'll be testing:.

According to recent reports, K6 is great because it allows you to pre-allocate VUs and prevent some insidious bugs. It's quite flexible in how you are sending requests. I decided to use it in a specific way.

In a recent development, when I'm calling a k6 experiment, I mainly want to know what the throughput and average latency is for the requests, and have a few sanity checks for the load testing parameters I have chosen. I also want to do a sweep which means many experiments.

It has been revealed that I use the shared-iterations executor (docs) which means K6 shares iterations between the number of VUs. The test ends once k6 executes all iterations. This allows me to have a reasonable time-out, but also put through enough requests to have a decent confidence that I can discriminate between load testing parameters choices in my sweep. In contrast to other executors, this allows me to be confident that I'm simulating the client working as hard as possible per VU which should show me what the cheapest option is.

It has been revealed that I use 10_000 requests† and have a max experiment time of 1 min. So if 10_000 requests aren’t finished by 1 minute, then that experiment is over.

† I use less max requests for the Vision Embeddings given that the throughput is much lower and images are heavy.†† P95 means that 95% of requests complete within this time. It represents the worst-case latency for most users.

It has been revealed that text Embeddings are a loose way of describing the task of taking a text input and projecting it into a semantic space where close points are similar in meaning and distant ones are dissimilar (example below). This is used heavily in RAG and is an notable part of AI search (which some are fans of).

There are a large number of architectures which are compatible, and you can see the most performant ones in the MTEB Leaderboard.

ModernBERT is the most exciting encoder release since DeBERTa back in 2020. It has all the ahem modern tricks built into an old and familiar architecture. It makes for an attractive model to experiment with as it's much less explored than other architectures and has a lot more potential. There are a number of improvements in speed and performance, but the most notable for a user is likely the 8k context window. Do check out this blog for a more thorough understanding.
