It has been revealed that pose detection in the browser is a solved problem. You can load a model, point it at a webcam, and get a skeleton tracking a human body in real time, on a laptop, with no server involved.

And then you have a skeleton that follows someone around the screen, which is a toy.

The gap between that toy and a feature someone would pay for is smaller than most developers expect, and it isn't made of machine learning. It's made of trigonometry you already know. This article builds a working bicep-curl rep counter to show exactly where that line falls — and more importantly, which side of it your bugs live on.

I'm using MediaPipe Pose Landmarker from Google AI Edge, which is Apache-2.0 licensed and runs entirely in the tab. Here's the whole setup:.

In a recent development, point that at a element carrying a camera stream and call detectForVideo. What comes back, per frame, is this:.

Thirty-three points. Each one is a normalised coordinate — x and y run 0 to 1 across the frame, z is a relative depth estimate — plus a visibility score saying how confident the model is that it can actually see that joint.

That's the entire output. Coordinates and confidences.

The model has no concept of exercise. It doesn't know what an arm is for. It has never heard of a bicep curl. It reports where it thinks your joints are, thirty-odd times a second, and stops.

Everything that turns that into a product is yours, and it's ordinary code.

A bicep curl is a change in the angle at the elbow. The elbow angle is defined by three of those 33 points: shoulder, elbow, wrist. In MediaPipe's pose topology those are indices 11, 13 and 15 on the left side, 12, 14 and 16 on the right.

Getting the angle is two vectors and a dot product:.

This is the same maths you'd use to point a game character in a direction. Nothing about it is machine learning, and that matters for a reason I'll come back to.

Recent findings suggest that one thing to notice: I'm ignoring z entirely. The depth estimate is relative, not metric — it's good enough for working out which parts of a body are nearer the camera, and not good enough to measure anything. For a 2D elbow angle, using it adds noise and buys nothing.

Here's where almost everyone's first attempt breaks.

The naive version looks at the angle and counts whenever the arm is up:.

Sources indicate that run that at 30 frames a second and one slow curl gives you about twenty reps. You haven't counted repetitions. You've counted frames in which the arm happened to be bent.

Recent findings suggest that A rep isn't a state. It's a transition between states:.

Fifteen lines, and that's the feature. The counter increments exactly once per cycle, on the edge, because the guard on phase makes every other frame in that cycle a no-op.

If you used a single threshold — say, 100 degrees — you'd get a counter that fires repeatedly whenever someone holds their arm near 100 degrees and the estimate jitters by a degree either side. Every tiny fluctuation across the line is a transition, and every transition is a rep.

Two widely separated thresholds give you hysteresis. Once the arm is "up," it has to travel all the way past 150 degrees before the counter will consider another rep. Noise of a few degrees can't produce a count because no amount of jitter near 55 crosses 150.

It has been revealed that this is the same trick a thermostat uses to avoid switching the heating on and off every few seconds, and it's the single most useful pattern in this whole category of work. Any time you turn a continuous signal into discrete events, you want two thresholds, not one.

visibility is the field people skip, and skipping it is how you get phantom reps.

Industry observers note that when a joint goes out of frame or gets occluded, the model still returns a coordinate for it. It is obliged to return 33 points. What it does is return a guess, with a low visibility score attached — and a guessed wrist position can swing wildly between frames, which looks exactly like a very fast curl.

Returning null and having patch bail out means an occluded frame holds the current state rather than corrupting it. The arm stays "up" until the model can actually see it come down.

In a recent development, if you want to be stricter, smooth the angle over the last three or four frames with a rolling median before it reaches the state machine. A median rejects single-frame outliers in a way a mean doesn't.

Once you've written one of these, you start recognising the shape everywhere:.

According to recent reports, none of those require a different model. They're the same 33 coordinates with different geometry sitting on top, and the geometry is a few dozen lines each.

Here's why I keep insisting on the distinction between coordinates and meaning.

Sources indicate that when my rep counter miscounts, I don't retrain anything. I don't collect a dataset, I don't label examples, I don't spin up a training job. I look at two things: my thresholds, and my state machine. One of them is wrong.

That's a normal bug in normal code, and you already know how to find it. You can log the angle. You can set a breakpoint on the transition. You can write a unit test that feeds a synthetic sequence of angles through revision and asserts the count — no camera, no model, no fixtures:.

The hard part of this problem — turning pixels into joint positions — was solved by a research team and shipped to you as a file you can download. The part that's left is the part you're already good at.

You are not blocked on machine learning knowledge. You were blocked on nobody telling you this was available.

I set delegate: 'GPU' above without comment, and it deserves one. MediaPipe Tasks lets you choose between a CPU path and a GPU path, and availability of the GPU path varies by browser, platform and graphics driver.

The practical consequence is that you have to test the CPU path, because for some meaningful share of your people it isn't a fallback — it's the only path they will ever take. If you develop on a machine where the GPU delegate works and never exercise the CPU one, you have shipped something you've never run.

Sources indicate that that, and the question of how often you should run the model at all, is a bigger subject than this article. It's the next one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, S&P Global Ratings, one of the world’s largest rating agencies, confirmed that it’s putting Nvidia’s credit rating on watch as the company faces a possible downgrade. The agency states that the challenges surrounding Jensen Huang regarding export control violations, as well as his resignation and subsequent reinstatement 11 days later, reveal the weakness of Nvidia’s management team and board oversight.

Sources indicate that “We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence,” the rating agency said in its press release. It also added, “Concerns related to Nvidia’s China exposure also raise questions regarding geopolitical risk management and internal controls. While Nvidia management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the ‘key man’ risk to the forefront. The departure, then reinstatement of the CEO, does not sufficiently answer our questions regarding board oversight of executive code of conduct.”.

According to recent reports, nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang resigned from the job on November 12, after multiple allegations of affairs, especially with Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, who’s also accused of enabling the smuggling of $7.5 billion worth of AI GPUs into China. Even though Huang left the company he founded in disgrace, he was reinstated to the position by the Nvidia board on November 23. This was a major surprise, especially as it had previously refused to bring him back due to the ongoing national security investigation into Jensen.

However, it seems that Nvidia’s board of directors has folded to the pressure, especially after President Donald Trump himself said that he talked to them directly, with the board saying that it “received input from senior levels of the United States” that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Despite those assurances, the Nvidia chief still faces multiple investigations, including an internal inquiry at Nvidia, a private meeting with the House of Representatives’ Select Committee on China, and a public testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee, among others.

Even though the AI chipmaker’s risk profile remains unchanged, S&P Global Ratings’ warning is a sign that the market is uneasy about the situation regarding stricter export controls and the allegations of chip diversion. The ratings agency remarked that the downgrade could happen in the next 90 days after it concludes its due diligence, although it expects any potential drop to “be limited to one notch, unless investigations or disclosures lead us to believe Nvidia’s reputation or future business prospects have been harmed.”.

Both pre-trained and instruction tuned models are released. Gemma-3-4B-IT beats Gemma-2-27B IT, while Gemma-3-27B-IT beats Gemini 1.5-Pro across benchmarks.

Industry observers note that gemma 3 is Google's latest iteration of open weight LLMs. It comes in four sizes, 1 billion, 4 billion, 12 billion, and 27 billion parameters with base (pre-trained) and instruction-tuned versions. Gemma 3 goes multimodal! The 4, 12, and 27 billion parameter models can process both images and text, while the 1B variant is text only.

According to recent reports, the input context window length has been increased from Gemma 2’s 8k to 32k for the 1B variants, and 128k for all others. As is the case with other VLMs (vision-language models), Gemma 3 generates text in response to the user inputs, which may consist of text and, optionally, images. Example uses include question answering, analyzing image content, summarizing documents, etc.

It has been revealed that while these are multimodal models, one can use it as a text only model (as an LLM) without loading the vision encoder in memory. We will talk about this in more detail later in the inference section.

The three core enhancements in Gemma 3 over Gemma 2 are:.

In this section, we will cover the technical details that lead to these enhancements. It is interesting to start with the knowledge of Gemma 2 and explore what was necessary to make these models even better. This exercise will help you think like the Gemma team and appreciate the details!

Scaling context length to 128k tokens could be achieved efficiently without training models from scratch. Instead, models are pretrained with 32k sequences, and only the 4B, 12B, and 27B models are scaled to 128k tokens at the end of pretraining, saving significant compute. Positional embeddings, like RoPE, are adjusted—upgraded from a 10k base frequency in Gemma 2 to 1M in Gemma 3—and scaled by a factor of 8 for longer contexts.

Recent findings suggest that KV Cache management is optimized using Gemma 2’s sliding window interleaved attention. Hyperparameters are tuned to interleave 5 local layers with 1 global layer (previously 1:1) and reduce the window size to 1024 tokens (down from 4096). Crucially, memory savings are achieved without degrading perplexity.

Sources indicate that gemma 3 models use SigLIP as an image encoder, which encodes images into tokens that are ingested into the language model. The vision encoder takes as input square images resized to 896x896. Fixed input resolution makes it more difficult to process non-square aspect ratios and high-resolution images. To address these limitations during inference, the images can be adaptively cropped, and each crop is then resized to 896x896 and encoded by the image encoder. This algorithm, called pan and scan, effectively enables the model to zoom in on smaller details in the image.

Recent findings suggest that similar to PaliGemma, attention in Gemma 3 works differently for text and image inputs. Text is handled with one-way attention, where the model focuses only on previous words in a sequence. Images, on the other hand, get full attention with no masks, allowing the model to look at every part of the image in a bidirectional manner, giving it a complete, unrestricted understanding of the visual input.

One can see in the figure below that the image tokens are provided with bi-directional attention (the entire square is lit up) while the text tokens have causal attention. It also shows how attention works with the sliding window algorithm.

To make a LLM multilingual, the pretraining dataset incorporates more languages. The dataset of Gemma 3 has double the amount of multilingual data to improve language coverage.

To account for the changes, the tokenizer is the same as that of Gemini 2.0. It is a SentencePiece tokenizer with 262K entries. The new tokenizer significantly improves the encoding of Chinese, Japanese and Korean text, at the expense of a slight increase of the token counts for English and Code.

For the curious mind, here is the technical report on Gemma 3, to dive deep into the enhancements.

The LMSys Elo score is a number that ranks language models based on how well they perform in head-to-head competitions, judged by human preferences. On LMSys Chatbot Arena, Gemma 3 27B IT reports an Elo score of 1339, and ranks among the top 10 best models, including leading closed ones. The Elo is comparable to o1-preview and is above other non-thinking open models. This score is achieved with Gemma 3 working on text-only inputs, like the other LLMs in the table.

Industry observers note that gemma 3 has been evaluated across benchmarks like MMLU-Pro (27B: 67.5), LiveCodeBench (27B: 29.7), and Bird-SQL (27B: 54.4), showing competitive performance compared to closed Gemini models. Tests like GPQA Diamond (27B: 42.4) and MATH (27B: 69.0) highlight its reasoning and math skills, while FACTS Grounding (27B: 74.9) and MMMU (27B: 64.9) demonstrate strong factual accuracy and multimodal abilities. However, it lags in SimpleQA (27B: 10.0) for basic facts. When compared to Gemini 1.5 models, Gemma 3 is often close—and sometimes better—proving its value as an accessible, high-performing option.

How to Build Conference Talk Slides With AI Without Looking Generic

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that weekly.
  • Conference talks fail on slides more often than on content.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Industry observers note that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Conference talks fail on slides more often than on content. The speaker knows the material and has something worth saying, but the deck is a wall of bullets, or a template everyone in the room has seen before, or forty slides for a twenty-minute slot. AI presentation makers can now produce a complete deck from an outline in minutes, which solves the time problem and creates a new one: the output tends toward exactly the uniform, stock-image, bullet-heavy style that audiences have learned to tune out.

This article explains how conference slides differ from other decks, why AI-generated decks look generic and what specifically causes it, a workflow that uses an AI presentation maker for speed while keeping the talk distinctive, how to handle the slide types that matter most in a talk (the opening, the demonstration, the data, the close), and a checklist to run before the talk.

A conference talk is spoken, timed and performed to a room. That changes the rules compared with a reading deck or a business presentation.

The causes are specific and therefore fixable.

Sources indicate that template uniformity. Every slide uses the same layout family, so the deck has no visual rhythm. Audiences read the sameness as mass-produced.

In a recent development, bullet default. Given a paragraph, the tool produces three to five bullets. Given twenty paragraphs, twenty bullet slides.

Stock imagery. Icons and photos chosen by keyword match the topic superficially and add no meaning. A talk about database indexing gets a picture of a filing cabinet.

Label titles. “Introduction”, “Background”, “Key Challenges”, “Conclusion”. Titles that name the category rather than make the point.

Sources indicate that flattened emphasis. The tool does not know which of your ideas is the one the audience should leave with, so every slide gets equal weight.

It has been revealed that no pacing. Every slide carries the same amount of content, so there is no build, no pause, no payoff.

Each of these is a default that can be overridden, either in how the input is prepared or in a short editing pass afterwards.

It has been revealed that step 1: Write the talk before the slides. Not a script necessarily, but the argument: what the audience knows at the start, what they know at the end, and the four to six moves that get them there. Write the one sentence you want them to repeat to a colleague afterwards. If this is not clear, no deck will fix it.

Step 2: Write the slide titles as the things you will say. Each title is a sentence, in your voice, that states the point of that moment in the talk. “Indexes make reads fast by making writes slower” is a title. “Index trade-offs” is not. Read the titles in order; they should be the talk in miniature.

According to recent reports, step 3: Mark the pacing. Next to each title, note whether the slide is a hold (a key point, stays up while you talk for a minute or more), a beat (a quick slide in a sequence), or a reveal (something shown, a demo, a result). This tells you where to put effort.

Step 4: Generate. Paste the titles with one or two sentences of content under each into an ai presentation maker. Ask for a slide count close to your title count. Pick the plainest theme available; distinctiveness will come from your content, not the template.

Step 5: Strip the bullets. On every hold slide, delete the bullets and leave the title, or the title plus one image or one number. On beat slides, keep at most one short line. The content that was in the bullets goes into speaker notes, which is where it belonged.

Step 6: Replace every stock image. Delete icons. Replace keyword-matched photos with your own material: a screenshot, a diagram you drew, a chart from your data, a photograph you took, a single large word. If a slide has no genuine visual, a title alone on a plain background is better than a filler image.

It has been revealed that step 7: Build the reveals by hand. Demos, before-and-after comparisons, the key chart. These are the slides the audience will remember, and they need more care than a generator can give. See the section below.

According to recent reports, step 8: Break the layout rhythm deliberately. Make the two or three most important slides look different: full-bleed image, a single enormous number, a black slide with one line of white text. Contrast is what makes a moment land.

Step 9: Rehearse with a timer. The slide count will be wrong in the first rehearsal. Cut, merge or split until the pacing matches the time.

The opening. Not a title slide with your name and a logo while you say hello. Open on something that earns attention: a surprising number, a question, a screenshot of the problem, a single provocative sentence. Your name and affiliation can come on slide two, or be said rather than shown.

In a recent development, the problem statement. One slide, one sentence, stays up while you explain why the audience should care. No bullets.

The demonstration. If the talk has a demo, record it. Live demos fail in rooms with unreliable connections and unfamiliar projectors. A recorded demo with the audio off, narrated live, gives the same effect with none of the risk. If you must go live, have the recording ready as a fallback.

Sources indicate that the data. One chart per slide, one message per chart, the message in the title. Strip gridlines, legends and secondary series. Highlight the one line or bar that matters in colour and grey out the rest. Label directly. Type large enough to read from the back.

Recent findings suggest that the “so what.” After the evidence, a slide that states what it means in one sentence. This is a hold slide; give it time.

In a recent development, the close. The one sentence you want them to repeat, alone on the final slide. Not “Thank you” or “Questions?”; those can be said. The last thing on screen while you take questions should be your point.

Because the slides are now sparse, two things need handling.

First, the speaker notes must carry what you intend to say, in cue form: the key phrases, the number you must not forget, the transition to the next slide. The generator will have put the stripped bullet content there; edit it into cues rather than prose.

Recent findings suggest that second, the shared deck. Attendees who download a sparse deck afterwards get little from it. Options: export with notes visible; publish a companion blog post or document; or build a second “reading” version with more text on each slide. Many speakers do the first and link to a post.

For a twenty-minute talk, fifteen to twenty-five slides is typical once hold and beat slides are counted. For a forty-five-minute talk, thirty to fifty. Build-up sequences of several quick beats inflate the count without inflating the time, which is fine. What is not fine is a deck of forty dense slides for twenty minutes; that is a talk that will run over and leave the audience behind.

In a recent development, rehearse at least twice with a timer, once alone and once with a listener. Cut the content you rush. Nobody has ever complained that a talk finished two minutes early.

Recent findings suggest that lightning talks (five to ten minutes). Five to eight slides, almost all holds. One idea, one piece of evidence, one takeaway. Cut everything else.

In a recent development, workshops and tutorials. More slides, more text, because attendees will refer back and follow along. The reading-deck rules apply more here; still, keep each step to one slide.

It has been revealed that panel contributions. Often no slides at all, or two or three for a specific point. Resist bringing a full deck.

It has been revealed that keynotes. Fewer slides, longer holds, more full-bleed images and single sentences. The speaker carries almost everything; the slides punctuate.

In a recent development, remote talks. The screen is small and the audience is distracted. Larger type still, more frequent slide changes to hold attention, and a recorded demo is essential because screen-sharing a live one adds another failure point.

According to recent reports, how much of the deck should the AI tool produce? The structural first draft: layouts, consistency, speaker notes populated. Expect to edit every slide and rebuild the key ones.

Is it acceptable to have slides with only a title? Yes, and it is often the strongest format for a spoken talk. The audience listens instead of reading.

Industry observers note that what about code on slides? Short excerpts only, in a large monospace type, with the relevant lines highlighted and the rest dimmed. Anything longer belongs in the companion post.

Should I use animations? Simple builds (revealing elements in sequence) help pacing. Transitions and effects distract. Keep to the former.

Breaking: Xet is on the Hub

📅 18 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Click here to read about joining the Xet waitlist (or head over to join immediately).
  • Over the past few weeks, Hugging Face’s Xet Team took a major step forward by migrating the first Model and Dataset repositories off LFS and to Xet storage.
  • This marks one of many steps to fulfill Hugging Face’s vision for the Hub by empowering AI builders to build, iterate, and collaborate more effectively on massive models and datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Click here to read about joining the Xet waitlist (or head over to join immediately).

Over the past few weeks, Hugging Face’s Xet Team took a major step forward by migrating the first Model and Dataset repositories off LFS and to Xet storage.

This marks one of many steps to fulfill Hugging Face’s vision for the Hub by empowering AI builders to build, iterate, and collaborate more effectively on massive models and datasets. If you're interested in deeper dives on the technology itself, check out the following posts:.

But this post isn't about the core technology. It's a behind-the-scenes view of getting Xet on the Hub; taking you through our proof-of-concept to the first migration of repositories.

The migration shifted ~6% of the Hub’s download traffic onto Xet infrastructure, validating several integral components and testing integrations with the myriad of ways repositories are accessed (e.g., via local development environments, different libraries, CI systems, cloud platforms, etc.). With nearly two million developers working on over two million public repositories, it’s real-world usage that’s the ultimate proving ground. Engineering a complex system like Xet storage is a balancing act. You strategy for scale, performance, and reliability, but once bytes start moving, challenges emerge. The trick is knowing when to move from design and theory to practice.

LFS, the storage system behind repositories today, stores large files in a separate object storage outside of the repository. LFS deduplicates at the file level. Even tiny edits create a newly introduced revision to upload in full; painful for the multi-gigabyte files found in many Hub repositories.

Recent findings suggest that in contrast, Xet storage uses content-defined chunking (CDC), to deduplicate at the level of bytes (~64KB chunks of data). If you edit one row in a Parquet file or tweak a small piece of metadata in a GGUF model, only those changed chunks are sent over the wire.

Recent findings suggest that this provides significant benefits to large file transfers. For example, the Xet team keeps an internal ~5 GB SQLite database that powers a metrics dashboard. With LFS, appending 1 MB (around the average enhancement currently) requires re-uploading the entire 5 GB file. With Xet storage, we push only the fresh data.

This means uploads for the dashboard take a tenth of a second (at 50Mb/s) instead of the 13 minutes if the database were backed by LFS.

Making this work requires coordination between the following components:.

Recent findings suggest that before moving to production, the system was rolled out into an ephemeral environment, where we built a steel thread of functionality to enable uploading and downloading via the huggingface_hub. The video below demonstrates our progress one month in:.

Sources indicate that after the heady highs of a quick proof-of-concept, the team settled into battling gnarly integration points (privacy, backward compatibility, fragmentation, etc) with the complex ecosystem that is the Hub. Eventually, the infrastructure moved into production for Hugging Face team members. With real usage now rolling in, we moved forward with the first large-scale migration.

It has been revealed that on February 20th at 10 a.m., it was all hands on deck. In the weeks prior the team had built the internal tooling to migrate files from LFS to Xet and, just as importantly, roll back a repository to LFS if necessary. Now it was time to put it to the test. Grafana and Kibana lit up with new logs and metrics, showing the load shift in real time.

The picture is the same in Kibana, only here you can tell when we took a lunch break:.

Sources indicate that by the end of the day, we had successfully migrated all target repositories for a total of 4.5 TB into Xet storage. Downloads from each repository were now served by our infrastructure.

Sources indicate that no launch is without its lessons. The system handled the load smoothly and migrations went off without any major disruptions, but as the bytes flowed through various components we began to see some trends.

Reviewing network throughput post-migration, we saw that CAS was downloading four times more data than it was returning to clients:.

Upon further investigation we found the vast majority of requests to CAS were for 10MB ranges of data within files. These requests come from users that are using hf_transfer to accelerate their downloads of large files. The requested ranges do not align on block boundaries and the block format doesn’t provide uncompressed chunk lengths to facilitate skipping directly to the data within the block. Instead, CAS streams the block starting at the beginning and reads until it finds the requested data.

According to recent reports, given a block with an average size of 60MB and multiple partial requests to ranges within that block, the overhead accumulates. CAS reads 210MB for just 60MB delivered, a ratio of 3.5 bytes downloaded : 1 byte sent to the client. At scale across blocks of irregular sizes and ranges that can span several blocks, the 4 bytes downloaded : 1 byte sent ratio is matched.

As usual, an image is worth a thousand words:.

To fix this, we updated the block format to store chunk-length metadata, enabling CAS to download only what each request actually needs. This format change required coordinated updates across:.

All of which were undertaken without downtime. Not only did this result in a balanced ratio in CAS downloads to returned data, but also reduced GET latency by ~35% across the board.

According to recent reports, at the same time, we also saw an unexpected load imbalance across our CAS cluster. One pod would spike to hundreds of active uploads while other pods chugged along at single digits. Swapping the load balancer’s routing algorithm (from round-robin to least outstanding requests) and adding more nodes made little difference in the moment.

It has been revealed that digging deeper we realized that during uploads, CAS writes to a temporary file for validation before uploading without calling fsync, allowing the OS to buffer writes in the page cache. When a spike of uploads comes in, the unflushed page cache leads to increased memory pressure.

As the OS tries to flush the page cache to disk, the pod experiences throughput throttling from block storage, causing increased latency on uploads. While uploads slowly process, latest requests continue to come in, pushing more to the disk. This creates a vicious cycle, leading to a backlog of uploads and the imbalance that we saw during the migration:.

To keep a pod from getting in this state, we put a limit to the number of concurrent uploads each machine accepts before rejecting requests that, when reached, pushes requests on to other pods in the cluster. If all pods in the cluster get in this state, then our autoscaling policies kick in. Longer-term solutions might include forcing disk syncs, removing the on-disk buffering, or switching to ephemeral storage with better throughput.

These two issues led to important architectural improvements, but they weren’t the only challenges the team tackled in the weeks following the migration. We also addressed other performance issues, a memory leak (which we fixed but still can't definitively root cause), and on advice from AWS to migrate the LFS Bridge from an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to a Network Load Balancer (NLB) to improve scalability during bursts of traffic.

According to recent reports, in short, real-world load was essential for exposing these challenges, and incremental migrations let us tackle them safely. That’s how we’re ensuring Xet-backed repositories scale reliably for the entire Hugging Face community with faster uploads, fewer bottlenecks, and minimal disruption all the way.

With the initial migration complete, Xet is now on the Hugging Face Hub.

We’re finalizing an official integration with the huggingface_hub that will mean you get the benefits of Xet without any significant changes to your current workflow. To get going:.

Sources indicate that if you have any questions, drop us a line in the comments 👇 or open a discussion on the Xet team page. And stay tuned as we roll out more pieces (faster web uploads, faster Git workflows), bringing faster substantial-file collaboration to every AI builder on Hugging Face!

While Nvidia is only allowed to sell its most advanced AI chips to whitelisted companies, it appears that two of its Californian customers are actually fronts for Chinese companies. Further, one of the Californian companies was renamed after its Chinese parent organization was blacklisted, CBS News reports. The other one, which is on Nvidia's list of "preferred partners," is owned by a Chinese firm whose CEO graduated from a Chinese military university. It's reported that U.S.-based, Chinese-owned companies have been used as a way to work around export controls designed to prevent Nvidia's chips from being sold wholesale to China. Chips are routinely sold to companies in the U.S. before being leased or shipped to other companies in Southeast Asia.

Recent findings suggest that while Nvidia isn't allowed to sell its most capable AI chips to China, it can still do business with the country. It can sell graphics cards for use in personal gaming PCs as well as AI chips that don't use the firm's latest, most capable technologies. But that hasn't stopped those chips from turning up in the most unlikely of places. Illegal Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs have been spotted in use inside China Telecom's network, and last year alone, it's believed that around $1 billion worth of Nvidia chips were smuggled into China. Earlier this year, nine people were indicted over the illegal export of Nvidia GPUs, while even older Nvidia hardware has seen huge price increases due to the unavailability of newer hardware.

It has been revealed that megaspeed is one firm that is accused of facilitating the breaking of export controls. The company is under criminal investigation right now, and it was recently blacklisted as a result. The company also happens to be a former employer of Alice Huang, the woman whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with when he resigned from the company earlier this month. Alice Huang is also believed to be a Chinese Spy, while her husband has even closer connections to a Chinese spy agency.

In a recent development, back in the U.S., RiCloud AI is an Nvidia customer owned by Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Limited, an outfit with headquarters in Shenzhen, China. Yuxing's CEO and co-owner, Cong Yu, reportedly has a degree in National Defense Mobilization from the People's Liberation Army Command College, a university operated by the Chinese military. Among RiCloud AI's customers is Agencia Comercial Spirits, a small whisky importer that pivoted to AI in 2025. Since then, it has committed to AI data center deals worth up to $598 million.

Industry observers note that airvres is presently listed as an "elite" partner on Nvidia's website, yet it was previously called Inspur, the same name used by its Chinese parent company. The name change came after Inspur-related firms were added to a federal blocklist in March 2023. Airvres reportedly exported at least $5.6 billion of chips to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February 2026, including Nvidia's top-of-the-line Blackwell silicon. The chips went to two companies in Malaysia, one of which was Alice Huang's Megaspeed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At its annual GTC conference, NVIDIA has unveiled a trio of groundbreaking open-source releases aimed at accelerating physical AI development. Release of a upcoming suite of world foundation models (WFMs) with multicontrols called Cosmos Transfer, a highly curated Physical AI Dataset, and the first open model for general humanoid reasoning called NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1 - represent a significant leap forward in physical AI technology, offering developers powerful tools and resources to advance robotics systems, and enhance autonomous vehicle technology.

Cosmos Transfer, the latest addition to NVIDIA's Cosmos™ world foundation models (WFMs), introduces a new level of control and accuracy in generating virtual world scenes.

Available in 7 billion parameter size, the model utilizes multicontrols to guide the generation of high-fidelity world scenes from structural inputs, ensuring precise spatial alignment and scene composition.

The model is built by training individual ControlNets separately for each sensor modality used to capture the simulated world.

Input types include 3D bounding box map, Trajectory map, Depth map, Segmentation map.

Outputs from Cosmos Transfer varying environments and weather conditions.

Cosmos Transfer coupled with the NVIDIA Omniverse platform is driving controllable synthetic data generation for robotics and autonomous vehicle development at scale. Find more Cosmos Transfer Examples on GitHub.

Cosmos Transfer samples built using post-training base model are also available for autonomous vehicles.

Recent findings suggest that NVIDIA has also released Physical AI Dataset, an open-source dataset on Hugging Face for developing physical AI. This commercial-grade, pre-validated dataset consists of 15 terabytes of data representing more than 320,000 trajectories for robotics training, plus up to 1,000 Universal Scene Description (OpenUSD) assets, including a SimReady collection.

The dataset is designed for post-training foundation models like Cosmos Predict world foundation models, providing developers with high-quality, diverse data to enhance their AI models.

Another exciting announcement is the release of NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1, the world's first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model takes multimodal input, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks in diverse environments. The NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-N1-2B model is available on Hugging Face.

Isaac GR00T N1 was trained on an expansive humanoid dataset, consisting of real captured data, synthetic data generated using components of the NVIDIA Isaac GR00T Blueprint, and internet-scale video data. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks and environments.

Isaac GR00T N1 uses a single model and set of weights to enable manipulation behaviors on various humanoid robots, such as the Fourier GR-1 and 1X Neo. It demonstrates robust generalization across a range of tasks, including grasping and manipulating objects with one or both arms, as well as transferring items between arms. It can also execute complex, multi-step tasks that require sustained contextual understanding and the integration of diverse skills. These capabilities make it well-suited for applications in material handling, packaging, and inspection.

Isaac GR00T N1 features a dual-system architecture inspired by human cognition, consisting of the following complementary components:.

Post-training is the path forward to advancing autonomous systems, creating specialized models for downstream physical AI tasks.

Recent findings suggest that check out GitHub for Cosmos Predict and Cosmos Transfer inference scripts. Explore the Cosmos Transfer research paper for more details.

Recent findings suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-N1-2B model is available on Hugging Face. Sample datasets and PyTorch scripts for post-training using custom user datasets, which is compatible with the Hugging Face LeRobot format are available on GitHub. For more information about the Isaac GR00T N1 model, see the research paper.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, android’s source code is big – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by 2-3x. Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.

Sources indicate that we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.

Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.

ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.

In the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (Android.bp), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and Ninja executes the final build graph (see the Android build overview). Similar to the Make build tool, Ninja is timestamp-based. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.

Analyzing the AOSP code for Android 17 demonstrates the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.

Sources indicate that if you are looking for a reliable, everyday handset without spending flagship money, Samsung’s mid-range lineup is usually a safe bet. Right now, the Samsung Galaxy A56 has dropped to just $299 on Amazon, which makes a sizable $200 dent in its original $499 retail price.

Sources indicate that at under $300, the biggest selling point here isn’t just the upfront savings; it is the longevity. Samsung committed to six years of OS and security updates for the Galaxy A56, meaning this device will stay current and secure well into 2032. For a budget-tier purchase, getting that kind of software runway is hard to beat and only matched by Google with the Pixel 10a.

Hardware-wise, the A56 punches above this sale price. You get a crisp 6.7-inch 120Hz Super AMOLED display, an IP67 dust- and water-resistance rating, and a 5,000mAh battery with 45W wired charging, matching the charging speeds of Samsung’s flagship models. The triple-camera array, led by a 50MP main sensor with OIS, won’t win any photography awards against Ultra-tier phones, though it is plenty capable for casual snaps. Plus, One UI brings plenty of handy Samsung ecosystem features and baked-in AI tools like Object Eraser.

Of course, the Google Pixel 10a is the obvious rival in this space. If you can catch the Pixel 10a on sale around the $350 mark, its cleaner Android experience, seven-year update promise, and superior computational photography make it a very tempting alternative.

That noted, it hasn’t been available at that price point for a while and can only be picked up for $400 if you buy renewed. Which annoyingly means the Pixel is sitting closer to its $499 MSRP and has last years specs anyway, so in many ways that makes the Galaxy A56 potentially a smarter buy for your wallet despite being a year older.

In my opinion, for first-time smartphone owners, kids, or anyone who just wants a large, smooth screen and years of updates on a budget, $299 is tough to argue with.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that you can build an AI agent in an afternoon now.
  • Sources indicate that then it meets a real system with real permissions and real customers, and things get quiet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that you can build an AI agent in an afternoon now. Pick a model, write a loop, hand it a few tools and watch it book a meeting or open a pull request. The demo works, and everyone in the room is impressed.

Sources indicate that then it meets a real system with real permissions and real customers, and things get quiet. Gartner has predicted that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing rising costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Its analyst Anushree Verma described most current projects as early-stage experiments that are driven by hype and often misapplied. A forecast is not a measurement, but the pattern it describes matches what many teams report: the agent is rarely what breaks. The workflow around it is.

This article covers where that workflow tends to fail, with a focus on permissions, tool connections and human approval. It includes a small, runnable policy gate in JavaScript, compares the main safeguards and notes their limits. Standards and guidance change swiftly in this area, so check the linked sources for the current versions.

In a recent development, A year or two ago the model was often the differentiator. Today many teams can reach the same frontier models through the same kinds of APIs, so if the intelligence is similar, the advantage has to come from somewhere else.

Anthropic’s guide to building effective agents reached a similar conclusion after working with teams building agents. It reports that the most successful implementations were not using complex frameworks or specialized libraries, and were building with simple, composable patterns instead. It also separates workflows, where code paths are predefined, from agents, where the model chooses its own steps, and advises using the simplest approach that works and adding complexity only when measurement indicates it helps.

Industry observers note that that should change where developers spend their time. Frameworks matter, but three less glamorous questions matter more: what can the agent touch, when does it stop, and who checks its work?

According to recent reports, the OWASP guidance on Excessive Agency names what goes wrong here. It covers agents that can do more than they need to, and it traces the problem to three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy.

In practice this looks familiar. An agent that only needs to read tickets is given a token that can also close them. A summarization tool connects with an admin account because that was quicker to set up. A generic “run shell command” tool is exposed when the agent only ever needs to write one file.

Sources indicate that the fix is ordinary engineering discipline applied to a upcoming kind of caller. OWASP’s recommendations include giving each tool only the functions and permissions it needs, preferring narrow tools over open-ended ones, running actions under the user’s own scoped identity, requiring human approval for high-impact actions and enforcing authorization in the downstream system rather than letting the model decide. The last point is the key one: a model can be talked out of a rule written in a prompt, but an API that checks scopes cannot.

Make the risky properties of a tool explicit in its definition so your orchestration layer can act on them:.

Nothing clever is happening there, which is the point. The decision about what needs a human is made by a developer at design time, not by a model at runtime.

Industry observers note that the definitions above only help if something enforces them. The sketch below is a policy gate that sits between the model and your tools. It checks that the tool exists, that the caller was granted the scope, and whether the action is reversible, and it records each decision. It runs on Node.js 18 or later with no dependencies.

It has been revealed that A short test file indicates the behavior. Unknown tools and missing scopes are denied, reads run, and the irreversible send waits for a person:.

This is deliberately minimal. A real system would load scopes from the user’s actual session, enforce the same scopes again in the downstream API, and store the audit log somewhere durable. The gate is a second line of defense, not a replacement for authorization in the systems the agent calls.

The Model Context Protocol has become a common way to connect agents to tools. Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, in December 2025. Block contributed goose and OpenAI contributed AGENTS.md as founding projects, which demonstrates how central the ecosystem has become.

Recent findings suggest that A standard protocol is good news. It also means you can install a tool server in minutes and expose every endpoint of your glitch tracker, repository or CRM to your agent, whether it needs them or not. Easy connection quietly pushes more power to the agent.

Industry observers note that the protocol’s own security best practices document covers several relevant risks, including confused deputy problems in proxy servers, token passthrough, local server compromise and scope minimization. For scopes, it recommends starting with a minimal set and elevating only when a privileged operation is first attempted, and it lists wildcard or omnibus scopes as a common mistake.

A sensible rule is to treat every tool server like a third-party dependency running with production credentials. Review the tools it exposes, switch off the ones the workflow does not use, pin versions and log every call. If you would not let a newly introduced contractor do it on day one, the agent should not do it either.

Human-in-the-loop design is often implemented as “approve everything”. That fails in a predictable way: people click approve forty times a day and stop reading by lunchtime.

A better rule is to gate on reversibility. Reads run freely, reversible writes run and get logged, and irreversible actions such as sending, paying or deleting wait for a person. Everything leaves a trace that a developer can replay when something looks odd. The gate above implements exactly this split.

It has been revealed that some teams build these pieces themselves, and others buy them. Elsewhen, a London-based consultancy that works on agentic operations for enterprise teams, describes its own service in similar terms. Its page lists approval gates where people sign off consequential decisions, an audit trail of what each agent read and which systems it touched, and a shared layer of permissions and guardrails that is reused across workflows. Elsewhen also says its Planet Agent report found that agents tend to start at the edges of an organization, where tasks are repeatable and mistakes are cheap, and then move toward the core. Treat that as the vendor’s own finding, and ask for the underlying evidence before relying on it.

The same logic applies outside engineering. The first question worth asking any AI partner is what they have actually put into production, and developers can ask the same of their own work.

According to recent reports, no single control is enough. The table summarizes what each safeguard does well and where it falls short.

It is the OWASP term for an agent that can do more than it needs to, caused by excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy.

A prompt rule can be bypassed or ignored, while a scope check in the downstream API is enforced regardless of what the model says.

Usually not. Gating on reversibility keeps humans focused on actions such as sending, paying and deleting, and avoids approval fatigue.

Treat them like any third-party dependency. Review the tools they expose, limit scopes, pin versions and log calls.

The agentic projects that survive the next two years will probably not be the ones with the most ambitious autonomy. They will be the ones where someone sat down early and decided what the agent could touch, what it had to ask about and how anyone would know what it did.

That work does not demo well and it will not trend on social media. It is still the part that decides whether your agent becomes infrastructure or ends up among the projects that get cancelled.

AI Policy @🤗: Response to the White House AI Action Initiative RFI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On March 14, we submitted Hugging Face's response to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy's request for information on the White House AI Action Proposal.
  • Open approaches to AI development are not only (typically) more transparent, adaptable, and scientifically sound, they have also consistently reproduced or surpassed the performance of widely-used API-only commercial offerings on many tasks; and are increasingly doing so on shorter timelines, with increased resource efficiency.
  • The most advanced AI systems to date all stand on a strong foundation of open research (attention mechanisms, transformer architectures, cheaper post-training algorithms) and open source software (PyTorch, Hugging Face libraries, supercomputer operating systems) — which highlights the critical value of continued support for openness in sustaining further progress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On March 14, we submitted Hugging Face's response to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy's request for information on the White House AI Action Proposal. We took this opportunity to (re-)assert the fundamental role that open AI systems and open science play in enabling the technology to be more performant and efficient, broadly and reliably adopted, and meeting the highest standards of security. This blog post provides a summary of our response, the full text is available here.

Open approaches to AI development are not only (typically) more transparent, adaptable, and scientifically sound, they have also consistently reproduced or surpassed the performance of widely-used API-only commercial offerings on many tasks; and are increasingly doing so on shorter timelines, with increased resource efficiency. Our team's recent OlympicCoder outperforming Claude 3.7 on complex coding tasks with 7B parameters and an open-source post-training recipe, or AI2's fully open OLMo 2 models (with open training data) matching o1-mini performances, are two of the most recent compelling examples. These successes show that a robust AI strategy must leverage open and collaborative development to best drive performance, adoption, and security of the technology. We make three major recommendations in this direction.

The most advanced AI systems to date all stand on a strong foundation of open research (attention mechanisms, transformer architectures, cheaper post-training algorithms) and open source software (PyTorch, Hugging Face libraries, supercomputer operating systems) — which highlights the critical value of continued support for openness in sustaining further progress. Investment in systems that can freely be re-used and adapted has also been shown to have a strong economic impact multiplying effect, driving a significant percentage of countries' GDP. As AI systems with open weights and training techniques become increasingly attractive options for developers in terms of both performance and cost, prioritizing public research infrastructure and broad access to compute, customizable models, and trusted open datasets — especially for smaller developers and researchers — will be essential to the further technical and economic success of AI technology.

Recent findings suggest that addressing the resource constraints of organizations adopting and adapting AI technology will be essential to supporting its diffusion and fostering innovation from adopters across the entire development chain. Smaller models (that may even be used on edge devices), techniques to reduce computational requirements at inference, and efforts to facilitate mid-scale training for organizations with modest to moderate computational resources all support the development of models that meet the specific needs of their use context, especially in high-risk settings such as healthcare where fully generalist models have proven unreliable. More efficient and purpose-designed AI systems facilitate better in-context evaluation, better resource utilization, and enable organizations to build technical capacity at all stages of the AI development chain to ensure that all customers can leverage the system that best fits their needs.

According to recent reports, finally, if decades of information security and cybersecurity in open source software are any indication, open and transparent AI systems will have a fundamental role to play in securing AI development and deployment especially in the most critical settings — with different levels of openness needed for different security requirements. Fully transparent models providing access to their training data and procedures can support the most extensive safety certifications. Open infrastructure and open-source tooling implementing the latest training techniques can empower organizations to train the models they need in fully controlled environments. Open-weight models that can be run in air-gapped environments can be a critical component in managing information risks. Prioritizing adoption of the most transparent systems, supporting the development of the open resources outlined, and building capacity to leverage them especially in critical settings of AI adoption are essential to enabling more secure AI adoption.

Please refer to the full response for our more detailed recommendations!

Following its short-lived Galaxy Z TriFold, Samsung appears to have a sequel on the way that’s set to arrive in the Galaxy Z Fold 9 lineup.

The Galaxy Z TriFold debuted a few months after the Galaxy Z Fold 7, carrying the codename “Q7m.” GalaxyClub now reports that “Q9m” has surfaced, implying that Galaxy Z TriFold 2 will be based on the Galaxy Z Fold 9 series.

That tells us a couple of things.

In a recent development, for one, don’t expect a upcoming TriFold to arrive in the same schedule as the first one. The original Galaxy Z TriFold introduced in late 2025 before expanding to other regions in early 2026. This also tells us that the Galaxy Z TriFold 2 will be based on the Galaxy Z Fold 9 series, likely including the latest chipset and Samsung’s Android 18 build.

There’s no guarantee yet about when the next TriFold might debut, how much it might cost, or where it might launch. GalaxyClub notes that the codename subtly suggests there’s no EU release in the plans, but it can’t be completely ruled out either.

Whatever happens with Galaxy Z TriFold 2, let’s just hope it lasts longer than the original.

We will set up OlympicCoder 7B, the smaller of the two OlympicCoder variants, and we’ll use a quantized variant for optimum local inference. Here’s the stack we’re going to use:.

It’s important to say that we chose this stack purely for simplicity. You might want to experiment with the larger model and/or different GGUF files. Or even alternative inference engines like llama.cpp.

According to recent reports, LM Studio is like a control panel for AI models. It integrates with the Hugging Face hub to pull models, helps you find the right GGUF file, and exposes an API that other applications can use to interact with the model.

In short, it lets you download and run them without any complicated setup.

The GGUF files that we need are hosted on the hub. We can open the model from the hub in LMStudio, using the ‘Use this model’ button:.

This will link to the LMStudio application and open it on your machine. You’ll just need to Choose a Quantization. I went for Q4_K_M because it will perform well on most devices. If you have more compute, you might want to try out one of the options with Q8_*.

If you want to skip the UI, you can also load models with LMStudio via the command line:.

This is the crucial part. We now need to integrate VScode with the model served by LMStudio.

Most of the core AI features in vscode are available via this setup, for example:.

Industry observers note that olympicCoder is not Claude. It’s optimised on the CodeForces-CoTs dataset which is based on competitive coding challenges. That means that you should not expect it to be super friendly and explanatory. Instead, roll up your sleeves and expect a no-holds barred competitive coder ready to deal with tough problems.

You might want to mix up OlympicCoder with other models to get a rounded coding experience. For example, if you’re trying to squeeze milliseconds out of a binary search, try OlympicCoder. If you want to design a user facing API, go for Claude-3.7-sonnet or Qwen-2.5-Coder.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that following his recent resignation from the organization and his return as CEO earlier this week, Jensen Huang has received a glowing statement of support from Denny's, the chain where he famously began his working life before founding Nvidia. The diner chain Denny's posted a 200-word statement to X in which it sought to maintain its links to the Nvidia founder, saying that there are "some things you just don’t take off the menu." Denny's, famously, is the diner where Huang came up with the idea for Nvidia before founding the then-GPU company, now an AI server outfit.

Every story starts somewhere. We’re proud to be part of Jensen’s. https://t.co/WpWJdLFmIsNovember 25, 2026.

Notably, the chain also noted that it has restored a plaque commemorating the occasion to "where it belongs," days after it was removed amid growing controversy over Huang and his affair with former Megaspeed employee Alice Huang. Megaspeed is now under criminal investigation over its involvement in bypassing U.S. export controls relating to Nvidia's advanced AI chips. It's also believed that Alice Huang's husband, Kang Wei, may also be a spy with connections to China's Ministry of State Security.

Despite all of that, Denny's has very much hitched its trailer to Huang and his reputation, for better or worse. The diner's statement ends by reminding him that his booth "is always waiting and the coffee's on," although it's unclear whether he'll be able to make time for a visit between his upcoming visit to Congress to discuss the last few weeks' goings-on and joining board meetings with U.S. President Donald Trump. There is good news for Huang, though, even if he's found to have broken the law during his trysts with the suspected spy. Trump states that a pardon is "always an option," meaning Huang could be free to visit all the Denny's diners he wants to in the future.

As for Nvidia, its share price has suffered the same fate as other tech stocks in recent weeks. It rallied after initially nosediving around the time of Huang's resignation, but has since continued its downward trajectory, having fallen almost 2.4 percentage points in the last five days and over 30 points in the last month.

Industry observers note that we realized that our analytics dashboard needed a refresh. Since we debug a lot of endpoints ourselves, we’ve felt the same pain as our owners. That’s why we sat down to plan and make several improvements to provide a better experience for you.

Just open the dashboard and get instant insights.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gradio’s gr.Dataframe component is one of our most popular components, we've seen it used in a variety of awesome apps, like leaderboards, dashboards, and interactive visualisations. Although we hadn't made any changes to the dataframe in quite some time, our backlog of problems had been growing, and some improvements had been in demand for a while.

It has been revealed that well — we’re now super excited to release a host of new updates to Gradio’s dataframe component. Over the last 6 weeks, we’ve closed over 70 dataframe issues - including bugs, improvements and enhancements.

You can select multiple cells at once! Copy or delete values across your selection with ease.

According to recent reports, add row number columns and keep critical columns in view while navigating wide datasets using the pinned_columns parameter. No more losing track of what you're looking at!

According to recent reports, easily copy cell values into a comma-separated format with our new copy button. Need a better view? The full screen button gives you interactivity without distractions and can be enabled with the show_full_screen parameter.

Sources indicate that look at all that data! Now we can just scroll to the top.

Improved keyboard navigation makes gr.Dataframe more accessible than ever. You can also take control of your dataframe’s look with a dedicated styler parameter and enhance the user experience of your app.

Access entire row data in select events for more intuitive interactivity and data manipulation.

Customise the interactivity of your dataframe by specifying non-editable columns using the static_columns parameter.

Rapidly find the data you need with our powerful search feature by setting the show_search parameter to "search".

Narrow down your dataset to focus on exactly what you need with flexible filtering options with show_search set to "filter".

Experience smoother, more intuitive cell selection that behaves the way you expect.

Recent findings suggest that with over 70 concerns closed, we’ve made huge improvements, but there’s always more for us to work on. Looking ahead, we still have more ideas to implement and we’re excited to keep refining accessibility, performance, and integration. Look out for some cool demos on our socials using the dataframe on Gradio’s X.

In a recent development, the updated dataframe is live in the latest Gradio release. Update your installation with pip install --upgrade gradio.

Sources indicate that check out the Gradio documentation for examples and tutorials to get started with these fresh features. We’re eager to see what you create! Got thoughts or suggestions? Share them by raising an problem in our GitHub repo.

This is awesome, I hope it can get into Streamlit, which is a great library for making interactive dashboards in Python.
