#150652. Industry News: Training and Finetuning Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 26 Mar 2025 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2483 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Training and Finetuning Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 26 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more.
  • Finetuning reranker models involves several components: datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class itself.
  • Lastly, in the Evaluation section, I'll show you that my small finetuned tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-base-gooaq-bce reranker model that I trained alongside this blogpost easily outperforms the 13 most commonly used public reranker models on my evaluation dataset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a reranker model (also known as a cross-encoder) that beats all existing options on exactly your data. This method can also train extremely strong new reranker models from scratch.

Finetuning reranker models involves several components: datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class itself. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong reranker models.

Lastly, in the Evaluation section, I'll show you that my small finetuned tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-base-gooaq-bce reranker model that I trained alongside this blogpost easily outperforms the 13 most commonly used public reranker models on my evaluation dataset. It even beats models that are 4x bigger.

Repeating the recipe with a bigger base model results in tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce, a reranker model that blows all existing general-purpose reranker models out of the water on my data.

If you're interested in finetuning embedding models instead, then consider reading through my prior Training and Finetuning Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost as well.

According to recent reports, reranker models, often implemented using Cross Encoder architectures, are designed to evaluate the relevance between pairs of texts (e.g., a query and a document, or two sentences). Unlike Sentence Transformers (a.k.a. bi-encoders, embedding models), which independently embed each text into vectors and compute similarity via a distance metric, Cross Encoder process the paired texts together through a shared neural network, resulting in one output score. By letting the two texts attend to each other, Cross Encoder models can outperform embedding models.

Recent findings suggest that however, this strength comes with a trade-off: Cross Encoder models are slower as they process every possible pair of texts (e.g., 10 queries with 500 candidate documents requires 5,000 computations instead of 510 for embedding models). This makes them less efficient for large-scale initial retrieval but ideal for reranking: refining the top-k results first identified by faster Sentence Transformer models. The strongest search systems commonly use this 2-stage "retrieve and rerank" approach.

Throughout this blogpost, I'll use "reranker model" and "Cross Encoder model" interchangeably.

Reranker models are often tasked with a challenging problem:.

Which of these kkk highly-related documents answers the query the best?

General-purpose reranker models are trained to perform adequately on this exact question in a wide range of domains and topics, preventing them from reaching their maximum potential in your specific domain. Through finetuning, the model can learn to focus exclusively on the domain and/or language that matters to you.

In the Evaluation section end of this blogpost, I'll show that training a model on your domain can outperform any general-purpose reranker model, even if those baselines are much bigger. Don't underestimate the power of finetuning on your domain!

Training reranker models involves the following components:.

Let's take a closer look at each component.

In a recent development, the CrossEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use your local data in whatever format you prefer (e.g. CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL).

Note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets in the Hugging Face Hub.

Recent findings suggest that some datasets, like nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual, have multiple subsets with different data formats. You need to specify the subset name along with the dataset name, e.g. dataset = load_dataset("nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual", "de", split="train").

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in certain file formats:.

You can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict if your local data requires pre-processing. This allows you to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:.

Each key in the dictionary becomes a column in the resulting dataset.

It is important that your dataset format matches your loss function (or that you choose a loss function that matches your dataset format and model). Verifying whether a dataset format and model work with a loss function involves three steps:.

For example, given a dataset with columns ["text1", "text2", "label"] where the "label" column has float similarity score ranging from 0 to 1 and a model outputting 1 label, we can use it with BinaryCrossEntropyLoss because:.

Be sure to re-order your dataset columns with Dataset.select_columns if your columns are not ordered correctly. For example, if your dataset has ["good_answer", "bad_answer", "question"] as columns, then this dataset can technically be used with a loss that requires (anchor, positive, negative) triplets, but the good_answer column will be taken as the anchor, bad_answer as the positive, and question as the negative.

Additionally, if your dataset has extraneous columns (e.g. sample_id, metadata, source, type), you should remove these with Dataset.remove_columns as they will be used as inputs otherwise. You can also use Dataset.select_columns to keep only the desired columns.

The success of training reranker models often depends on the quality of the negatives, i.e. the passages for which the query-negative score should be low. Negatives can be divided into two types:.

The strongest CrossEncoder models are generally trained to recognize hard negatives, and so it's valuable to be able to "mine" hard negatives to train with. Sentence Transformers supports a strong mine_hard_negatives function that can assist, given a dataset of query-answer pairs:.

Recent findings suggest that loss functions help evaluate a model's performance on a set of data and direct the training process. The right loss function for your task depends on the data you have and what you're trying to achieve. You can find a full list of available loss functions in the Loss Overview.

Most loss functions are easy to set up - you just need to provide the CrossEncoder model you're training:.

You can customize the training process using the CrossEncoderTrainingArguments class. This class lets you adjust parameters that can impact training speed and help you understand what's happening during training.

For more information on the most useful training arguments, check out the Cross Encoder > Training Overview > Training Arguments. It's worth reading to get the most out of your training.

Here's an example of how to set up CrossEncoderTrainingArguments:.

To track your model's performance during training, you can pass an eval_dataset to the CrossEncoderTrainer. However, you might want more detailed metrics beyond just the evaluation loss. That's where evaluators can help you assess your model's performance using specific metrics at various stages of training. You can use an evaluation dataset, an evaluator, both, or neither, depending on your needs. The evaluation strategy and frequency are controlled by the eval_strategy and eval_steps Training Arguments.

Sentence Transformers includes the following built-in evaluators:.

You can also use SequentialEvaluator to join multiple evaluators into one, which can then be passed to the CrossEncoderTrainer. You can also just pass a list of evaluators to the trainer.

Sources indicate that sometimes you don't have the required evaluation data to prepare one of these evaluators on your own, but you still want to track how well the model performs on some common benchmarks. In that case, you can use these evaluators with data from Hugging Face.

The STS Benchmark (a.k.a. STSb) is a commonly used benchmarking dataset to measure the model's understanding of semantic textual similarity of short texts like "A man is feeding a mouse to a snake.".

Feel free to browse the sentence-transformers/stsb dataset on Hugging Face.

Preparing data for CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator can be difficult as you need negatives in addition to your query-positive data.

The mine_hard_negatives function has a convenient include_positives parameter, which can be set to True to also mine for the positive texts. When supplied as documents (which have to be 1. ranked and 2. contain positives) to CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator, the evaluator will not just evaluate the reranking performance of the CrossEncoder, but also the original rankings by the embedding model used for mining.

Recent findings suggest that note that by default, if you are using CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator with documents, the evaluator will rerank with all positives, even if they are not in the documents. This is useful for getting a stronger signal out of your evaluator, but does give a slightly unrealistic performance. After all, the maximum performance is now 100, whereas normally its bounded by whether the first-stage retriever actually retrieved the positives.

You can enable the realistic behaviour by setting always_rerank_positives=False when initializing CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator. Repeating the same script with this realistic two-stage performance results in::.

The CrossEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. We only have to specify the trainer with the model, training arguments (optional), training dataset, evaluation dataset (optional), loss function, evaluator (optional) and we can start training. Let’s have a look at a script where all of these components come together:.

In this example I'm finetuning from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, a base model that is not yet a Cross Encoder model. This generally requires more training data than finetuning an existing reranker model like Alibaba-NLP/gte-multilingual-reranker-base. I'm using 99k query-answer pairs from the GooAQ dataset, after which I mine hard negatives using the sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 embedding model. This results in 578k labeled pairs: 99k positive pairs (i.e. label=1) and 479k negative pairs (i.e. label=0).

I use the BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, which is well suited for these labeled pairs. I also set up 2 forms of evaluation: CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator which evaluates against the NanoBEIR benchmark and CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator which evaluates the performance of reranking the top 30 results from the aforementioned static embedding model. Afterwards, I define a fairly standard set of hyperparameters, including learning rates, warmup ratios, bf16, loading the best model at the end, and some debugging parameters. Lastly, I run the trainer, perform post-training evaluation, and save the model both locally and on the Hugging Face Hub.

It has been revealed that after running this script, the tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-base-gooaq-bce model was uploaded for me. See the upcoming Evaluation section with evidence that this model outperformed 13 commonly used open-source alternatives, including much bigger models. I also ran the model with answerdotai/ModernBERT-large as the base model, resulting in tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce.

It has been revealed that evaluation results are automatically stored in the generated model card upon saving a model, alongside the base model, language, license, evaluation results, training & evaluation dataset info, hyperparameters, training logs, and more. Without any effort, your uploaded models should contain all the information that your potential people would need to determine whether your model is suitable for them.

The CrossEncoder trainer supports various transformers.TrainerCallback subclasses, including:.

These are automatically used without you having to specify anything, as long as the required dependency is installed.

Refer to the Transformers Callbacks documentation for more information on these callbacks and how to create your own.

Typically, top-performing general-purpose models are trained on multiple datasets simultaneously. However, this approach can be challenging due to the varying formats of each dataset. Fortunately, the CrossEncoderTrainer allows you to train on multiple datasets without requiring a uniform format. Additionally, it provides the flexibility to apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps to train with multiple datasets at once:.

Each training/evaluation batch will only contain samples from one of the datasets. The order in which batches are sampled from the multiple datasets is defined by the MultiDatasetBatchSamplers enum, which can be passed to the CrossEncoderTrainingArguments via multi_dataset_batch_sampler. Valid options are:.

Cross Encoder models have their own unique quirks, so here’s some tips to help you out:.

CrossEncoder models overfit rather quickly, so it’s recommended to use an evaluator like CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator or CrossEncoderRerankingEvaluator together with the load_best_model_at_end and metric_for_best_model training arguments to load the model with the best evaluation performance after training.

In a recent development, crossEncoders are particularly receptive to strong hard negatives (mine_hard_negatives). They teach the model to be very strict, useful e.g. when distinguishing between passages that answer a question or passages that relate to a question.

Don’t underestimate BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, it remains a very strong option despite being simpler than learning-to-rank (LambdaLoss, ListNetLoss) or in-batch negatives (CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, MultipleNegativesRankingLoss) losses, and its data is easy to prepare, especially using mine_hard_negatives.

In a recent development, I ran a reranking evaluation of my model from the Trainer section against several baselines on the GooAQ development set with both always_rerank_positives=False and with always_rerank_positives=True in the reranking evaluator. These represent the realistic (only rerank what the retriever found) and evaluation (rerank all positives, even if the retriever didn't find it) formats, respectively.

As a reminder, I used the extremely efficient sentence-transformers/static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 static embedding model to retrieve the top 30 for reranking.

The larger tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce took less than an hour to train, and is in a league of its own with a massive 79.42 NDCG@10 in the realistic setting. The GooAQ training and evaluation dataset aligns very well with what these baselines were trained for, so the difference should be even larger when training for a more niche domain.

According to recent reports, note that this does not mean that tomaarsen/reranker-ModernBERT-large-gooaq-bce is the strongest model here on all domains: It's simply the strongest in our domain. This is totally fine, as we just need this reranker to work well on our data.

Don't underestimate the power of finetuning reranker models on your domain. You can improve both the search performance and the latency of your search stack by finetuning a (small) reranker!

How to Add Idempotency Keys to a Node.js API with PostgreSQL

According to recent reports, A mobile app sends POST /orders. The server creates the order, but the response is lost when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 4G. The app sees a timeout and retries. Now the customer has two orders, and your support team has a refund to process.

Retrying is the right thing for a client to do. The problem is that POST is not idempotent: RFC 9110 defines GET, PUT and DELETE as idempotent methods, but not POST or PATCH. Repeating a POST can repeat its side effects.

An idempotency key fixes this. The client generates a unique key for each logical operation and sends it with every attempt. The server does the work once, stores the response against the key, and returns the stored response for any retry. The IETF HTTPAPI working group is standardizing this pattern as the Idempotency-Key HTTP header field, and this tutorial follows its recommendations.

We'll build it with Node.js, Express 5 and PostgreSQL. By the end you'll have a table that stores keys, a function that safely claims a key under concurrent requests, an Express route that replays stored responses, and a client that retries without creating duplicates.

Sources indicate that the client's job is simple: generate a key, usually a UUID, and send the same key on every retry of the same operation. The draft defines the header value as a quoted string:.

The server's job is harder, because every request falls into one of five cases:.

To tell case 3 from case 4, the server stores a fingerprint of the request alongside the key. A matching fingerprint means a genuine retry; a different one means key reuse. Case 5 is the one most implementations get wrong, because it only demonstrates up under concurrency. A database constraint handles it for us.

Create a project and install the two dependencies:.

The key table records who sent the key, the request fingerprint, whether the work has finished, and the response to replay:.

According to recent reports, two details matter here. The primary key includes client_id, so keys are scoped per client: two customers who happen to generate the same value can't see each other's responses. And locked_until lets the server recover a key whose request crashed halfway, which we'll use in Step 3.

It has been revealed that the draft defines the header value as a structured field string, which means it arrives wrapped in double quotes. Many clients send it without quotes, so the parser below accepts both and limits the characters and length it will store:.

The fingerprint has to be identical for identical requests, even if a client serializes the JSON body with its properties in a different order. Sorting object keys before hashing takes care of that. The hash uses SHA-256 from Node's built-in crypto module:.

Including the method and path means a key reused on a different endpoint counts as a mismatch, not as a retry.

The tempting approach is to SELECT the key, and insert it if nothing comes back. Under concurrency that fails: two retries arriving a few milliseconds apart both see no row, and both do the work.

In a recent development, instead, let the primary key decide. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING either inserts the row or does nothing, atomically, even across many application processes. The PostgreSQL INSERT documentation describes this behavior in detail. If the insert returns a row, this request owns the key. If not, we read the existing row and decide which case we're in:.

Sources indicate that the UPDATE in the last step is also atomic. If two retries find the same expired lock, only one of them matches the locked_until < now() condition and gets the key. If the row disappears between the two queries, for example because it was released after a failure, the function reports in_progress and the client simply retries.

Set LOCK_SECONDS comfortably above the slowest time your operation takes. If the lock expires while the original request is still running, a retry can take over and run the work a second time.

In a recent development, once a request owns the key, it creates the order and marks the key as completed. Both writes happen in one transaction, so there is no moment where the order exists but the key still claims in_progress, or the other way round. Note that a transaction in node-postgres has to use a single client checked out from the pool, as the node-postgres transaction documentation explains:.

It has been revealed that releaseKey runs when the work fails. Deleting the claim lets the client retry with the same key instead of waiting for the lock to expire. It only deletes rows that are still in progress, so a completed response is never thrown away.

The route validates the body first. A request with invalid input never touches the key table, so the client can fix the input and resend with the same key. Error responses use the application/problem+json format from RFC 9457, which the idempotency draft also uses in its examples:.

The server side only works if the client keeps the key stable. The most common client bug is generating a latest key inside the retry loop, which turns every retry into a new operation. Generate the key once per logical action, before the first attempt:.

The catch branch is the reason idempotency keys exist. After a timeout, the client can't know whether the order was created. With a stable key, retrying is safe either way: if the first attempt succeeded, the retry returns the stored order; if it didn't, the retry creates it. The random jitter spreads retries out, so many clients recovering from the same outage don't all hit the server at once.

In a browser or mobile app, store the key with the pending action, for example in the form state or a local queue. If the user taps "Place order" again after an error, reuse it. Only generate a fresh key when the user starts a genuinely new action.

Sources indicate that keys can't live forever, or the table grows without limit. The draft leaves the retention period to the server but states it should be published in the API documentation, so clients know how long a retry stays safe. Twenty-four hours covers most retry scenarios. A scheduled job can delete older rows in batches:.

Recent findings suggest that run it every few minutes from cron or your job scheduler until it deletes zero rows. Deleting in batches keeps each transaction short, and the created_at index from Step 1 keeps the inner query fast. A retry that arrives after its key has expired is treated as a upcoming request, which is why the retention period belongs in your documentation.

Start the server with node server.js, then send the same request twice:.

The second request lists the properties in a different order, and it's still recognized as a retry because of the canonical fingerprint. Both responses carry the same order ID, and the orders table contains one row.

Now change the quantity while keeping the key. The server answers 422, because the key now belongs to a different request:.

To see the concurrent case, add await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 3000)); before completeKey in the route, restart the server, and fire two requests with a new key at the same time:.

According to recent reports, one request prints 201 and the other 409. Without the ON CONFLICT claim, both would have printed 201 and created two orders. Remove the delay when you're done.

This design guarantees that the database work in Step 4 happens once per key. Two situations need extra care:.

Sources indicate that idempotency keys don't replace other safeguards either. A unique constraint on a natural business key, such as one payment per invoice, still catches duplicates that arrive with different keys, for example when a user submits the same form from two tabs.

In a recent development, with one table, an atomic claim and a transaction that stores the response next to the work, POST endpoints become safe to retry. Clients get a simple rule: generate one key per action, reuse it on every retry. The server takes care of the rest, including the concurrent retries that a SELECT-then-INSERT approach misses.

The same pattern works for PATCH endpoints and for webhooks you send to other systems. Start with the endpoints where a duplicate costs real money or confuses a customer, and publish your key format and retention period in the API documentation so client developers know what to send.

Open R1: Patch #4

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this week, a upcoming model from DeepSeek silently landed on the Hub.
  • Industry observers note that the model has the same architecture as the original DeepSeek-V3 and now also comes with an MIT license, while the previous V3 model had a custom model license.
  • The DeepSeek team has evaluated the model on a range of math and coding tasks and we can see the model’s strong capabilities compared to other frontier models:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this week, a upcoming model from DeepSeek silently landed on the Hub. It’s an updated version of DeepSeek-V3, the base model underlying the R1 reasoning model. There isn’t much information shared yet on this new model, but we do know a few things!

Industry observers note that the model has the same architecture as the original DeepSeek-V3 and now also comes with an MIT license, while the previous V3 model had a custom model license. The focus of this model release was on improving the instruction following as well as code and math capabilities. Let’s have a look!

The DeepSeek team has evaluated the model on a range of math and coding tasks and we can see the model’s strong capabilities compared to other frontier models:.

Clearly, the model plays in the top league: often on par with GPT-4.5 and generally stronger than Claude-Sonnet-3.7.

To summarise the model has seen significant improvements across benchmarks.

Specifically, in the model card the DeepSeek mentions targeted improvements in the following areas:.

So the question might pop-up: how did they actually do this? Let’s speculate a bit!

Given the naming and architecture it is fairly safe to assume that the newly introduced model is based on the previous V3 model and trained on top of it. There are two possible areas how they improved the models:.

Until the team releases a technical report we don’t know for sure what they tweaked but the post-training pipeline is quite likely and potentially also adding a bit of pretraining. So have a look at how to use the models next!

You can use Hugging Face’s Inference Providers to quickly experiment with this model. It’s available through Fireworks, Hyperbolic, and Novita.

Industry observers note that here’s an example using the huggingface_hub library. You can also use the OpenAI client library like in this example.

Industry observers note that TGI supports running DeepSeek V3-0324 with its latest release as well. You can use it directly with the tagged docker image on a node of H100s.

SGLang supports running DeepSeek V3-0324 out of the box along with the Multi Latent Attention and Data Parallelism optimisations as well. To use you can simply just run the following on a node of H100s. For more information follow along here.

Dynamic Quants from Unsloth and Llama.cpp.

It has been revealed that running large LLMs like DeepSeek V3-0324 can be quite compute intensive and would require a large amount GPU VRAM to run. This is where Quantization comes in, it allows the end user to use the same model but with much lower VRAM consumption with a small trade-off in downstream performance.

According to recent reports, unsloth AI created Dynamic quantisations which allow one to run DeepSeek V3 with half the amount of compute as one node of H100 and can run with llama.cpp without as much degradation in benchmarks. Read more about it here: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V3-0324-GGUF.

Running language model safely has always been at the center of attention, ever since the first GPT models have been released. With the immense popularity of the DeepSeek models and their origin the question has found new interest. Let us run down the things that are safe to do and areas where some caution is a good idea. This is not DeepSeek specific but true for any open model!

First of all - is it safe to even download the model?

Yes, downloading the model is safe. There are a few precautions on the Hub side that make sure it’s safe to download and run models:.

Industry observers note that so downloading the weights is safe, and upon code review so is executing the modeling code. This means you can run the DeepSeek model locally without the risk of backdoors or malicious code execution.

So what would be the main risks outside of downloading and running the model? It depends on what you do with the model outputs!

The advice that follows is not specific to any model, and applies to both open and closed models: whether considering risks stemming from built-in secret behaviours in the model or from a model accidentally producing bad outputs.

We’ll cover risks in three areas: alignment, code generation and agents.

Industry observers note that alignment mismatch: Every model provider chooses how and to which values their models are aligned. What these values are and how they are chosen typically remains opaque and they might also change over time (see this study). The advantage of open models is that the alignment can be changed with custom fine-tuning at a later stage still as the example of Perplexity’s DeepSeek 1776 reveals.

As a rule, owners should be aware that any LLM is biased in one way or another and treat the model outputs accordingly.

According to recent reports, code generation: One of the most popular use-cases of LLMs is as coding assistants. However, this is also where indiscriminate usage of the model outputs can have the most negative effects. Models are trained on vast amounts of published code, upcoming and old. This typically includes potentially malicious code or code that contains known vulnerabilities. So models might produce similar vulnerabilities when proposing code solutions.

So, how can you prevent security concerns when using LLMs for code development? Run thorough code reviews of the proposed changes and scan the code with appropriate tools for vulnerabilities, as you would with any other code contribution.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped.
  • Pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record.
  • iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped. The results land as a stalled bill to ban sweepstakes casinos and raise sports betting taxes runs out of time.

Pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record. Online casinos contributed a record $278.8 million, up 11.1%. The total cleared the previous single-month mark of $625.5 million, which was set in May 2026.

iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase. A year earlier, online casino revenue was $251,097,586, itself a record at the time. Total gaming tax revenue in October 2025 was $252,287,937, against a record $274 million this October.

Two licensees led the iGaming field. Hollywood Casino at Penn National generated $114.4 million, up 16%. Valley Forge Casino Resort followed with $75.2 million, up 5.3%.

Industry observers note that october was a stronger month than September. In September, total gaming revenue was $555,036,870, a 4.07% year-over-year increase. iGaming table revenue slipped 0.63% that month.

The October pattern mirrors the last fiscal year. iGaming revenue in fiscal 2025/26 was $2,933,453,989, an 18.42% gain over the prior year. It generated $1,337,414,660 in tax. Combined gaming revenue reached $7,005,987,435, an all-time fiscal-year high. Taxes and fees returned to the state totaled $3,098,193,583.

Pennsylvania’s online casino growth is in line with a slowing iGaming trend nationally. US iGaming revenue rose 12.3% year over year to $1.03 billion in August 2026. For the state budget, the vertical is now a central source of gaming tax.

According to recent reports, sports betting moved the other way on volume. Handle fell to $903 million from $968.5 million in October 2025. Revenue still rose, to $65.1 million from $60.7 million. The same split showed up across fiscal 2025/26. Handle dropped from $8,721,795,533 to $8,448,101,928. Sports wagering revenue rose 35.95% to $662,947,631.

The record arrives as Harrisburg weighs a gaming modernization package. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced House Bill 2801 with four co-sponsors. On September 24, 2026, it was referred to the House Gaming Oversight Committee. Titled ‘Skill Games & Gaming Modernization,’ the bill would rewrite large parts of the state’s gaming code.

Recent findings suggest that house Bill 2801 would make operating or promoting online sweepstakes games illegal in Pennsylvania. Fines would range from $50,000 to $500,000 per violation.

The bill would also raise the sports wagering tax from 34% to 36%. The state presently taxes online slots at 54%. A higher sports rate would apply to a product whose handle is shrinking even as its revenue climbs.

The bill has not moved. HB 2801 had no recorded committee hearing or vote as of mid-November, according to Legal Sports Report. The legislative session ends November 30. Bills that do not pass by then do not carry into 2027.

In addition, the team needed a solution that adhered to infrastructure-as-code practices, supported project-by-project secret management, and provided a smooth balance between automation and manual control during deployments.

The engineering team seized the opportunity to re-examine their internal project structure, splitting projects into distinct infrastructure and application domains. This allowed them to implement a clearer separation of concerns and standardize secret rotation practices—a priority in the wake of a recent security incident.

According to recent reports, by leveraging Terraform, which was previously used to create Kubernetes secrets from AWS configurations, they found the transition to the Infisical Kubernetes Operator exceptionally smooth. This integration enabled security improvements while standardizing secrets management across all environments.

According to recent reports, kubernetes is at the heart of Hugging Face’s production environment, and Infisical's Kubernetes Operator has been instrumental in automating secret updates. The Operator continuously monitors for changes to any secret in Infisical and ensures that these updates are propagated to the corresponding Kubernetes objects. Whenever a change is detected, it can automatically reload dependent Deployments, ensuring that containers always run with the most recent secrets.

Industry observers note that A new secret is required by an application running in Kubernetes. The secret can be created via the Infisical's CLI or the web UI, then the developer creates an InfisicalSecret resource in Kubernetes that specifies which secret from Infisical should be synced:.

Once the CRD is applied, the Infisical Operator continuously watches for updates. When changes are detected in Infisical, the Operator automatically updates the Kubernetes secret (my-app-k8s-secret).

Better yet, since the application's Deployment references my-app-k8s-secret as an environment variable source or mounted volume, the Operator can automatically trigger a container reload when the secret changes.

In a recent development, in practice, Hugging Face engineers favor waiting for manual redeployments despite the Operator’s ability to automatically trigger container restarts. This decision was driven by the need for precise control over deployments, particularly when high traffic (over 10 million requests per minute) and numerous replicas are involved.

According to recent reports, for local development, Infisical’s CLI streamlines workflows by injecting secrets directly into development environments. This removes the need for insecure local .env files, aligning local configurations with production standards and reducing onboarding friction.

In a recent development, security improvements form the backbone of this migration. By integrating Infisical with existing identity providers such as Okta, Hugging Face established a fine-grained RBAC system. Permissions are automatically mapped from Okta groups, ensuring that developers retain administrative rights over their projects, while frontend and backend teams receive appropriately restricted read or write access.

According to recent reports, additionally, the secret sharing functionality allows secure credentials sharing among ML/AI researchers at Hugging Face. The centralized Infisical platform also simplifies auditing and managing secret rotations—a necessity highlighted by previous security incidents.

Seamless integration with CI/CD pipelines further enhanced the overall security posture. Infisical was embedded into the deployment pipeline via GitHub Actions using OIDC authentication and Terraform integration. By operating self-hosted runners within a secure environment, every deployment adhered to production-grade security standards. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the US Senate has unanimously passed a bill that would ban death, war and terrorism contracts on CFTC-registered prediction-market exchanges. The vote would turn regulatory discretion into a statutory ban just as the CFTC proposes looser rules, and the House has only weeks to act.

Recent findings suggest that sens. Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act. It is the first prediction-market bill the Senate has passed this Congress. The measure now heads to the House.

Under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations. Sports contracts are not covered.

Industry observers note that curtis made a moral case for the bill on the Senate floor. “There should be no financial incentive to profit from terrorism, war, or the death of another human being,” he noted.

Whether such contracts can trade presently rests on the CFTC’s discretion. The bill would replace that discretion with a prohibition written into statute.

The timing puts lawmakers and the regulator on different tracks. CFTC Chair Selig plans to rewrite the prediction-market rules. The agency’s proposed rule would amend Regulation 40.11 and add Appendix F to Part 40. The agency would use that framework to decide when a contract linked to war, terrorism, assassination, gaming or illegal conduct is against the public interest.

Sources indicate that that framework would give the agency more room, not less. The proposal would say only that the CFTC may find such contracts contrary to the public interest, dropping the categorical prohibitions in the current rule, according to the Congressional Research Service. The agency withdrew a stricter 2024 proposal in February 2026.

For exchanges, the difference is significant. An agency can revise a rule through its own process. A ban in statute would keep those categories off the table regardless of how the CFTC’s rules change.

The DEATH BETS Act targets a specific set of contracts. Sports is a different matter for operators. Schiff and Curtis have also introduced the Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act. That bill would bar sports-betting and casino-style contracts on these exchanges.

Sources indicate that A unanimous vote on death and war contracts does not prove the same support exists for a sports ban. It does show that senators are willing to legislate directly on what prediction markets can list, rather than leave the question to the CFTC.

Sources indicate that that makes the vote an early sign of how much support Congress has for limiting these platforms. It comes while the exchanges are fighting state gambling regulators in court. Operators now face pressure from state regulators, the CFTC’s rulemaking and Congress at the same time.

The House now has a short window. So far, the chamber’s leadership has given no word on putting the bill to a floor vote, FinanceFeeds reported.

Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients.
  • It has been revealed that to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters.
  • Recent findings suggest that to address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

It has been revealed that to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

Recent findings suggest that to address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

DiLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

The Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This issue is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

Sources indicate that in multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

Streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

Using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

Efficient Request Queueing – Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 02 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Serving LLMs to many applications and users in parallel is challenging because they compete for limited GPU resources.
  • An inference engine like vLLM or HuggingFace TGI consists of.
  • Industry observers note that why do we need a queue here?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Serving LLMs to many applications and users in parallel is challenging because they compete for limited GPU resources. This article is the first in a series on LLM performance, based on our experience with serving self-hosted LLMs at TNG Technology Consulting GmbH. In the first part, we focus on the impact of queuing and discuss different scheduling strategies.

An inference engine like vLLM or HuggingFace TGI consists of.

Industry observers note that why do we need a queue here? Because calculations on the GPU are more performant and resource-efficient when they are done batch-wise instead of isolated for individual requests. This backend queue allows the scheduler to pick multiple requests and put them on the same batch to be processed.

Note that typically each inference engine serves only a single model, and we have multiple deployments running for different models in parallel.

When a single user "A" sends a large number of requests, they will quickly fill up the queue. Other users ("B" and "C") that send their requests only shortly after are blocked from using the same model (until all requests from "A" have been processed). Note that the picture focuses on vLLM as inference engine, but the problem is more general and applies to other backends as well.

In a recent development, at TNG, users don't send requests directly to the vLLM backend but to an API Server (what we call "LLM-Server"). Here we can have separate queues for each user (and model), and a scheduler that is not FIFO (first in - first out) but goes round-robin through all user queues. This achieves some "fair scheduling": for example, in the diagram users B and C send their request a bit later, when user A's first request has already been scheduled. At that time, three requests from user A had been waiting already for some time, but user C has to wait for only one request from user A to be completed.

It has been revealed that the key idea is: prioritize requests from different consumers in our own component and not in the inference backend! Typically, you can't change the order of requests once they have been sent to the inference engine, so you have to bring them in the right order while they are still in the LLM-Server, where we have full control.

You can consider different aspects in order to decide what "fair" scheduling is. In the above example, any new user with a single request should be served before any user is served two or more times in a row. This is "fair" on a number-of-requests level. But you could also look at processing time: how long does a request keep the backend busy? Long prompts and long generations will "block" the LLM for other users for a longer time, so maybe shorter requests should have precedence? Unfortunately, it is very difficult to estimate the generation length. While there are some requests with a "max_tokens" limit, a typical chat message from an interactive AI assistant has no token limit, and can vary between a very short generation ("summarize this text") and a very long one ("tell me a story" / "write all code for xyz").

Depending on the prompts, there can be some benefit in arranging requests based on similarity, so that vLLM can maximize cache hits, which speeds up the performance. This kind of KV-cache-aware routing has recently gained attention by frameworks like NVIDIA Dynamo and AIBrix.

In a business context, and for hosted LLMs, the cost of individual requests can be another metric to consider, but comes with similar challenges.

Sources indicate that the solution can also be extended by having not only one queue per user (and model) but several queues with different priorities. For example, interactive applications like TNG's AI Assistant with chat interface should have higher priority because users who don't see any progress within five seconds will think the application is broken. Users who generate code reviews for tens of files and several thousand lines of code, however, will expect the LLM requests to take some time. And some use cases (like benchmark runs, scheduled via a batch API) should have such low priority that they don't disturb other use cases and are just scheduled when nothing else is running.

Sources indicate that consider again the scenario that one user A sends a lot of requests at once, and some time later a fresh user C joins and wants to schedule a single request. If the scheduler on LLM-Server side sent every request (according to the fair prioritization) immediately to the backend, all requests from A would accumulate again in the FIFO queue. The new user C would have to wait again until all previously received requests have been processed. There would be almost no improvement to the initial scenario without LLM-Server.

Ideally, you could limit the number of maximum elements in the backend queue, but vLLM doesn't give you that option. Therefore, we have to dynamically adjust the rate at which the scheduler on LLM-Server side sends upcoming requests to the backend. Here, our goal is: keep the backend queue length short in order to minimize latencies experienced by new users.

(The simplest approach would be a static rate limit, but this would likely result in underutilization when most requests are short and hard to calibrate for different models and load patterns).

In order to make the backend queue length available in the LLM-Server, we need to fetch the respective Prometheus metrics from the vLLM /metrics endpoint. Our fair scheduler is only allowed to send requests to the backend as long as the backend queue length metric is smaller than three, for example. This target length for the backend queue can be lowered for an even shorter latency for upcoming people, until it results in under-utilized batches and a reduced efficiency - there is a trade-off. Keep in mind, though, that the target queue length does NOT reflect maximum concurrency; there can still be more than three requests being processed in parallel; vLLM will add queuing requests to the current batch as soon as there is sufficient space ("continuous batching").

In a recent development, once you have the feedback loop between backend queue and scheduler in the LLM-Server, you can easily extend the set of vLLM metrics used for making scheduling decisions. For example, for a good user experience in TNG's interactive AI Assistant we aim for a high token generation speed (e.g., >7 tokens/s, that is ~150ms per token), and if the reported time-per-output-token metric rises above 150ms, no upcoming requests will be scheduled.

It has been revealed that you can also program different metric thresholds for different request priorities. For example, for low-priority requests from the batch API we only schedule a request when the backend queue is completely empty: we rather risk short periods of underutilized GPUs than causing increased latencies for any later request with higher priority.

In a recent development, there is quite some potential for optimizations: for example, if you allow scheduling for a backend length shorter than three and the current metric is zero, you can immediately send three requests to the backend before having to fetch the metrics again. In the worst case, none of them fit into the current batch and all of them are in the backend queue (in which case the latest length is three, just fine).

Recently, vLLM added a priority-based scheduling option instead of sticking with FIFO. For this upcoming feature, requests are tagged with a priority before they are sent to the backend. And vLLM would regularly check if any higher-priority request is queuing and then sort all requests by priority (both the running batch and the waiting queue). This would not only let the high-priority request literally jump the queue but even move it directly to the processed batch. The price is (aside from some overhead due to sorting) that lower priority requests would be evicted from the running batch and put back in the waiting queue again.

vLLM understands the request priority as a continuous number. This does not only allow you to distinguish between default, high priority (interactive AI assistant) and low priority (batch API) but you could even make smaller decrements for every request that the user has already sent to the backend and where the response is pending. For example, users B and C send only single requests, which will have priority zero. User A sends four requests at once; the first one has priority zero, too, but the next ones will have priorities one, two, and three, and will be processed later (higher number = lower priority).

Overall, backend-side priority scheduling can be a good strategy for vLLM-based systems, because it simplifies queueing logic on the upstream LLM-Server. Unfortunately, in a realistic setting you cannot get rid of the LLM-Server as an additional scheduling layer, since you need some objective instance to assign priorities to individual requests.

According to recent reports, queueing and scheduling are crucial for applications with multiple consumers and clients of varying priorities, as they significantly impact the user experience. This is especially true in scenarios where multiple clients submit requests in parallel, benefiting from a dedicated "fair scheduling" strategy. Although backend features like priority scheduling can simplify optimization, an upstream gateway server is still necessary to fully manage these complexities.

According to recent reports, in the next part of this blogpost series, we will shift gears and focus on the token generation in the inference engine during prefill and decode phases. In particular, we will discuss resource utilization and strategies for concurrent processing of multiple requests.

yes, disaggregated prefill has improved by now, although it still takes some custom work to set it up correctly.The original challenge of multi-user serving with heterogeneous load patterns and priorities remains, though.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that two federal judges have now declined to protect Kalshi from Upcoming York's state-court gambling enforcement. The case moves to a state judge, and Kalshi disputes how far the proposed order would reach beyond New York.

U.S. District Judge Lorna Schofield denied the CFTC’s renewed emergency request on Friday, November 20, after a telephone hearing that began at 5 p.m. ET, ruling from the bench in Manhattan.

In a recent development, schofield found the CFTC was unlikely to show that the Commodity Exchange Act overrides state gambling laws. That includes licensing rules applied to prediction market operators. Her ruling came a day after Judge Vernon Broderick sent the case back to state court.

The agency’s earlier bid had gone before U.S. District Judge Jed Rakoff.

With the federal route closed for now, the case sits with Justice Melissa Crane of Fresh York County Supreme Court.

The proposed order would bar Kalshi from running an unlicensed gambling business within or from New York, or for people in the state. It covers sports, culture, election and other event contracts. It would also block consumers under 21 from trading.

The reach of that language is Kalshi’s central concern. In a Thursday-night letter to Crane, Kalshi’s Milbank lawyer Sean Murphy warned that the order would close the exchange to all customers everywhere, because the company is based in New York. The letter also pointed to the likely forced liquidation of all open positions. James’s office has mentioned that shutting Kalshi down nationwide is not what it is after.

The CFTC has tried to place event contracts beyond state reach. On April 24, 2026, it sued Newly introduced York in the Southern District of New York. It sought a declaration that it alone regulates event contracts. Similar suits had already targeted Arizona, Connecticut and Illinois.

On August 11, the agency issued an emergency order telling Kalshi to keep performing its functions as a designated contract market. Kalshi had warned the CFTC on August 1 that New York’s pending motion created a market emergency. The order was meant to reassure traders that one state cannot shut down a CFTC-registered exchange.

The financial exposure is large. Fresh York seeks a permanent injunction and full restitution to users. It also wants a $100,000 penalty for each attempt to offer sports wagering, plus a further penalty of three times Kalshi’s gains.

Recent findings suggest that the case lands on top of a 3-1 run of federal appeals court rulings against Kalshi. That record raises the chance the Supreme Court takes up whether states can regulate prediction markets. Separately, the Second Circuit denied relief on November 3 in Kalshi’s own suit against Newly introduced York regulators.

What an AI Marketing Agent Actually Does, and How to Build a Guarded One

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • It has been revealed that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • Industry observers note that an AI marketing agent is a system that pairs a language model with access to real tools, such as a CRM, an ad platform API or a CMS, and lets it work toward a goal instead of following a fixed script.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

It has been revealed that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Industry observers note that an AI marketing agent is a system that pairs a language model with access to real tools, such as a CRM, an ad platform API or a CMS, and lets it work toward a goal instead of following a fixed script. That is the core idea. Much of what gets labeled agentic marketing is either a wrapper around that loop or a scheduled job with a fresh name.

This article breaks down the mechanics in code terms, walks through a minimal guarded agent loop with tests, and gives a framework for deciding what to build, what to buy and what to keep away from any autonomous system. Product capabilities change rapidly, so check each vendor's current documentation.

● An agent is a goal, a tool set and a loop. The model chooses the next action at runtime instead of following branches you wrote in advance.

● Guardrails belong in code. Spend caps, allow-lists and approval thresholds should never depend on the prompt.

● The prototype is the easy part. Validation, retries, logging and evaluation are where the weeks go.

● Match autonomy to reversibility. Let agents do reversible, measurable work and keep irreversible actions supervised.

● Treat vendor claims as claims. Ask for logs and test on your own data.

Many marketing features have been renamed in the last couple of years. Email sequencing, lead scoring and campaign tools are now often described as agents. The honest question is whether a given product is a real architecture shift or marketing automation with a chat box added. Both exist: some systems run a perceive-reason-act loop with dynamic tool selection, while others are if/else branches with a model writing the subject line.

Strip away the marketing language and an agent has three parts:.

● A goal, expressed in natural language or as a measurable target.

● A tool set: functions the model is allowed to call, each described by a schema.

● A loop that runs until the goal is met, a limit is hit or a human steps in.

The reasoning step is a model call. You pass it the current state, the goal and the available tools, and it responds with text or a structured request to call a tool. Your code runs the call, feeds the result back and asks again. OpenAI's function calling guide describes this as a conversation between your application and the model, which is the primitive underneath most agent frameworks.

In a recent development, compare that with a cron job. A cron job runs a rule such as pausing ads below a click-through threshold every morning. It cannot decide that cost per acquisition matters more than click-through this week. An agent can, because the branching is chosen at runtime by a model rather than at write time by you. A useful test: if you can draw the full decision tree before the system runs, it is automation. If the path depends on what the model decides after seeing the data, it is an agent.

Recent findings suggest that ● Perceive. Read current state from an ad platform's reporting endpoint, a CRM webhook or a database. Ordinary code, no model involved.

Sources indicate that ● Reason. One model call containing the goal, the state, a summary of past actions and the schemas of every tool the agent may use.

Recent findings suggest that ● Act. The model returns a structured tool call. Your code validates the arguments against the schema and your guardrails, then executes.

● Observe. Capture the result, including failures. A rate-limit error or validation error is information for the next step.

According to recent reports, ● Patch memory. Record the action and outcome so the agent does not repeat itself.

● Repeat or stop. Loop until the goal is met, an iteration cap is reached or a guardrail escalates to a human.

It has been revealed that steps two and three rely on function calling, where tools are declared with typed parameters and the model returns matching arguments. The Hugging Face function calling guide highlights the same pattern. For connecting tools across systems, the Model Context Protocol is an open protocol for integrating LLM applications with external data sources and tools. Instead of writing an adapter for every CRM and ad account, you point an MCP client at a server that exposes those tools with discoverable schemas.

According to recent reports, lead scoring and routing. The agent reads CRM state, enriches it with lookups, scores the lead and writes back an owner and next action. It is agentic when it chooses which enrichment tools to call based on what is missing, and not agentic when the score is a fixed model output piped into a rule.

Recent findings suggest that ad creative generation and testing. The agent produces variations from brand inputs, debuts a structured test, reads performance data and shifts budget toward what works. This is among the clearest closed feedback loops because the outcome signal is numeric and fast.

According to recent reports, IBM's overview of AI agents in marketing frames a similar progression, from scripted chatbots at one end to agents that decide, design workflows and use function calling at the other. Most products sit somewhere in between.

In a recent development, vendors sometimes blur this line. Four criteria help even from the outside:.

Practical tests: give it a goal it has no preset workflow for and see whether it composes a path or returns an apology. Change the data mid-run and check whether the next step differs. Ask for the tool call log, because a real agent produces one. Ask what happens when a tool call fails; a script throws, while an agent should retry or re-blueprint.

Three questions decide this, and none are about how clever the model is: can errors be detected quickly, can the action be reversed, and what does one bad decision cost?

● Reasonable to hand over: drafting copy variations, summarizing campaign performance, flagging data mismatches, writing internal briefs, pausing clearly underperforming ads.

● Keep supervised: budget reallocation across accounts, legal, medical or financial claims, pricing and discount changes, messages to named customers and final brand-voice sign-off.

It has been revealed that A human approval step costs minutes. An unsupervised mistake in those areas can cost far more.

For many teams the practical answer is to build the orchestration that touches proprietary data and internal systems, and to evaluate off-the-shelf tools for narrow, high-volume tasks that other teams have already solved. What people underestimate when building is not the prototype, which can take an afternoon, but everything after: schema validation, retries, idempotency, rate-limit handling, prompt versioning, cost controls, an audit log and an evaluation harness.

Ad creative is a common candidate for the existing-tool route because volume is high and the loop is similar across businesses. Vendors in this space describe their products differently, so compare scope, integrations and pricing. As one example, Larven describes an AI marketing agent that runs Meta ads, pulls products and copy from a store such as Shopify, and connects to your own ad account. Treat any such description as the vendor's own, and verify it with a trial on your data before committing.

The goal: keep spend inside a daily cap while letting a model propose budget changes. The model is injected as a function, so you can wire in any provider's function-calling API or a stub for tests. The notable part is that every limit is enforced in code. The model proposes, and your code decides.

"""A minimal guarded agent loop. The model is injected as a function, so you can swap in any provider's function-calling API, or a stub for tests.""" from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Guardrails:     allowed_campaigns: set     daily_cap: float            # max total daily budget across campaigns     max_change_pct: float = 0.2 # larger single changes need a human     max_actions: int = 5        # per run @dataclass class State:     budgets: dict               # campaign_id -> daily budget     log: list = field(default_factory=list)     pending: list = field(default_factory=list) def check(call, state, g):     """Return 'run', 'approve' or ('deny', reason). Enforced in code, never by the prompt."""     if call["name"] != "adjust_budget":         return ("deny", "unknown tool")     cid, upcoming = call["args"]["campaign_id"], call["args"]["new_daily_budget"]     if cid not in g.allowed_campaigns or cid not in state.budgets:         return ("deny", "campaign not allowed")     if new < 0:         return ("deny", "negative budget")     others = sum(v for k, v in state.budgets.items() if k != cid)     if others + new > g.daily_cap:         return ("deny", "daily cap exceeded")     old = state.budgets[cid]     if old and abs(new - old) / old > g.max_change_pct:         return "approve"     return "run" def run(model, state, g):     """model(state) -> a tool call dict, or None when it has nothing to do."""     for in range(g.maxactions):         call = model(state)         if call is None:             break         verdict = check(call, state, g)         state.log.append({"call": call, "verdict": verdict})         if verdict == "run":             state.budgets[call["args"]["campaign_id"]] = call["args"]["new_daily_budget"]         elif verdict == "approve":             state.pending.append(call)     return state.

It has been revealed that the tests use a stub in place of a model. They confirm that small changes run, large changes wait for approval, the daily cap and allow-list are enforced, an unknown tool is denied, and a model that never stops is halted by the action limit with everything logged:.

from agent_loop import Guardrails, State, check, run G = Guardrails(allowed_campaigns={"a", "b"}, daily_cap=200) def call(cid, upcoming): return {"name": "adjust_budget", "args": {"campaign_id": cid, "new_daily_budget": new}} def test_small_change_runs():     assert check(call("a", 105), State({"a": 100, "b": 50}), G) == "run" def test_large_change_needs_approval():     assert check(call("a", 150), State({"a": 100, "b": 50}), G) == "approve" def test_cap_and_allow_list_are_enforced():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 90, "c": 10})     assert check(call("a", 115), s, G) == ("deny", "daily cap exceeded")     assert check(call("c", 11), s, G) == ("deny", "campaign not allowed")     assert check({"name": "delete_account", "args": {}}, s, G) == ("deny", "unknown tool") def test_loop_stops_at_action_limit_and_logs_everything():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 50})     g = Guardrails({"a", "b"}, 500, max_actions=3)     run(lambda st: call("a", st.budgets["a"] + 1), s, g)   # a model that never stops     assert len(s.log) == 3 and s.budgets["a"] == 103 def test_denied_and_pending_actions_do_not_change_budgets():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 50})     g = Guardrails({"a", "b"}, 500)     seq = iter([call("a", 150), call("a", 600), None])   # needs approval, then breaks the cap     run(lambda st: next(seq), s, g)     assert s.budgets["a"] == 100 and len(s.pending) == 1.

Run them with pytest. In a real deployment, the model function would call your provider with the state, the goal and the tool schemas, then return the parsed tool call.

● It handles one tool. A real agent needs several, such as reporting, pausing ads and requesting approval.

According to recent reports, ● It keeps state in memory. Production systems need a durable store and idempotent actions so a retry cannot apply a change twice.

In a recent development, ● The thresholds are placeholders. Set your own caps and percentages from your spend and risk tolerance.

Industry observers note that ● It validates the call but not the data. If upstream numbers are wrong, the agent will act on them.

Runaway spend. Budget APIs act instantly and changes compound. Without a hard ceiling in your own code, a reasoning error becomes a billing event.

According to recent reports, dirty upstream data. Stale CRM records, a broken product feed or a misattributed conversion. The agent can act confidently on wrong inputs and leave a tidy audit trail of well-reasoned bad decisions.

According to recent reports, missing audit trails. If you cannot reconstruct why an agent acted, you cannot fix or defend it. Deloitte's State of AI in the Enterprise reports that close to three-quarters of companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, and that only 21% of those companies report having a mature model for agent governance.

● Least-privilege credentials. A separate API key per agent, scoped to exactly what it needs, never a shared admin token.

● Hard caps in code. Daily spend ceilings and a maximum percentage change per adjustment, enforced outside the model.

It has been revealed that ● Human-in-the-loop thresholds. Define which actions always need approval.

According to recent reports, ● Log every tool call. Inputs, outputs, errors, model and prompt version, with timestamps you can query.

Sources indicate that ● Start read-only. Run in suggest mode and compare recommendations with what your team would have done.

Sources indicate that A system that pairs a language model with real tools and lets it pursue a goal. It reads state, decides on an action, executes it, observes the result and decides again.

Automation starts from a trigger and follows branches defined in advance. An agent starts from a goal and selects tools at runtime.

Not on current evidence. They handle high-volume, measurable, reversible work well. Strategy, positioning and final brand approval still sit with people.

Function calling, where tools are declared by schema and the model returns matching arguments, and increasingly the Model Context Protocol for connecting tools.

It depends on how swiftly errors are detected, whether actions are reversible and what a bad decision costs. Automate the cheap and reversible; supervise the rest.

Wrong tool calls, runaway spend, confident action on dirty data and brand drift at scale. Missing audit trails make all of them harder to diagnose.

Sources indicate that an AI marketing agent is less magic than it sounds: a goal, a set of tools and a loop with limits. The model's intelligence matters, but the system around it decides whether it is safe to run. Define the tools narrowly, enforce limits in code, log everything, start read-only and widen autonomy only as the evidence supports it.

Wyoming council backs felony sweepstakes casino ban that reaches payment and hosting suppliers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A bill now sponsored by Wyoming's Legislative Management Council would make running a dual-currency sweepstakes casino a felony.
  • In a recent development, wyoming is moving to outlaw dual-currency sweepstakes casinos.
  • Industry observers note that the gaming committee indicates casino-style sweepstakes games are already available in Wyoming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A bill now sponsored by Wyoming's Legislative Management Council would make running a dual-currency sweepstakes casino a felony. The draft also targets the vendors behind these sites, which raises the legal risk for payment processors and B2B suppliers.

In a recent development, wyoming is moving to outlaw dual-currency sweepstakes casinos. Its bill reaches past operators to the companies that keep them running. The draft reached the Legislative Management Council through Sen. John Kolb, co-chair of the Select Committee on Gaming. The council also agreed to sponsor two other gaming bills, one on pari-mutuel wagering breakage and one on background checks.

Industry observers note that the gaming committee indicates casino-style sweepstakes games are already available in Wyoming. These games let players wager with currency redeemable for money or prizes. The draft would state that the state’s prize-promotion laws do not authorize them. People who take part only as players are exempt.

Working draft 0.4 widens the definition of professional gambling. It covers anyone who knowingly provides services to an online sweepstakes game. Those services include geolocation, payment processing, hosting, game content and advertising. Vendors and processors would carry legal risk, not only the brands that face players.

The approach follows Oklahoma. Under SB 1589, companies that provide geolocation or payment services to a sweepstakes operator after November 1 face the same felony charges as the operator. Oklahoma lawmakers overrode Gov. Kevin Stitt’s veto of that bill. The votes were 34-10 in the Senate and 68-19 in the House.

Complaints to the regulator help explain the push. Wyoming Gaming Commission Executive Director Nick Larramendy described his office’s complaint load to lawmakers. Sweepstakes complaints arrive each week in greater numbers than complaints about any regulated form of gaming. Most come from players whose accounts were shut down when they tried to cash out a jackpot. The operators are often offshore, where the commission cannot reach them.

Taking such sites down would be easier with the ban in place, in Larramendy’s view, because the commission would have firmer ground for working with the Department of Justice and internet service providers. His testimony also pointed to a well-known payment processor. It serves offshore sweepstakes sites while holding a Wyoming online sports betting permit.

The bill has drawn broad support at each step. At its October 5-6 meeting, the gaming committee voted 6-0 in a roll call to recommend the amended draft. It also renamed the bill ‘Online sweepstakes prohibited.’ Lawmakers weighed a rival draft, 27LSO-0200, which would have regulated sweepstakes rather than banned them. Only the prohibition draft went to the council.

A sweepstakes ban bill in Pennsylvania has stalled. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced HB 2801 on September 24. The bill has had no hearing or vote in the House Gaming Oversight Committee. The state’s legislative session ends November 30.

Industry observers note that wyoming’s draft is written as a Senate File. It now goes to the 2027 General Session, which is scheduled to begin January 12, 2027. A general session can last no more than 40 legislative days. If passed, the ban would take effect July 1, 2027.
