Tech Report: Journey to 1 Million Gradio Consumers!

📅 04 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 5 years ago, we launched Gradio as a simple Python library to let researchers at Stanford easily demo computer vision models with a web interface.
  • It has been revealed that today, Gradio is used by >1 million developers each month to build and share AI web apps.
  • How did Gradio keep growing in the very crowded field of open-source Python libraries?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

5 years ago, we launched Gradio as a simple Python library to let researchers at Stanford easily demo computer vision models with a web interface.

It has been revealed that today, Gradio is used by >1 million developers each month to build and share AI web apps. This includes some of the most popular open-source projects of all time, like Automatic1111, Oobabooga’s Text Generation WebUI, Dall-E Mini, and LLaMA-Factory.

How did we get here? How did Gradio keep growing in the very crowded field of open-source Python libraries? I get this question a lot from folks who are building their own open-source libraries. This post distills some of the lessons that I have learned over the past few years:.

According to recent reports, 1. Invest in good primitives, not high-level abstractions.

Sources indicate that when we first debuted Gradio, we offered only one high-level class (gr.Interface), which created a complete web app from a single Python function. We swiftly realized that developers wanted to create other kinds of apps (e.g. multi-step workflows, chatbots, streaming applications), but as we started listing out the apps people wanted to build, we realized what we needed to do: go lower.

It has been revealed that instead of building many high-level classes to support different use cases, we built a low-level API called Gradio Blocks that let consumers assemble applications from modular components, events, and layouts. Despite generally being more work to use, gr.Blocks today represents 80% of the usage of Gradio—including the highly popular apps mentioned above.

In a recent development, with a small team, a focus on low-level abstractions has necessarily meant that we could not chase many tempting, high-level abstractions. But this focus saved us from two common pitfalls:.

Customization-maintenance trap: high-level abstractions are easy to use, but customers request extra parameters to customize them, which in turn leads to increased maintenance burden since every abstraction and parameter needs to be implemented, maintained, and tested to avoid bugs.

The productivity illusion: using high-level abstractions seems like less work, until a user needs functionality that is not supported (which can be hard to predict at the beginning of a project), forcing the developer to do a costly rewrite.

The first problem wastes our time as maintainers of Gradio, while the second problem wastes our people’ time. To this day, Gradio only includes two high-level abstractions (gr.Interface and gr.ChatInterface) which themselves are built with Blocks.

The advantage of having good primitives is even more dramatic in the age of AI-assisted coding, where we find that LLMs are generally good at combing through documentation and building complex applications out of primitives (see all the games being built with three.js for example). It doesn’t take much extra time to write low-level code if the AI is writing the code for you.

In a recent development, the best ambassador for your library is not you, but an enthusiastic user. It follows, then, that you should find ways for customers to share your library or its products as part of their workflow. Gradio’s early growth was fueled by our “share links” feature (which created a temporary public link for your Gradio app in a single line of code). Instead of having to worry about packaging or hosting their code on a web server with the right kind of compute, Gradio users could share their apps with colleagues immediately.

Sources indicate that after joining Hugging Face, we also benefited from being the standard UI for Hugging Face Spaces—widely used by the machine learning research community. The most viral Spaces drew millions of visitors, exposing developers to Gradio, who in turn shared and built their own Gradio apps, using those same Spaces (whose code was publicly available) as a resource to learn how to use Gradio.

Sources indicate that 3. Build for a (growing) niche use case.

In a recent development, early on, we faced a critical decision: should Gradio be a general-purpose Python web framework, or should we focus specifically on building machine learning web apps? We chose the latter, and this has made all the difference.

In the crowded ecosystem of Python web libraries, we are frequently asked, "How is Gradio different from X?" Our concise answer—that Gradio is optimized for machine learning web apps—is memorable and fundamentally accurate. Each Gradio app ships with features particularly suited to ML workflows, such as a built-in queue that can manage long-running ML tasks efficiently, even with thousands of concurrent consumers. The components we have designed are specifically tailored to ML use cases. On the other hand, for a long time, Gradio did not even include features like link buttons, simply because our core users never needed it. By narrowing our focus, Gradio quickly became the go-to choice among machine learning developers—the default "UI for AI.".

Recent findings suggest that of course, we benefited tremendously from choosing a niche that itself was growing. The recent headwinds that have propelled all things AI-related benefited us tremendously and we likely would not have experienced the same kind of growth if we had focused on data science or dashboards for example.

It has been revealed that 4. Your only roadmap should be rapid iteration.

In a recent development, unlike some other libraries, Gradio doesn’t publish roadmaps. Instead, we track emerging trends in machine learning and ship accordingly. In open-source software generally, and AI specifically, shipping features based on the needs of the community (and deprecating features that are no longer needed) is key to continuous growth. As a concrete example, in the early versions of Gradio we built specific functionality to allow developers to show the “interpretation” of their machine learning models—as this was a very popular use case around 2020-21. As interest in interpretation waned, we deprecated this and instead poured our efforts into audio/video streaming and chat-related features.

It has been revealed that our internal process is decentralized as well. Each of the 11 engineers and developer advocates on the Gradio team is encouraged to identify impactful ideas, prototype quickly, engage directly with the open-source community via GitHub, Hugging Face, and social media. Each team member brings these ideas back to the team and we continuously build and rebuild consensus around what ideas are likely to be impactful as we keep growing the most impactful directions.

5. Maximize ways customers can consume your library's outputs.

It has been revealed that when you create a Gradio app and “launch()” it, you get a web application running in your browser. But that’s not all -- you also get an API endpoint for each Python function, as well as automatically-generated documentation for each endpoint. These endpoints can be consumed via Python or JavaScript Clients that our team has built, or directly using cURL.

The reason that we do this is because we want each minute that a developer spends with Gradio to be maximally useful. A single Gradio app should run locally or be deployed without any code changes on Hugging Face Spaces or on your server, or integrate into larger applications programmatically, or even be harnessed by AI agents through MCPs (more on that soon!). By focusing on maximum usability, we hope that developers can continue to get more and more out of the Gradio library.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are incredibly excited to welcome the next generation of large language models from Meta to the Hugging Face Hub: Llama 4 Maverick (~400B) and Llama 4 Scout (~109B)!
  • Released today, these powerful, natively multimodal models represent a significant leap forward.
  • This is just the start of our journey with Llama 4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are incredibly excited to welcome the next generation of large language models from Meta to the Hugging Face Hub: Llama 4 Maverick (~400B) and Llama 4 Scout (~109B)! 🤗 Both are Mixture of Experts (MoE) models with 17B active parameters.

Released today, these powerful, natively multimodal models represent a significant leap forward. We've worked closely with Meta to ensure seamless integration into the Hugging Face ecosystem, including both transformers and TGI from day one.

This is just the start of our journey with Llama 4. Over the coming days we’ll continue to collaborate with the community to build amazing models, datasets, and applications with Maverick and Scout! 🔥.

In a recent development, llama 4, developed by Meta, introduces a newly introduced auto-regressive Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. This generation includes two models:.

It has been revealed that both models leverage early fusion for native multimodality, enabling them to process text and image inputs. Maverick and Scout are both trained on up to 40 trillion tokens on data encompassing 200 languages (with specific fine-tuning support for 12 languages including Arabic, Spanish, German, and Hindi).

It has been revealed that for deployment, Llama 4 Scout is designed for accessibility, fitting on a single server-grade GPU via on-the-fly 4-bit or 8-bit quantization, while Maverick is available in BF16 and FP8 formats. These models are released under the custom Llama 4 Community License Agreement, available on the model repositories.

To help the community leverage these state-of-the-art models immediately, we're thrilled to announce the following integrations:.

The Llama 4 models were pre-trained with a context length of 256K. The Instruct models were fine-tuned to support much larger context lengths: 1M in the large 128 experts version (Maverick), and 10M (!) for the 16 experts version (Scout).

Recent findings suggest that these large context lengths come with a few very interesting architecture choices. Until an official technical report is published, this is what we know so far.

Sources indicate that noPE (cute name, +1 charisma points), which was explored as far back as 2022, just forgoes the traditional positional encoding schemes, such as RoPE, that are most times applied in transformers models. In the case of Llama 4, NoPE layers are used every 4 layers. These layers are crucial for long context, as they use the full causal mask over the context.

For RoPE layers (three out of 4), chunked attention is used.

Meta refers to the interleaved use of NoPE layers, together with temperature scaling (as explained below), as the iRoPE architecture.

If you want to learn more about positional encodings, we recommend Chris' recent post.

As a way to reduce memory requirements, Llama 4 uses chunked attention in the layers that work with traditional RoPE positional encodings (three out of 4 decoder layers). The best way to visualize how chunked attention works is through this ASCII representation that was extracted from the transformers source code:.

This diagram highlights the attention mask that would be used if the chunked attention length was 3. In the case of Llama 4, chunked attention length is 8192. This means that RoPE layers can only keep track of context in 8K blocks, while NoPE layers have access to the full context. You can see it as a more memory and compute efficient version of Sliding Window Attention.

Attention blocks applied to long contexts have a problem: the attention probability scores fade closer to zero as the sequence length increases. This is a known consequence of applying the softmax function to very long sequences. To address this problem, Llama 4 uses a scaled softmax, which the model refers to as temperature tuning. This is applied in the NoPE layers, but not in the RoPE ones as these attend to shorter sub-sequences.

This method is a way to improve generalization for arbitrary context lengths, and probably one of the key factors to achieve 10M context length in Llama 4 Scout.

Llama Scout (the 16 experts version) uses an additional RMS normalization without learnable parameter of the Query and Key states in RoPE layers, after RoPE embeddings have been applied.

Llama Scout is a full MoE consisting of 16 experts. Llama Maverick uses 128 experts, but MoE and dense layers alternate. Therefore, experts are applied in half of the layers.

Llama Maverick was co-distilled from a larger model, Llama Behemoth, using a novel loss function that weight dynamically the student and teacher logit.

The models leverage MetaP, a methodology likely inspired by MuP, to optimally tune hyperparameters across different dimensions including training budget and model size.

Getting started with Llama 4 using transformers is straightforward. Make sure you have transformers v4.51.0 or later installed (pip install -U transformers huggingface_hub[hf_xet]). Here's a quick example using the instruction-tuned Maverick model responding about two images, using tensor parallel for maximum speed. You need to run this script on an instance with 8 GPUs, using a command like:torchrun –nproc-per-instance=8 script.py.

Make sure to check the model cards on the repos (Llama 4 Maverick (~400B) and Llama 4 Scout (~109B)) for detailed usage instructions, including multimodal examples, specific prompt formats (like system prompts), quantization details, and advanced configuration options!

Evaluation results confirm the strength of these models, showing state-of-the-art performance that significantly outperforms predecessors like Llama 3.1 405B. For instance, on reasoning and knowledge tasks, the instruction-tuned Maverick achieves 80.5% on MMLU Pro and 69.8% on GPQA Diamond, while Scout scores 74.3% and 57.2% respectively.

Releasing a giant like Llama 4 takes a colossal effort across teams, geographies and a lot of VMs. In no particular order we’d like to thank Arthur, Lysandre, Cyril, Pablo, Marc, Mohammed from the Transformers team. We are grateful to the full vLLM team for rich discussions, insights, shared testing and debugging during this intense integration with many challenges. With larger optimisation needs, we’d like to thank Mohit for single-handedly adding support to Llama 4 in TGI. These chonky models require some serious engineering at the storage level. This took a lot of effort from Ajit, Rajat, Jared, Di, Yucheng and the rest of the Xet team too.

There are a lot of people involved in this effort, thanks a lot to the rest of the Hugging Face, vLLM and Meta Llama teams for the brilliant synergy!

#150634. When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks ↗ Open Full Page

When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is “Face with Bags Under Eyes” (🫩) and that notes a lot.
  • It has been revealed that technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do.
  • It has been revealed that it’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been a… year, huh? I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is “Face with Bags Under Eyes” (🫩) and that notes a lot. One thing is for sure: the industry we make a living in is in flux, regardless of the outcomes of the AI bubble. Let’s take a look at how we can try and navigate that situation as best we can. But first….

It has been revealed that technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do. This is true regardless of if they fail or somehow succeed in their quest to have everyone paying a subscription fee for their Large Language Model (LLM) technology, which is marketed to us as AI. I’ll refer to this technology as AI for the rest of this article for simplicity.

It has been revealed that it’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either. Everywhere you go, you will see some slop, somewhere. Be it a flyer, website, a village poster or a food truck menu. Heck, people are even using LLMs to work out what’s special about their own children. The effects of this technology are far-reaching, way beyond our own industry.

Sources indicate that the technology has hit us all in tech especially hard though. Mid-last year, I did some investigating because I suspected that so-called AI mandates were becoming increasingly popular and what I learned from conversations then feels like some sort of utopia compared to now. In the space between that piece being published and now, we went from token maxxing to companies realizing that actually, this technology is extremely expensive and not returning the promised outcomes.

Sources indicate that the mandates have cooled, sure, but the demands to use AI to produce more volume, regardless of whether that volume is actually needed or not are still very much there. I’m in a fortunate position to have friendships with people all across the industry, from tech hyperscalers, to tiny little studios, and the stories I have heard from their work life are nothing short of horrifying. No one really seems to be happy with their work either.

This is such a long way away from even a handful of years ago where yes, there was a lot of problematic culture and outcomes from the tech industry, but people were generally quite happy with the work they were doing at least.

The sudden urge to sprint towards AI technologies over the last few years has had a devastating effect in so many places. The technology has encouraged suicide, devastated communities with the data center build-out and of course, displaced thousands of people’s careers. It’s worth noting that I’ve mentioned only a tiny sample of the harms there. If I listed them all, this article would be unbearably long and depressing.

Industry observers note that some harms I do want to touch on though are the effects on our communities in tech. The community spirit of open source and open knowledge was the foundation of the industry’s — especially the web industry’s — rapid success. At the root of everything there was people happy to share knowledge and build everyone up with them. Those people still do exist — myself included — but being one of those people is increasingly difficult.

As the numbers go up in the AI world, the numbers very much go down for independent educators, publishers and community conferences. There’s a developing and worrying culture of “I don’t need to skill up now because I can use AI for work”, so allow me to break down why that reductive view of your work and your career is harmful in the long term.

And don’t ever forget that! Let’s have a think for a second about what actually makes you a good developer, because typing characters in a text editor certainly isn’t it. What makes us good is experience, knowledge, nuance and above all else, creativity.

Look, I get it, AI really can feel like it’s a miracle machine, but it’s important to take a wider view. Along with the published studies on cognitive decline and the widening skills gap, it’s more important than ever to invest in your brain to keep your skills sharp because you’re not getting that repetitive reinforcement that writing code every day gives you anymore if AI tools do everything for you. There’s a reason that I often build most of my teaching around a linear build-along because the tangible nature of repeating patterns you’ve learned really helps that knowledge to sink in.

It has been revealed that as always, this article is addressed to everyone, but I want to talk directly to founders (like me), decision makers, and managers for a second. A substantial part of our job, in fact, the most important part, is to ensure that our workers are looked after. I’m not just talking about compensation and perks here. I’m talking about our responsibility to ensure that our workers’ skills are kept sharp, their professional curiosities are satisfied and above all else that they are happy in the work they are doing. Our workers are much more than “number go up” vehicles.

Industry observers note that you should be giving your developers more time to learn, rather than chasing endless volume. If AI enthusiasts are to be believed, there’s hours upon hours of time efficiencies created by this technology. Don’t fill that time with more volume. Instead, invest that time in developing your worker’s skills. It’s going to avoid burnout which yep, daily LLM use will likely cause in the long term.

One thing that is increasingly clear is that the health of the AI industry is not good. The bubble has already effectively burst in China and more worryingly for economy enjoyers, the “picks and shovels” — AKA the chips industry in Korea — has seen dramatic downturns. This is not how an “inevitable” outcome is supposed to happen!

It has been revealed that the U.S. AI industry is on very shaky ground too. Circular financing, unbelievable levels of debt and a data center build out that simply cannot keep up with the required power levels to turn profits for hyperscalers and startups, mixed with a genuine hatred of the technology by the general public, creates enough risk in itself. Recent events, such as the Democrats dominating the midterms causing AI stocks to drop and as well as Nvidia’s stock because of its CEO being caught up in a spying scandal shine a light on the fragility of the industry. A healthy industry doesn’t work like this.

With all that in mind, what would be a really silly thing to do? Yeh, you guessed it: put AI at the heart of everything in your business. Sure, there’s open source models — which I think is the logical destination of the technology — but how many companies are going to be willing to maintain their infrastructure needs? Not many. The low barrier of entry of commercial AI technology is the selling point, let’s be honest.

Sources indicate that above everything, people need to be invested in, not pushed aside by technology like AI. As I mentioned earlier, it’s experience, knowledge, nuance, and creativity that sets humans far apart from AI. That technology does indeed keep evolving, but even the most ardent of AI supporters will concede that the rate of frontier model improvement is very much levelling out.

There’s never been a more notable time to keep human skills sharp, so here’s some ideas on how to do that.

Sources indicate that this is not just directed at individuals but also at founders, decision makers and managers. Our industry has been historically excellent at investing in skilling people up and we need to bring that back.

Give staff the time and budget to learn, to develop their skills and to engage with the community at conferences. You already know the positive outcomes that brings, so bring it back to your organization. At the absolute worst case, it’ll make the usage of AI in your organization more efficient and when the token subsidies inevitably end, more cost effective.

Again, token subsidies will inevitably end. So, getting thousands of dollars of worth from a $200 a month subscription will be something you’ll look fondly back on. When hallucinations from AI tools are suddenly costing thousands, does it make sense to force your staff to produce as much volume as possible? Of course not.

According to recent reports, my advice is to re-evaluate those prior decisions and invest saved costs back into developing your workers instead, while there’s still a hope of them not burning out completely. Make sure you include your workers in these decisions and discuss the impacts of mandates on them. It’s key for you to understand the impact of these sort of decisions.

Recent findings suggest that this advice is more aimed at developers, but stay paying attention, managers. As I noted earlier, repetition (especially typing) reinforces new learning and existing knowledge. The slower pace also allows your brain to think, which from a quality of output perspective, is imperative. Doing none of that atrophies skills over time.

It has been revealed that I recently read Jenn Schiffer’s great post. She did the Weird Web October challenge and wrote this:.

[…] i encourage anyone who uses ai and/or vibe codes to consider doing an exercise like this without those tools as a way to challenge your brain and you can continue doing your regular work the way you do your regular work.

Sources indicate that I think that’s a very good idea, even if it’s messing around with a little side project — if you’ve got the energy from Producing Value all day, of course. Guess what bosses: this is another way you can make your staff happier, by giving them time to do this on the clock.

It has been revealed that at the end of the day, you’ll miss the soul when it’s gone. It’s not gone yet though. Far from it. Independents like CSS-Tricks, my publication, Piccalilli, and Smashing Magazine are trying hard to keep the soul of our industry alive by sharing high quality educational content with the community.

Most of this content is free at the point of entry, but it certainly isn’t free to produce. We all pay writers fairly to share their knowledge with the community and we are all tiny organizations. We’re certainly not in this game to make huge profits, that’s for sure.

Recent findings suggest that all of us could do more though, but funding is the ultimate barrier. For both companies and individuals, purchase courses, join the membership programs, and purchase ad space. With the right financial support, publications like ours can be a real force in pushing the good stuff back into our industry and bringing everyone up with us. That’s what we do it for.

Some course producers I recommend are Miriam, Sara, Mat, Scott, Brad and Ian, Josh, Ahmad, Christine, Vitaly, Ben and of course, myself! All of these will have generous Black Friday deals, so go ahead and ask your boss to invest in you.

Now, share this post with your boss.

  • As part of our ongoing efforts, we are excited to share the following updates:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at Inception, we have been working to enhance AI model evaluations within the Arabic language context. Previously, we introduced AraGen, one of the first generative Arabic leaderboards, serving as a benchmark for evaluating Arabic LLMs on generative tasks.

As part of our ongoing efforts, we are excited to share the following updates:.

The following sections provide details about each of these updates.

Industry observers note that arabic-Leaderboards is a comprehensive and unified space for all Arabic evaluations and tasks. It is meant to serve as a central hub covering a broad spectrum of evaluations, for models across modalities. Right now, it has AraGen-03-25 and Arabic Instruction Following as live leaderboards. We proposal to expand this space with more leaderboards and tasks for Arabic AI models across various modalities.

We invite interested contributors to reach out to us through the community tab or directly through email in order to discuss how to integrate their work/leaderboards as additional tabs into this space.

In December 2024, we introduced the AraGen Benchmark as the foundation for the AraGen Leaderboard. A key feature of this leaderboard is its dynamic nature, with evaluation datasets remaining private (blind testing) for three months to ensure fair and unbiased assessments. Adhering to the same philosophy, we are publicly releasing the AraGen-12-24 benchmark, along with all model responses evaluated by Claude-3.5-Sonnet following the 3C3H guidelines.

By sharing this benchmark and model responses, we aim to encourage the community to review them, identify any unexpected behaviors we may have missed and help us refine our evaluation framework.

According to recent reports, in this latest AraGen release, we have expanded the dataset to include 340 pairs of questions and answers, up from 279 in the previous version. The distribution remains relatively similar:.

This allocation reflects the primary focus on question answering as the main use cases of any Language-Model/Chatbot/AI-Assistant, while still addressing other evaluation areas, particularly given the complexity of generating challenging queries in Arabic grammar and orthography.

Additionally, we refined the judge system prompt to enhance clarity, even for smaller/weaker judge models.

Maintaining consistency and reliability in our benchmark and evaluation pipeline is crucial as we introduce dynamic evaluation cycles. To ensure this, we analyzed ranking variations among the top 10 models across different dataset versions and system prompt configurations.

We analyzed model performance under two evaluation scenarios:.

It has been revealed that the overall rankings were stable, with the top-performing model (o1-2024-12-17) consistently maintaining its lead. Notably, we observed a swap in rankings between two Claude models, underscoring the sensitivity of our evaluation approach, especially given their initially close scores.

The only significant change in rankings was for the gpt-4o-2024-08-06 model, whose performance markedly improved with the updated dataset and prompt. This sudden jump is at the moment under investigation as part of our ongoing benchmarks-design research.

No major variations occurred solely due to changes in the system prompt, indicating good reproducibility as long as the same judge model (claude-3.5-sonnet) is used. However, we anticipate potential variations with smaller or weaker models as judges, where employing the second system prompt (SP2) may enhance consistency.

Sources indicate that as a summary, the robust, consistently top-ranking performance of o1-2024-12-17—whose top score dropped from 82.67% to 70.25%—continues to reinforce its reliability for Arabic applications under the more challenging updated benchmark. While recent updates to the evaluation pipeline introduced minor ranking shifts, the overall framework remained stable, with top and bottom performers showing consistent positions. Many observed ranking adjustments likely reflect typical evaluation error margins due to minor score differences. Notably, scores for the second- through fifth-ranked models, previously between 70–78%, are now between 51–57%. This highlights that the updated AraGen dataset poses a markedly more difficult benchmark aligned with ongoing advances in reasoning models. Despite these shifts in absolute scores, it is encouraging that leaderboard positions remained largely consistent, underscoring the robustness of the evaluation approach moving forward.

Recent findings suggest that as part of our December release, we introduced 3C3H as a fresh evaluation measure of the chat capability of models, aimed at assessing both the factuality and usability of LLMs’ answers. Over the past three months, we have observed some interesting findings, which we share in this section.

One emergent trend is that the various dimensions are almost perfectly correlated. In most cases, correct answers are scored as both highly helpful and harmless, while most models fail to maintain this correlation for the conciseness dimension. This generally reflects the way we train these models today, where more verbose answers are often rewarded as more helpful. This trend has recently caught the attention of the research community, as exemplified by the release of OpenAI’s GPT-4.5 model. According to their use cases section, answers from GPT-4.5 are more concise than those from GPT-4, while still being equally helpful.

A model that stood out in this analysis is “silma-ai/SILMA-9B-Instruct-v1.0”, which exhibited a higher conciseness score compared to other open-weight models—even those with larger sizes. However, this gain in conciseness came at the cost of helpfulness and other dimensions when compared to its base model, “google/gemma-2-9b-it”. We believe that this analysis, along with optimizing for 3C3H, will enable the community to develop better models through curated datasets while maintaining the correlation across all dimensions.

This is an ongoing effort to better understand how these dimensions are interconnected and how various scenarios and training recipes affect this relationship. Below, we provide a space where you can generate heatmaps for any combination of models of your choice. We hope the community finds it helpful in spotting additional trends that we may not have noticed. Ultimately, we aim for this tool to foster more discussion about evaluation and 3C3H, serving as a resource for others’ work.

We believe that one limitation of this analysis is the zeroing rule, whereby we do not evaluate the other dimensions if the answer is not correct. In the future, we proposal to investigate further whether an answer can be helpful despite being incorrect, and how dimensions such as conciseness and harmlessness factor into this evaluation if the answer is not correct.

Recent findings suggest that one of the core capabilities of large language models (LLMs) is their ability to understand and follow human instructions. This skill is crucial for building reliable chatbots, virtual assistants, and AI systems that do what owners ask. Without strong instruction-following, a model might generate correct information but in the wrong format, ignore user-specified constraints, or produce unwanted content. Instruction-Following benchmark is standardized, objective way to measure a model's instruction adherence and compare models fairly to drive improvements.

Sources indicate that our work took inspiration from the IFEval dataset. IFEval, originally introduced by Google, provides a structured benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs on their ability to follow verifiable instructions. It consists of prompts containing specific, objectively measurable commands such as “use exactly three bullet points,” “include the word ‘innovation’ twice,” or “limit your answer to 100 words.” English IFEval dataset contains around 500 prompts covering 25 different types of such verifiable instructions. Evaluation within IFEval is conducted through Python functions that automatically verify whether instructions are followed, avoiding the need for human evaluators or another AI judge. This makes the evaluations reproducible and unbiased. While IFEval has become the standard for assessing LLMs responding in English, a similarly detailed and structured resource is absent for Arabic.

Sources indicate that construction of our Arabic IFEval dataset began by carefully adapting approximately 300 prompts from the original English IFEval. This wasn't a straightforward, word-for-word translation; instead, we thoughtfully adjusted prompts to clearly reflect Arabic linguistic nuances and cultural contexts. Instructions that made little sense in Arabic, such as those involving English-specific vowel constraints, were either adapted to equivalent Arabic linguistic challenges or omitted entirely. Cultural references specific to English-speaking contexts were replaced with culturally relevant or Arabic-language equivalents to maintain contextual clarity. Additionally, we created unique Arabic-specific samples from scratch, specifically designed to emphasize distinctive Arabic phonetics, orthographic characteristics, and morphology, such as the careful use of diacritical marks (tashkīl), phonetic constraints like avoiding certain letters (e.g., writing without using the letter Alef (ا)), and leveraging root-based morphology to challenge models' word-selection abilities. All prompts underwent rigorous expert validation by Arabic linguists and domain experts who ensured grammatical accuracy, cultural appropriateness, and unambiguous clarity of each instruction.

Arabic IFEval dataset is publicly available for the research community to utilize, test, and contribute to. It is available on Huggingface under inceptionai/Arabic_IFEval.

In a recent development, prompt (Ar):فسر كيف يمكن للتقنيات الحديثة مثل الذكاء الاصطناعي أن تسهم في الحفاظ على الأدب العربي، مع تضمين 12 كلمة تنتهي بأحد الحروف الرافسة (د، ذ، أ، ر، ز، و)، وأن تكون الإجابة مكتوبة بأسلوب موجز لا يتجاوز 120 كلمة. يجب أن لا تحتوي إجابتك على أي فواصل.

Your answer should include at least 12 words ending with one of these specific Arabic letters (د، ذ، أ، ر، ز، و), be concise, and should not exceed 120 words. Your response must not contain any commas.

According to recent reports, to evaluate the models, we adopted a comprehensive methodology combining both explicit and implicit evaluation techniques. Explicit evaluation involved using automated scripts to assess whether instructions were strictly followed, focusing on elements such as correct formatting and specific word usage. Implicit evaluation addressed more nuanced linguistic expectations, such as maintaining the intended response language and avoiding repetitive patterns.

Industry observers note that additionally, we utilized scoring metrics introduced by Google in the IFEval framework, applying these metrics at both prompt-level and instruction-level granularity. These metrics were measured using strict criteria accuracy, which requires adherence to the provided instructions. The prompt-level score is notably harder, reflecting the user's viewpoint by asking, "Did I get everything I requested?" If a prompt included multiple requirements, failing to meet any single requirement would mean the user's request was not fully satisfied. In contrast, the instruction-level score is more lenient, allowing us to evaluate partial compliance.

In our analysis, we will emphasize the prompt-level strict accuracy as it provides the most rigorous assessment of a model's instruction-following capabilities.

We evaluated a broad range of LLMs on both the English IFEval benchmark and our newly introduced Arabic IFEval. This encompassed closed-source models (such as OpenAI's GPT series and Anthropic's Claude models) and open-source alternatives (including the Jais series, Meta’s LLaMA-2 variants, and various open bilingual models). Below, we present a summary of results for a representative subset of these models, comparing their prompt-level accuracy on both English and Arabic IFEval. Accuracy is reported using both strict and loose criteria, with values expressed as the percentage of prompts successfully completed.

It has been revealed that the first sign of trouble is rarely a crash. It is the invoice.

Recent findings suggest that A small team ships a Node.js app on a serverless platform because it is quick to set up. Traffic grows, and the bill grows with it, in ways that are hard to forecast. Some visitors also wait a beat longer for their first response, because the function has to start up before it can answer.

The usual alternative is a virtual private server (VPS). The price is fixed, but the work is not. Someone has to patch the operating system (OS), configure the web server, renew SSL certificates and keep backups running.

Recent findings suggest that between the two sits a third option: managed hosting for Node.js. Here is how the three compare, and how to choose.

According to recent reports, platforms such as AWS Lambda charge for what runs. Lambda's event functions are priced on the number of requests and on duration, measured in GB-seconds, and the memory you choose sets the CPU and the cost per second.

That suits small or spiky workloads. A newly introduced app with little traffic can sit inside the free tier, which covers one million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds a month.

The surprises come with growth. Billed duration is multiplied by the number of requests, so even small inefficiencies in a handler can turn into significant costs at scale.

Then there is the cold start. When the platform has to create a newly introduced execution environment, the first request waits. AWS's own decision guide puts Lambda cold starts at roughly 100 milliseconds to over 1 second.

Since August 2025, AWS bills for that initialization (INIT) phase across all function configurations, so a cold start now reveals up on the invoice as well as in the response time.

Sources indicate that AWS's own analysis found they occur in under 1% of invocations, so steady traffic makes them far less. For a checkout page that does hit one, it is still a pause the customer feels.

There are fixes. Provisioned concurrency keeps functions initialized and ready, but it is billed for the time it is enabled. Newer options let one execution environment handle several requests at once, which means fewer cold starts.

Sources indicate that limits matter, too. A Lambda function can run for 15 minutes at most, and accounts start with a default of 1,000 concurrent executions. Long-running jobs need a different home.

A VPS fixes the pricing problem. A plan costs the same every month, whatever traffic does.

On an unmanaged VPS, the team owns everything above the hardware. That means operating system updates, a firewall, a web server such as NGINX in front of the app, a process manager such as PM2 to restart it if it crashes, SSL certificate renewals and backups that someone has to test.

Sources indicate that none of it is exotic. All of it is a job. Left undone, it is how small teams end up with unpatched servers and no way to restore one.

For a team without a sysadmin, the real price of a VPS is the hours.

Managed Node.js hosting sits between the two. The app runs on a persistent infrastructure, so there is no scale-to-zero and no cold start between requests. The price is a flat monthly initiative. The provider handles the work around it.

Cloudways Velocity is one example. It patches the OS, manages SSL and domain mapping, and runs backups automatically.

The stack is NGINX and PM2, pre-configured with caching, and PostgreSQL is provisioned on all plans. Deployment is by Git push with built-in CI/CD, and a WAF, malware protection, DDoS mitigation and Cloudflare Enterprise CDN are included.

Industry observers note that it ships presets for 12 project types, including Next.js, Remix, Express, Fastify, Astro, Nuxt, Angular and n8n. Anything that builds to SSR or a static bundle and starts with a Node command can run under "Other". Runtime versions are selectable, with Node.js LTS 22.x and 24.x listed.

Recent findings suggest that the trade-off is scaling. Velocity scales vertically: you pick a server size and move up when the app outgrows it. A traffic spike beyond that server's capacity is a capacity problem, not something the platform absorbs by adding instances.

Sources indicate that look at the traffic first. If it comes in bursts with long quiet gaps, serverless often wins. If it is steady, a server is usually simpler to reason about.

Recent findings suggest that take one handler and keep the assumptions the same throughout. Each request runs for half a second on 1 GB of memory. The rates are AWS's published x86 prices: $0.20 per million requests and $0.0000166667 per GB-second, after the free tier, as shown earlier.

Now compare Velocity's looks, which use a pay-as-you-go model billed on an hourly basis according to the selected proposal, ranging from Starter at $20 a month (2 GB RAM, 2 vCPU, 5 apps) to Business at $400 (64 GB RAM, 16 vCPU, 150 apps). More importantly billing is strictly tied to the server plan rather than incoming traffic, a sudden spike in visits will not automatically raise your hourly compute rate.

The Lambda figures leave out API gateway charges, data transfer and logging. A single server has a ceiling, so load-test before assuming one proposal carries 100 million requests.

And Velocity has metered extras: $0.033/GB for offsite backup storage, $0.02/GB for CDN bandwidth beyond the plan's allocation, and $1 per 10 GB of extra disk.

If you want to test managed hosting, you can try Cloudways Velocity during Black Friday with the promo code BFCM802 for 80% off for 2 months plus unlimited migrations, valid through December 4, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the point is the shape, not a winner. Serverless cost tracks usage. A server's cost tracks its size. Choose the one you can forecast.

The strongest case is also the most common one: steady traffic, a small team and a budget that has to be forecast.

Sources indicate that when cloud hosting costs have to fit a budget, a flat monthly plan beats a meter. Velocity's plans give you Node.js hosting with predictable pricing, so finance can see the number in advance and it does not move with every spike.

Because the server stays on, there is no cold start between requests, and the first visitor after a quiet spell is not left waiting.

Recent findings suggest that cloudways says Velocity patches the operating system, manages SSL and domain mapping, and runs backups automatically. The people who built the product keep building it.

Industry observers note that APIs, full-stack apps and automation workflows such as n8n need a process that stays up. A persistent server is built for exactly that.

When the app outgrows its server, you move up a size, and you can move back down if you don't need it.

For most small teams, that adds up to a simple choice. Velocity trades the theoretical ceiling of serverless for something many teams value more: costs they can forecast and an app that stays ready, without a DevOps hire.

Teams whose traffic is extreme, or who need code running at the edge, may still prefer a specialist platform, but that is the exception.

In a recent development, serverless is strongest when work is irregular. A VPS is strongest when you want control and have the time. Managed Node.js hosting suits the large group in between: teams with steady traffic, a small headcount and no appetite for server upkeep.

Teams looking for managed hosting can explore Cloudways Velocity to deploy and scale Node.js applications efficiently.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Still slinging hardware – now with added AI and attendant risks or opportunities.

  • It has been revealed that the two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Still slinging hardware – now with added AI and attendant risks or opportunities.

Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”.

It has been revealed that the two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different tech giant” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.”.

On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.”.

HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player.

Sources indicate that dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure organization.

Clarke said he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead.

Sources indicate that dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with”.

“Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.”.

Sources indicate that HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent.

In a recent development, the CEO noted HPE expects better growth ahead, because upcoming server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year.

In a recent development, dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anyone who has been working in web development for a while will be familiar with this now-legendary meme from xkcd.
  • That’s why it’s vital to use fallbacks to build a robust front end, either to quietly and discreetly avoid the error or to communicate it to our people.
  • According to recent reports, the issue of robustness is so crucial that it is actually one of the four principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anyone who has been working in web development for a while will be familiar with this now-legendary meme from xkcd. It illustrates just how fragile the technical infrastructure of a website or app can be.

That’s why it’s vital to use fallbacks to build a robust front end, either to quietly and discreetly avoid the error or to communicate it to our people.

According to recent reports, the issue of robustness is so crucial that it is actually one of the four principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)! So how can we provide a modern front end without excluding customers who use browsers and hardware that are only partially compatible or not compatible at all?

The answer lies in implementing multiple safety nets in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, so that we are prepared for the worst-case scenario and can provide our users with the best possible experience.

The main difference between the use of fallbacks and progressive enhancement lies in the directions in which the two approaches aim.

While progressive enhancement is about automatically making certain features available as long as they are supported (forward), fallbacks are about what happens when something is not available or accessible (backward).

In a recent development, for example, we can offer a shiny new CSS feature that makes interacting with our website even more enjoyable. But if this feature isn’t available in some browsers, no one will notice, because a version that’s supported by older browsers is available instead. Progressive enhancement in action!

Another example: If JavaScript cannot be loaded for a critical application, we provide a fallback that either offers basic functionality or, at the very least, displays a message explaining what the problem is.

Sources indicate that while one doesn’t necessarily exclude the other, their approaches are quite different. My personal recommendation is to always work with progressive enhancement as a guiding principle and to consider fallbacks whenever possible.

To evaluate upcoming features intended for production, we must first determine the extent to which a feature is supported.

Sources indicate that since 2023, the Interop project has been in place, in which major browser vendors collaborate to release new features for the web platform more or less simultaneously. This serves as a general overview.

Related to this is the Baseline project, which demonstrates, for specific features, the extent to which they are supported and how long they have been available. However, it is extremely important to note that it does not track browser support for accessibility features built into the web platform!

It has been revealed that another crucial resource for checking compatibility is Can I Use. Here, you can get a quick overview of browser support for various features.

Let’s start with the foundation of the World Wide Web: HTML. Modern tech stacks place a strong emphasis on client-side rendered JavaScript, which can offer many benefits to customers in more complex applications. However, there can be just as many reasons why JavaScript might fail to load, so we need a strategy to address this.

In the event of a total failure, we should redirect users to an appropriate error page where they receive information about what went wrong and what not only they, but also we, can do to prevent this in the future. If you want to know how to write error messages that actually help users rather than frustrate them, check out Amy Hupe’s amazing article.

Because this kind of error feedback is so essential, the static site generator Astro, for example, offers the ability to add custom 404 and 500 error pages. You could discuss other possible error codes with your back-end team to implement additional safeguards.

Industry observers note that but what if we also want to make individual sections or components more robust in case JavaScript isn’t available? For this, we can use the  tag, which, according to Can I Use, has excellent browser support. Here’s a highly simplified example of a fictional dashboard component:.

If JavaScript is not available, we will still display the components, but explain in simple and clear terms that they cannot be loaded at the moment and why that is the case.

We give users the option to reload that specific component so they can resolve the issue themselves. We also offer them the option to contact us directly via email if the problem persists.

Recent findings suggest that here, you could add a pre-written text to the  tag, which could include, for example, an internal error code specific to that component in the subject line and have a corresponding body text. This way, they would only need to click the button and could send the email directly using their email program of choice. Support would then have all the necessary information to resolve the problem without needing to ask for additional details.

No matter what your use case is, this pattern can be universally adapted and extended, and ensures that it works even if everything else goes wrong.

Let’s stick with our fictional dashboard component. Say we want to use the CSS anchor() function to display the data, which is fairly newly introduced and has solid, but not great, browser support.

Recent findings suggest that since this is a feature that can include multiple attributes, we need to check whether the ones we want to use are actually available. This is exactly where the @supports CSS rule comes into play! Here, it’s recommended to use the and operator: It should only be used if all attributes are available. If not, the more robust CSS with better browser support is used.

Here’s another fictional, simplified example:.

This approach also serves as documentation: Once the feature has been around for a while and is more well-established, you can look directly for the @supports rule in your code base and check whether it is still necessary, along with its fallback.

According to recent reports, javascript offers us the ability to make our front end even more resilient with minimal effort. To do this, we can use the if…else statement to check whether a specific feature is available. For example, if we want to use the relatively fresh Navigation API, we could check for it as follows:.

If we use a component-based approach, where HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are all contained in a single file, we can also use the conditional ternary operator to display this component or parts of it, or do nothing at all.

Our fictional dashboard component relies on data from the back end, and it only makes sense to display it once the data has successfully reached the front end. So, for example, we could do the following:.

It has been revealed that depending on the use case, it makes sense to display a fallback or even nothing at all. You could also define the conditions more specifically, depending on how robust you want it to be.

My experience so far at various companies has been that the topics of fallbacks and robustness haven’t played as prominent a role as they really should have.

This is surprising, because as we’ve learned, it doesn’t take much to implement various safety nets on the front end, as long as you think ahead about what (shouldn’t) happen if something goes wrong.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript provide us with specific elements and functions to ship robust code and thus avoid upsetting our users and, in the worst case, causing them to turn away from us.

In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we revealed how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs. Real-world AI agents, however, rarely finish their job in a single turn. They have to reason over partial observations, invoke tools, observe environment feedback, and adapt their strategy across multiple steps. So in this post, we will walk through how to train a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix's agentic reinforcement learning pipeline on Cloud TPU v6e-8. You can find the complete code in this GitHub repository.

We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host. Plane Strike is played on a 6x6 grid (A1 to F6) where one 8-cell plane is hidden in one of 4 orientations. Each turn, the agent sees the result of its previous strike and the raw visible board (. untried, X hit, O miss), thinks through candidate placements, and calls the strike(cell="...") tool to strike one cell. The game ends when all 8 plane cells are hit, or after 23 strikes.

Visual Salamandra: Pushing the Boundaries of Multimodal Understanding

📅 11 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Language Technologies Lab takes a major step forward in multimodal artificial intelligence with the release of Visual Salamandra, extending the capabilities of the Salamandra large language model (LLM) to both images and video.
  • Designed with vision-language alignment at its core, Visual Salamandra builds on top of the Salamandra Instructed 7B model by integrating Google’s SigLIP encoder (SigLIP-So400m), a 2-layer MLP projector, and advanced late-fusion techniques to bridge the gap between visual and textual modalities.
  • The resulting architecture enables Visual Salamandra to comprehend and generate contextually accurate responses from diverse inputs, ranging from single and multiple images and videos to purely textual instructions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Language Technologies Lab takes a major step forward in multimodal artificial intelligence with the release of Visual Salamandra, extending the capabilities of the Salamandra large language model (LLM) to both images and video. Visual Salamandra is based on the 7 billion parameters foundational model maintaining its compactness and efficiency while extending it to multimodal tasks.

Designed with vision-language alignment at its core, Visual Salamandra builds on top of the Salamandra Instructed 7B model by integrating Google’s SigLIP encoder (SigLIP-So400m), a 2-layer MLP projector, and advanced late-fusion techniques to bridge the gap between visual and textual modalities.

The resulting architecture enables Visual Salamandra to comprehend and generate contextually accurate responses from diverse inputs, ranging from single and multiple images and videos to purely textual instructions. This development reflects a broader commitment by the Lab to support robust, multilingual, and multimodal AI systems—especially those that prioritize European linguistic diversity.

In a recent development, to adapt Salamandra for visual inputs, the Lab implemented a four-phase training process centered on late-fusion architecture. In this setup, a pre-trained image encoder (SigLIP, 14 patches at 384x384 resolution) generates image embeddings, which are then aligned with the LLM via a custom-trained multilayer perceptron (MLP) projector.

The four training phases include:.

• Phase 1: Projector Pre-training – Only the projector is trained to map image features into the LLM’s latent space.

• Phase 2: High-Quality Vision Pretraining – Using refined datasets (e.g., OCR and re-captioned images), the entire architecture (encoder, projector, and LLM) undergoes joint training.

• Phase 3: Instruction Tuning – The model learns to follow user instructions via visual question answering (VQA), OCR, and other grounded vision tasks.

• Phase 4: Full Multimodal Tuning – Incorporates single/multi-image and video data, along with text-only examples, to optimize the model’s generalization to real-world, multi-input scenarios.

Data diversity played a crucial role throughout training. A total of 6.1 million instruction-tuning instances were used, including 842,000 text-only samples. The training corpus featured data from sources like AI2D, Cambrian, and LLaVA Next, chosen to enhance visual grounding, document understanding, mathematical reasoning, and OCR.

In a recent development, figure 1. Data distribution during the Visual Salamandra 7B training process.

As with previous models from the Language Technologies Lab, Visual Salamandra continues the commitment to multilingual inclusivity, with a strong focus on European languages.

It has been revealed that this approach guarantees that underrepresented languages benefit from instruction tuning and alignment with vision tasks, helping to close the resource gap in multimodal AI research. Visual Salamandra is one of the first models of its kind to integrate such linguistic plurality into a multimodal instruction-tuned framework.

Figure 2. Multilingual generation examples with the model trained with Text Regularization and merged with the original backbone LLM.

Visual Salamandra unlocks a wide range of applications at the intersection of language and vision, such as:.

• Visual Question Answering (VQA): Ask questions about an image or video and receive context-aware, accurate responses.

• Optical Character Recognition (OCR): Accurately read and transcribe text from documents, scenes, and charts.

• Document and Chart Understanding: Analyze complex visual documents or graphical content with embedded text.

• Mathematical Reasoning: Solve visually grounded math problems through multimodal reasoning.

• Instruction-based Image Interaction: Follow detailed instructions in visual contexts, including image captioning and localization tasks.

The inclusion of video capabilities also opens the door for further developments in video summarization, event detection, and multimodal storytelling...

With Visual Salamandra, the Language Technologies Lab demonstrates its ongoing leadership in creating inclusive, high-performing foundational models. By harmonizing state-of-the-art vision encoders with strong multilingual LLMs, the team is setting the stage for next-generation AI systems that see, understand, and communicate—across modalities and languages.

While Visual Salamandra indicates strong multimodal capabilities, it is notable to note its limitations:.

• It may hallucinate plausible but incorrect answers, especially when visual inputs are ambiguous.

• Performance on complex OCR and dense document layouts is still challenging.

• The model was trained with filtered and licensed datasets, but users should remain vigilant about potential biases or inaccuracies, particularly when deployed in sensitive applications.

We recommend using Visual Salamandra in contexts where human oversight is possible and avoiding high-stakes applications without proper evaluation.

Visual Salamandra is released under a Apache License, Version 2.0, allowing for research and non-commercial use.

Stay tunned for future releases and tools built on Visual Salamandra, and explore the full model details in our paper.

The Language Technologies Lab team.

This work has been supported and funded by the Ministerio para la Transformación Digital y de la Función Pública and the Plan de Recuperación, Transformación y Resiliencia – funded by the EU through NextGenerationEU, within the framework of the Modelos del Lenguaje project.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article is adapted from a lesson in Writing Resilient CSS, the newest module in Kevin’s course, CSS Demystified.
  • According to recent reports, modifiers have been with us for a long time, often with modifier classes, but also with attribute selectors.
  • For a lot of use cases, either of those approaches work great, but when it comes to layout, a lot of the time we want the context of where the element is being used to control things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article is adapted from a lesson in Writing Resilient CSS, the newest module in Kevin’s course, CSS Demystified. The module covers configuration options with custom properties, math functions, relative colors, :has(), style queries, and more, all put to work in practical, reusable patterns. The course is 32% off until December 2, 2026.

According to recent reports, modifiers have been with us for a long time, often with modifier classes, but also with attribute selectors. Some common examples are things like different versions of alerts and buttons.

For a lot of use cases, either of those approaches work great, but when it comes to layout, a lot of the time we want the context of where the element is being used to control things.

A card is a nice example of this, where we might have several versions.

In a recent development, the issue here is, if I’m using .card--compact, I probably want to do that for all the cards within a section. That can be annoying to apply to each card, but that’s rendered moot since most people are doing some sort of looping in a template like this these days.

And this works great, as long as we always want the cards to be compact.

However, you might put this together and send it off to the design team for approval, only for them not to like that when the compact cards are lower down the page, the smaller padding isn’t needed to create visual separation between the two sections. Instead of helping with the hierarchy, it’s simply creating a strange visual inconsistency.

We could use something like a resize observer to try and deal with this, but we have a better tool at our disposal: Container Style Queries, which are now Baseline Newly Available.

While they all start with container, for the rest of this article I interchangeable use container query or size query for a container size query, and style query for what we’re talking about here.

Before we get into the good stuff, a quick look at the basics of style queries.

It has been revealed that you’re probably familiar with size queries, which work similar to @media but look at the size of a container, rather than the viewport. Container style queries use the same @container at-rule as container size queries, but instead of looking at a size, they look at the value of a custom property.

This reads as, “if the nearest container has --theme: high-contrast, style the .card like this.”.

A couple of key notes about them:.

Just like with size queries, style queries look at an ancestor, not the element itself. That means this won’t work:.

Industry observers note that the custom property needs to be set on something above the card. Sometimes this can be annoying, and it always tends to catch people out, but because of how I use them, I don’t find this to be much of a limitation.

if() is also on the way, and allows for style queries as well, but if() is able to see the value of custom properties on the element it’s being used. The big difference is it can only be used for a single property, while style queries can be used for rules with multiple properties.

Let’s take a look at a card again, first with a modifier like we might do now. To change it up, we’ll use an attribute modifier instead of a class.

Switching this up to use a style query, we could do something like this instead:.

In a recent development, if we’re in the mindset of how we’re used to using modifiers, this feels like a lot more work with no real payoff, but now, anything that can set a custom property can switch it: a media query, a container query, a :has() selector, or a parent section. The styles for the alternative layout are written once, and there are lots of ways to switch them on, making it so much more versatile.

Sources indicate that one easy win here is if you’re working with a CMS. Now, the author of the page can chose from an option, which just sets one custom property value for a section of the page, and the appropriate styles kick in.

Where I feel like this has the most potential is when dealing with conditional styles like the sidebar we looked at earlier, where we can enable the compact card layout however we want:.

Here’s an overflow grid pattern I use quite a bit:.

The problem is that it always overflows, even if I don’t have enough children to warrant it. Like here, the first row, the third card is just barely overflowing, making it awkward more than anything.

One solution is to use a container query and :has(), where we let the items fill the space when there are fewer than five of them, and there’s enough space:.

In a recent development, and this works really well! But sometimes, we might need to make some bigger changes depending on where the elements are being used.

In a recent development, let’s say, for example, our page has a hero component that goes to two columns on larger screens, with a heading on one side and a set of featured articles in an overflow grid on the other. The container query is making sure the overflow is on in the narrow space, but horizontal scrolling there seems a little awkward.

When the split happens, I’d rather the grid scrolled vertically instead, and we can leverage style queries to pull this off.

First, we give the overflow grid a configuration option for its direction, defaulting to columns:.

Now the split can change when it goes to two columns:.

And this works, but the result isn’t great. The grid is still sized for horizontal scrolling, so we end up with a tall, awkward column, and no overflow at all.

This is where style queries come in. The overflow grid can “listen” for the direction change and adjust its own styles to match.

In a recent development, the split section isn’t styling the overflow grid directly, which is possible, but always awkard, and leads to fragile code bases. Instead, we created some configurable settings on that grid, and simply adjusted them as needed.

Industry observers note that I don’t think style queries mean it’s time to throw out modifier classes (or data modifiers). They still work great, especially since a style query can’t look at the element it’s styling. If I simply want my button to be an accent button, or a pill shape, then a modifier makes a lot of sense.

On top of that, a regular media query or container query, or even an intrinsic pattern might get the job done, and that’s great too.

Sources indicate that where style queries shine is when the condition and the styles need to live in different places, or when one condition needs to affect several things at once, like the split above. Instead of a layout reaching in and styling its children, it changes a few settings, and each component decides how to respond.

That’s a big part of what I think of as writing resilient CSS: components that keep working, and adapt sensibly, no matter where they end up.

This article is adapted from a lesson in Writing Resilient CSS, the newest module in my course, CSS Demystified. The module covers configuration options with custom properties, math functions, relative colors, :has(), style queries, and more, all put to work in practical, reusable patterns.
