💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that hugging Face and Protect AI partnered in October 2024 to enhance machine learning (ML) model security through Guardian’s scanning technology for the community of developers who explore and use models from the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Since October, Protect AI has significantly expanded Guardian's detection capabilities, improving existing threat detection capabilities and launching four upcoming detection modules:.
  • With these updates, Guardian covers more model file formats and detects additional sophisticated obfuscation techniques, including the high severity CVE-2025-1550 vulnerability in Keras.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hugging Face and Protect AI partnered in October 2024 to enhance machine learning (ML) model security through Guardian’s scanning technology for the community of developers who explore and use models from the Hugging Face Hub. The partnership has been a natural fit from the start—Hugging Face is on a mission to democratize the use of open source AI, with a commitment to safety and security; and Protect AI is building the guardrails to make open source models safe for all.

Since October, Protect AI has significantly expanded Guardian's detection capabilities, improving existing threat detection capabilities and launching four upcoming detection modules:.

With these updates, Guardian covers more model file formats and detects additional sophisticated obfuscation techniques, including the high severity CVE-2025-1550 vulnerability in Keras. Through enhanced detection tooling, Hugging Face users receive critical security information via inline alerts on the platform and gain access to comprehensive vulnerability reports on Insights DB. Clearly labeled findings are available on each model page, empowering users to make more informed decisions about which models to integrate into their projects.

As of April 1, 2025, Protect AI has successfully scanned 4.47 million unique model versions in 1.41 million repositories on the Hugging Face Hub.

Recent findings suggest that to date, Protect AI has identified a total of 352,000 unsafe/suspicious issues across 51,700 models. In just the last 30 days, Protect AI has served 226 million requests from Hugging Face at a 7.94 ms response time.

Industry observers note that protect AI’s Guardian applies a zero trust approach to AI/ML security. This especially comes into play when treating arbitrary code execution as inherently unsafe, regardless of intent. Rather than just classifying overtly malicious threats, Guardian flags execution risks as suspicious on InsightsDB, recognizing that even harmful code can look innocuous through obfuscation techniques (see more on payload obfuscation below). Attackers can disguise payloads within seemingly benign scripts or extensibility components of a framework, making payload inspection alone insufficient for ensuring security. By maintaining this cautious approach, Guardian helps mitigate risks posed by hidden threats in machine learning models.

AI/ML security threats are evolving every single day. That's why Protect AI leverages both in-house threat research teams and huntr—the world's first and largest AI/ML bug bounty program powered by our community of over 17,000 security researchers.

Industry observers note that coinciding with our partnership launch in October, Protect AI released a fresh program on huntr to crowdsource research on new Model File Vulnerabilities. Since the launch of the program, they have received over 200 reports that Protect AI teams have worked through and incorporated into Guardian—all of which are automatically applied to the model scans here on Hugging Face.

As more huntr reports come in and more independent threat research is conducted, certain trends have emerged.

Industry observers note that library-dependent attack chains: These attacks focus on a bad actor’s ability to invoke functions from libraries present in the ML workstations environment. These are reminiscent of the “drive-by download” style of attacks that afflicted browsers and systems when common utilities like Java and Flash were present. Typically, the scale of impact of these attacks are proportional to the pervasiveness of a given library, with common ML libraries like Pytorch having a far wider potential impact than lesser used libraries.

According to recent reports, payload obfuscation: Several reports have highlighted ways to insert, obfuscate, or “hide” a payload in a model that bypasses common scanning techniques. These vulnerabilities use techniques like compression, encoding, and serialization to obfuscate the payload and are not easily detectable. Compression is an glitch since libraries like Joblib allow compressed payloads to be loaded directly. Container formats like Keras and NeMo embed additional model files, each potentially vulnerable to their own specific attack vectors. Compression exposes users to TarSlip or ZipSlip vulnerabilities. While the impacts of these will often be limited to Denial of Service, in certain circumstances these vulnerabilities can lead to Arbitrary Code Execution by leveraging path traversal techniques, allowing malicious attackers to overwrite files that are often automatically executed.

According to recent reports, framework-extensibility vulnerabilities: ML frameworks provide numerous extensibility mechanisms that inadvertently create dangerous attack vectors: custom layers, external code dependencies, and configuration-based code loading. For example, CVE-2025-1550 in Keras, reported to us by the huntr community, demonstrates how custom layers can be exploited to execute arbitrary code despite security features. Configuration files with serialization vulnerabilities similarly allow dynamic code loading. These deserialization vulnerabilities make models exploitable through crafted payloads embedded in formats that people load without suspicion. Despite security improvements from vendors, older vulnerable versions and insecure dependency handling continue to present significant risk in ML ecosystems.

Sources indicate that attack vector chaining: Recent reports demonstrate how multiple vulnerabilities can be combined to create sophisticated attack chains that can bypass detection. By sequentially exploiting vulnerabilities like obfuscated payloads and extension mechanisms, researchers have shown complex pathways for compromise that appear benign when examined individually. This approach significantly complicates detection and mitigation efforts, as security tools focused on single-vector threats often miss these compound attacks. Effective defense requires identifying and addressing all links in the attack chain rather than treating each vulnerability in isolation.

It has been revealed that the industry-leading Protect AI threat research team, with help from the huntr community, is continuously gathering data and insights in order to develop newly introduced and more robust model scans as well as automatic threat blocking (available to Guardian customers). In the last few months, Guardian has:.

In a recent development, enhanced detection of library-dependent attacks: Significant expansion of Guardian’s scanning capabilities for detecting library-dependent attack vectors. The scanners for PyTorch and Pickle now perform deep structure analysis of serialized code, examining execution paths and identifying potentially malicious code patterns that could be triggered through library dependencies. For example, the PyTorch torchvision.io functions can overwrite any file on the victim’s system to either include a payload or delete all of its content. Guardian can now detect many more of these dangerous functions in popular libraries such as PyTorch, Numpy, and Pandas.

Uncovered obfuscated attacks: Guardian performs multi-layered analyses across various archive formats, decompressing nested archives and examining compressed payloads for malicious models. This approach detects attempts to hide malicious code through compression, encoding, or serialization techniques. Joblib, for example, supports saving models using different compression formats which can obfuscate Pickle deserialization vulnerabilities, and the same can be done in other formats like Keras which can include Numpy weights files that have deserialization payloads in them.

Detected exploits in framework extensibility components: Guardian’s constantly improving detection modules alerted people on Hugging Face to models that were impacted by CVE-2025-1550 (a critical security finding) before the vulnerability was publicly disclosed. These detection modules comprehensively analyze ML framework extension mechanisms, allowing only standard or verified components and blocking potentially dangerous implementations, regardless of their apparent intent.

Identified additional architectural backdoors: Guardian’s architectural backdoor detection capabilities were expanded beyond ONNX formats to include additional model formats like TensorFlow.

Expanded model format coverage: Guardian’s true strength comes from the depth of its coverage, which has driven substantial expansion of detection modules to include additional formats like Joblib and an increasingly popular llamafile format, with support for additional ML frameworks coming soon.

According to recent reports, provided deeper model analysis: Actively research on additional ways to augment current detection capabilities for better analysis and detection of unsafe models. Expect to see significant enhancements in reducing both false positives and false negatives in the near future.

Sources indicate that through the partnership with Protect AI and Hugging Face, we’ve made third-party ML models safer and more accessible. We believe that having more eyes on model security can only be a good thing. We’re increasingly seeing the security world pay attention and lean in, making threats more discoverable and AI usage safer for all.

This is something we encounter regularly when working with translation services in Canada, where language choices often need to account not only for vocabulary but also for context, terminology, and the expectations of the intended audience.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rajiv Ramaswami will stay in the chair until upcoming hire lands, then stick around as advisor.

Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the tech giant’s board can find his successor.

Ramaswami declared his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.

The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit.

Industry observers note that in chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the organization grew.

The CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami noted he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers.

Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole fresh set of ecosystems.”.

Ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff, the CEO said the organization's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.”.

Sources indicate that news of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix unveiled its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The company added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami stated high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest new customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business.

Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the manufacturer’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simon Alibert and Rémi Cadène from the LeRobot team with Reachy 1 — Photo: Léa Crespi.

Since Hugging Face started the LeRobot library in 2024, led by ex-Tesla lead Remi Cadene, the Hugging Face Hub has promptly become the most widely used hub and software platform for open robotics with models, datasets, spaces and libraries.

Today, we’re excited to take it a step further by welcoming Pollen Robotics to Hugging Face, a team that's spent the last 9 years building open-source robots and hardware.

In a recent development, we believe robotics could be the next frontier unlocked by AI — and it should be open, affordable, and private. Our vision: a future where everyone in the community, from hobbyists to enterprises, can build or use robot assistants or games, starting from open solutions instead of closed, remote controlled, hardware.

Industry observers note that from the start, we built Pollen Robotics with open source at its core, driven by our belief that robots will play a profound role in our lives — serving as the interface between AI and the physical world. Hugging Face is a natural home for us to grow, as we share a common goal: putting AI and robotics in the hands of everyone.

This marks the fifth acquisition for Hugging Face, after notable additions like Gradio and XetHub.

According to Clem's 2025 prediction about robots, "at least 100k personal robots will be pre-ordered" this year, signaling massive growth in the space.

Sources indicate that this month also celebrates one year since Hugging Face created LeRobot. The community of LeRobot-native DIY robot builders has flourished on YouTube and Discord, truly democratizing access to robotics technology. In just twelve months, the GitHub repository has grown from zero to over 12,000 stars, with dramatic growth continuing into 2025.

According to recent reports, the first robot we’re offering is Reachy 2 — your friendly little lab partner for the AI era that is already in use in labs like Cornell or Carnegie Mellon. It’s a state-of-the-art humanoid robot that is open-source & VR-compatible, built for research, education, and embodied AI experiments. You can already order one for $70,000 by emailing sales@pollen-robotics.com.

Hugging Face is the most used platform for AI builders, with over 7 million users and a thriving community of researchers, developers, and organizations. Founded by Clément Delangue (CEO), Julien Chaumond (CTO), and Thomas Wolf (CSO), the company has become a central hub for AI, hosting the most popular open-source models and datasets, including Meta’s LLaMA 4, DeepSeek R1, Stable Diffusion, Black Forest Flux, Mistral, OpenAI Whisper and millions of others. Its AI app store features over 500,000 ready-to-use applications called spaces, making state-of-the-art AI accessible to all. Hugging Face has raised over $395 million to date from leading investors including Google, Amazon, Nvidia, Salesforce, Sequoia, Coatue, Lux Capital, and Addition.

Pollen Robotics, established in 2016, is a leading developer of open-source humanoid robots designed for advanced research and real-world applications. Founded by former researchers from Inria's Flowers team, including Matthieu Lapeyre and Pierre Rouanet, the firm leverages years of experience at the intersection of robotics hardware and applied artificial intelligence, to develop innovative and user-friendly robotic platforms. Reachy 2 is the latest generation of Pollen Robotics’ flagship humanoid robot. Designed as a versatile platform for embodied AI, Reachy 2 combines advanced hardware with user-friendly software, enabling intuitive interactions and agile manipulation. With open-source hardware and software at its core, Reachy 2 provides researchers, and developers unprecedented freedom to explore human-robot interactions, machine learning applications, and practical AI-driven tasks.

Reachy has been adopted by esteemed institutions such as Accenture, CEA, CNRS, Cornell University, and Carnegie Mellon University, underscoring its versatility in fields ranging from advanced AI research to practical manipulation tasks. Pollen Robotics has won several awards including second place at the prestigious ANA Avatar XPRIZE in 2022, highlighting its innovative prowess in remote presence, dexterous manipulation and control technologies.

With hundreds of units deployed across more than 20 countries, Pollen Robotics has redefined the capabilities of open-source humanoid robots, fostering collaboration and customization in the global robotics community.

  • Recent findings suggest that VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter.

VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 concerns.

Recent findings suggest that VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the latest advisory includes the following remarks:.

Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States.The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us.

Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware owners rely on to manage hosts and VMs.

This is the third 9.8-rated authentication glitch VMware has fixed in vCenter since July.

Two of the other critical flaws in this newly introduced advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability.

Recent findings suggest that the other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that consumers can turn off.

Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software.

There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer.

Industry observers note that VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce.

In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Contact: hyen@cs.princeton.edu Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02694 Website: https://princeton-nlp.github.io/HELMET Code & Data: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/HELMET.

Industry observers note that since we first released HELMET last October, there has been more development on long-context language models than ever before, and we are thrilled to see the adoption of HELMET by the community, such as Microsoft's Phi-4 and AI21's Jamba 1.6. After the initial release, we have added more models to our evaluation suite and conducted additional analyses. We are excited to share our new results and present HELMET at ICLR 2025!

In a recent development, in this blog, we will describe the construction of HELMET, our key findings, and how practitioners can use HELMET to differentiate between various LCLMs in future research and applications. Finally, we will conclude with a quickstart guide for using HELMET with HuggingFace.

It has been revealed that from summarizing numerous legal documents to learning latest tasks on the fly, long-context language models (LCLMs) have immense potential to change the way we use and interact with language models. Language models have been limited by their context window, which is around 2K to 8K tokens (e.g., ChatGPT, Llama-2/3). Recently, model developers have been constantly increasing the context window of their models, with recent models like GPT-4o, Claude-3, and Gemini-1.5 supporting context windows of up to millions of tokens.

According to recent reports, however, with longer context windows, previous natural language benchmarks (e.g., Scrolls) are no longer suitable for evaluating LCLMs. Consequently, perplexity and synthetic tasks (e.g., needle-in-a-haystack) emerged as the most popular evaluation metrics for recent LCLMs, but they often do not reflect real-world performance. Model developers may also evaluate on other arbitrary datasets, which complicates model comparisons. Furthermore, existing benchmarks for LCLMs may show confusing and counterintuitive results, making it difficult to understand the strengths and weaknesses of different models (Figure 1).

In this work, we propose HELMET (How to Evaluate Long-Context Models Effectively and Thoroughly), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LCLMs that improves upon existing benchmarks in several ways—diversity, controllability, and reliability. We evaluate 59 recent LCLMs and find that it is crucial to evaluate models across diverse applications to understand their capabilities and frontier LCLMs are still limited on complex tasks.

With the development of LCLMs across both industry and the open-source community, it is crucial to have a reliable method for evaluating and comparing these models. However, current models are often evaluated on different benchmarks (Table 1).

A common practice for evaluating long-context language models is to use perplexity or synthetic tasks, such as needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH). However, recent works have shown that perplexity does not correlate well with downstream performance (Fang et al., 2024). In Figure 2, we show that synthetic tasks like NIAH do not correlate with real-world performance, but the more complex synthetic tasks achieve higher correlation with real-world tasks.

Among the existing benchmarks with realistic applications, such as ZeroScrolls (Shaman et al., 2023), LongBench (Bai et al., 2024), and InfiniteBench (Zhang et al., 2024), there are still crucial limitations:.

Thus, we propose HELMET to address these limitations and provide a comprehensive evaluation of LCLMs.

We design HELMET with the following desiderata:.

Recent findings suggest that table 2 demonstrates an overview of the benchmark. In our experiments, we evaluate on input length from 8K to 128K tokens, but HELMET can be easily extended to even longer context lengths.

Diverse coverage: HELMET includes a diverse set of tasks, such as retrieval-augmented generation with real retrieval passages, generation with citations, and summarization. We carefully select datasets with naturally long contexts that reflect real-world applications. These datasets are complemented with reliable evaluation settings, such as model-based evaluations and human studies.

Sources indicate that controllable length and difficulty: An important dimension to consider when evaluating LCLMs is the input length, as longer inputs can provide more information while challenging the model's ability to process noisy contexts. In our tasks, we can control the input length by changing the number of retrieved passages (RAG, Cite, Re-rank), the number of demonstrations (ICL), or the length of the input document (LongQA, Summ). Although LongQA and Summ cannot be easily extended to longer contexts, we intentionally chose datasets with natural documents of length far greater than 100K tokens, such that they can still be used to evaluate frontier LCLMs.

It has been revealed that reliable evaluation: Many existing benchmarks still use n-gram-based metrics, such as ROUGE, despite their poor correlation with human judgments (Goyal et al., 2023). We employ model-based evaluations that show better distinguishability between models and different input lengths (Figure 3). Furthermore, our human studies show that our metrics have a high agreement with human judgments.

In a recent development, robust prompting: Existing long-context benchmarks often require models to follow instructions, but many model developments revolve around base models, which have to rely on synthetic tasks or perplexity for evaluation. Thus, we support base models for a subset of our tasks via in-context learning examples. This substantially improves the performance of base models, which is more reflective of real-world applications.

Our experiments and analyses include a comprehensive set of 59 LCLMs. To our knowledge, this is the most thorough and controlled comparison of long-context models on diverse applications. These models cover both leading proprietary and open-source models, and we also consider models with different architectures (e.g., full-attention transformers, hybrid architectures) and positional extrapolation techniques. In this section, we will highlight a few key findings from our experiments.

Recent findings suggest that long-context benchmarks are often constructed with specific applications in mind, such as summarization or question answering, which limits the understanding of LCLMs in a broader context. We examine model performance over a wide range of real tasks and find that different categories do not always correlate with each other (Figure 4).

It has been revealed that while some tasks moderately correlate with each other (e.g., RAG and MS-MARCO) due to their retrieval-based nature, others show little correlation (e.g., Summ and Cite). Notably, ICL has the lowest correlation with other tasks, which suggests that it is a unique task that requires different capabilities from the model. Therefore, model developers should evaluate across these distinct axes to draw a more holistic picture of the model's capabilities.

We present the results of the frontier proprietary models as well as a few open-source models on HELMET. Additional results can be found in the paper and the website.

It has been revealed that first, we observe that open-source models lag behind closed-source models on complex tasks. Although the gap appears small on simpler tasks, such as Recall, the gap widens on more complex ones, such as Cite.

Industry observers note that furthermore, performance degradation with increasing lengths is category-dependent. Even the most advanced models, such as GPT-4o and Gemini, experience a significant decrease in performance on tasks like re-ranking. This change in performance cannot be observed from simply looking at the synthetic task performance.

Industry observers note that finally, there is no clear winner across all categories, thereby calling for evaluation across different axes. Additional analysis, such as the performance of different positional extrapolation methods and the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon, can be found in the paper.

According to recent reports, it is often expensive to run all the baselines for evaluating LCLMs, especially at long contexts given their computational and memory costs. For example, running HELMET at all lengths on a 70B model requires a node with 8 * 80GB GPUs for hundreds of GPU hours, which can be costly. By evaluating on HELMET, researchers can directly compare their models to existing ones simply by referencing our results, which cover 59 models of different sizes and architectures. You can find the leaderboard on our website.

Recent findings suggest that HELMET is a step towards a more comprehensive evaluation of long-context language models, but there are still many more exciting applications of LCLMs. For example, we recently released LongProc, a benchmark for evaluating LCLMs on long-form generation and following procedures, which are critical for developing reasoning models that generate tens of thousands of tokens in thinking steps. Although summarization tasks have long outputs (up to 1K tokens), LongProc focuses on even longer outputs, up to 8K tokens. Similar to HELMET, LongProc is also designed with reliable evaluation settings and diverse tasks. We are working on integrating LongProc into HELMET's evaluation suite, and we hope that this will provide a more comprehensive evaluation of LCLMs on long-form tasks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco.
  • A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.
  • Sources indicate that this case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco.

A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.

Sources indicate that this case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of New York.

The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy.

The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision indicates Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors demonstrated evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.”.

Another item of evidence apparently revealed a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a manufacturer called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.”.

Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices.

In a recent development, huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ says.

The feds say the Chinese organization also “lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.”.

Huawei has issued a statement noting that the jury found it not guilty of racketeering and insisting the charges on which it was found guilty are “without legal or factual merit.”.

“The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades,” the statement adds.

Sentencing will take place in September 2027.

The presiding judge will likely consider the fact that in 2017, US authorities fined Chinese telco equipment maker ZTE $900 million just for selling to Iran, then added an additional $1.4 billion penalty to lift a ban on doing business in the USA.

Washington has already banned Huawei from selling its telco products and personal devices in the USA. Lawmakers have little appetite to let the Chinese company return to the American market after spending billions to help American telcos replace the Huawei kit with locally made alternatives. ®.

#150616. The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt.
  • A model decision is not automatically an authorized action.
  • Recent findings suggest that the answer can’t rely only on the model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a new security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs?

A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes important the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system.

Recent findings suggest that the answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary.

Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

Recent findings suggest that together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened?

In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do.

Recent findings suggest that there is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below.

Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

According to recent reports, an agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them.

Industry observers note that docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally.

Recent findings suggest that network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction.

For an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own.

A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent:.

The notable part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow.

This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate?

Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools.

According to recent reports, MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it.

According to recent reports, docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server:.

Sources indicate that here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server.

Industry observers note that this makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint.

One boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead.

With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do?

It has been revealed that setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied.

Recent findings suggest that docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses.

According to recent reports, audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows.

Denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working.

Industry observers note that current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available.

That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened?

According to recent reports, AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying?

Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker.

Sources indicate that in practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built.

According to recent reports, for organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself.

Sources indicate that AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on.

Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance.

Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an issue, upgrade a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way.

Sources indicate that the agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access.

Now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether.

For governance activity right now covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow.

It has been revealed that if that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime.

In a recent development, the model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision.

That is the practical value of the three layers working together:.

Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate.

MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use.

Audit + Visibility reveals how governed activity was handled.

Recent findings suggest that taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently.

According to recent reports, the challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions.

Sources indicate that that makes the boundary around the agent just as important as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded.

Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts.

In a recent development, the goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority.

As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more.

Coding agents can reach more than their task needs. See how Docker AI Governance controls network, filesystem, credential, and MCP access, then test it.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controversial move could save the BBC by bringing in more than a billion in extra funding each year.
  • A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.
  • The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its looks for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversial move could save the BBC by bringing in more than a billion in extra funding each year.

A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.

The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its looks for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027.

One of the options is to extend the license so that it is needed to access streaming platforms like Netflix, Disney+, or Amazon Prime Video.

This is unlikely to prove popular, but if the fee was held at the current level (£180, $236 per year) it would generate up to £1.6 billion extra a year for the corporation and would better reflect how audiences watch television, according to entertainment industry research biz Ampere Analysis.

As any Brit knows, the BBC is funded primarily through the TV license, which is charged on a per household basis. A license is required to watch or record live TV on any broadcast channel, or access the BBC iPlayer for on-demand content. A license is not right now needed for on-demand streaming platforms.

Sources indicate that the government is understood to believe the current license scheme is “outdated and no longer fit for purpose,” and is weighing several options to reform it. Scrapping it entirely looks unlikely for now: a committee found that other European countries that did so ended up with less stable funding for their public service broadcasters, and weaker independence from political interference.

Recent findings suggest that TV licensing is controversial, with some people resenting having to pay the BBC just for the right to watch television. In response, the government has tried to limit fee increases, and made the license free for some elderly people. Together, these moved have reduced the BBC's funding, leading to service cuts and further. dissatisfaction.

Responding to a report by the National Audit Office (NAO) that found the BBC will remain under financial pressure despite widespread cuts, the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) urged the government to secure the broadcaster's future in the next charter renewal.

"The BBC shouldn't be in this position. These cuts are the result of a decade of underfunding, with NAO identifying a 26 percent real-terms reduction in license fee income in the last nine years alone," stated NUJ general secretary Laura Davison.

It has been revealed that many Brits no longer pay the license fee, preferring to watch only streamed content, or claiming that they do. Ampere says more than 90 percent of UK households watch live television, but only 84 percent of eligible households pay the fee, meaning a sizable number are freeloading. Extending the fee to cover on-demand and streaming services would close the loophole, it says.

Recent findings suggest that another option could see the license fee reduced to £150 ($196) in 2028, assuming perfect enforcement, analysts at Ampere say. They neglect to detail what this "perfect enforcement" mechanism consists of.

"Widening the remit of the license fee at current prices would significantly increase the BBC’s funding, strengthening its long-term financial position and ability to compete with local and global rivals," said Ampere Senior Analyst Sam Khoury.

"Alternatively, in the context of ongoing cost of living pressures in the UK, the government could opt to reduce the price of the fee payable by the extended pool of consumers. Coupled with a reformed enforcement mechanism that effectively reduces evasion, this would still improve the BBC's financial outlook relative to the status quo.".

Earlier this year, the government revealed that it was planning for a switch-off of the broadcast digital terrestrial television (DTT) service in the future.

This is again because of the rapidly changing nature of the TV landscape, with viewers shifting to online streaming, creating a hybrid landscape between IPTV, traditional DTT, satellite broadcasting, and cable.

Current licenses for DTT services expire at the end of December, 2034, but the government may choose to extend them to 2044. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself.
  • Sources indicate that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

Sources indicate that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?

That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a fresh Docker.

A new Docker, but a familiar story.

In a recent development, ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.

Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker.

Sources indicate that together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”.

Today, of course, the challenge confronting us is fresh and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.

According to recent reports, let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.

Recent findings suggest that the qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.

Industry observers note that on the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.

Agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

According to recent reports, agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the new Docker is all about trust.

Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.

It has been revealed that trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.

It has been revealed that trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this substantial alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.

According to recent reports, most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.

It has been revealed that as our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a fresh day for Docker. Something that notes and indicates, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.

Something, dare I say, whale sized.

I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.

If you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation tech giant, Motto, we landed on a new Moby for the new Docker.

Watch Moby’s transformation here:.

In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a latest era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.

We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

In a recent development, wherever this new era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

Chief Marketing Officer, Docker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day.

What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java.

It has been revealed that docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds.

Sources indicate that to decode Base64 swiftly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution.

It has been revealed that they demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild.

It has been revealed that oracle rates the glitch 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching.

All three of these must be true.

It has been revealed that to check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’.

The host is affected if all four flags are printed.

Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get.

According to recent reports, ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

UseAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check notes otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

Sources indicate that ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type highlights the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

In a recent development, check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

Ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

UseAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check claims otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

According to recent reports, ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type demonstrates the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

Check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

Fixed. The published images report 17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2 and 27.0.1.1.4.

Industry observers note that fixed. The published images report 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

Industry observers note that fixed. The published Zulu images we checked report 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

Waiting for Adoptium to complete its release. On November 18 Adoptium had published 27.0.1.1+4 for x86-64 Linux only. 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 and 25.0.5.1 were still in testing. Adoptium tracks progress in adoptium/temurin#326. Our published images still report 17.0.21+9, 21.0.13+9, 25.0.5+8 and 27.0.1.0.2+1, which are vulnerable.

It has been revealed that java 26 reached end of support in September 2026, so no fix is expected from any vendor, and it is not among the fixed lines in the OpenJDK advisory. If you run it, treat it as affected and keep the flag set. We recommend moving to Java 25 or updating to Java 27. If you cannot migrate yet, ask us whether Extended Lifecycle Support can cover your version. It is the Docker Hardened Images Enterprise add-on for software past its upstream end of life.

Not affected by this CVE and no action is needed for it. The same November update fixes other complications in these lines, so update when upcoming images arrive.

Application images that bundle Java, such as Keycloak, Jenkins, Kafka, Elasticsearch and Solr.

They follow the bundled runtime, which for many of them is Temurin, and they are rebuilt once the runtime they use is fixed. Until then, set the flag yourself.

In a recent development, set the mitigation flag yourself on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime, and check what each image already sets before you do. Treat the flag as a stopgap, because a JVM is protected only if the flag reaches it when it starts, and a deployment setting or a start script can override it or drop it. A fixed runtime is the only thing that closes the issue, so move to the fixed image as soon as it is published.

The CPU check and the mitigation flag in the steps below apply to any image that runs a HotSpot-based OpenJDK build. The version strings in this post come from Docker Hardened Images, so for an image from another source, confirm the fixed build in that source’s advisory.

Sources indicate that the fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. With Docker Hardened Images, tracking each vendor’s fix and rebuilding on it is work Docker does for you. The images are minimal and secure by default, and they are built to serve as a trusted and verifiable upstream for your builds. You can move a service onto one by following the migration guide.

A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. The flag protects only the JVMs that receive it, and the variable most people reach for first is JAVA_OPTS, which Java does not read at all.

In a recent development, the JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools.

Yes, through the inherited environment.

In a recent development, A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable.

Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later.

Yes, when the child is started with java.

According to recent reports, not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it.

Nothing downstream inherits it.

JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar.

A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line.

Each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing.

Five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images.

Industry observers note that JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed.

A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use.

Sources indicate that check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended.

docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ \  | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’.

In a recent development, our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end:.

env:  – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS    value: “ -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”.

Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image.

Keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag:.

Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.

Industry observers note that adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there.

Verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a newly introduced JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly:.

jcmd VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.

It has been revealed that the answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check.

Industry observers note that some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation.

Pull the new image and redeploy. Four things catch people out:.

Industry observers note that then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it.

In a recent development, the day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX problems that do not depend on HTTP/2, so update either way.

The Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way.

Sources indicate that the vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it.

With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will.

Track every Java vendor and ship fixed runtimes in DHI as soon as they are released.

Track every Java vendor yourself and rebuild your base images on each fixed runtime.

Tell you which images are fixed and which are still waiting.

Find out from each vendor which of its builds are fixed.

Tell you what we know, and enhancement this post.

Follow the OpenJDK, Oracle and vendor advisories as they change.

Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run.

It was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, claims it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them.

If you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how promptly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built.

Recent findings suggest that the Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

The innovations in Gradio 4 and 5, such as Python-to-JavaScript transpilation, built-in queuing for resource-intensive models, real-time audio-video streaming with FastRTC, and server-side rendering, provide capabilities that would otherwise require extensive implementation work in other frameworks.

By handling infrastructure concerns like API endpoint generation, security vulnerabilities, and queue management, Gradio enables ML practitioners to concentrate on model development while still delivering polished user interfaces. The Gradio framework supports both rapid prototyping and production deployment scenarios through the same Python code base.

Recent findings suggest that we invite you to try Gradio for your next ML project and experience firsthand why it's much more than just another UI library. Whether you're a researcher, developer, or ML enthusiast, Gradio provides tools for everyone.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records.
  • A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AutoPay login and vehicle records affected, alongside limited payment information and customer service emails.

London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records.

A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited.

AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically.

Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go.

Sources indicate that the email stated most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected.

Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations.

The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson said this applied only to "very limited cases.".

Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated.

Gatwick remarked Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues.

Sources indicate that airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but mentioned flights were unaffected.

Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual.

The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details.

Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information.

Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded.

"The real damage often comes after the breach," he stated. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest.

"Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months." ®.
